Hari said it led to the lower store; the officer below tried it and reported that it was locked. Mr Vale came to the landing with his keys. While he sorted through them, I remembered the storage rack. Kit had shown me a photograph of it when we were still speaking. One side leaned because a wheel had bent. She had put an arrow on the photograph and sent it to Mr Vale, with *please don’t store anything heavy here*. He’d replied that he’d look into it. I had teased her for adding the arrow. “The rack,” I said to him. “Was that moved?” “What rack?” “The metal one downstairs. Kit told you it was leaning.” Mr Vale’s hand stopped on the keys. “It was meant to be cleared.” “Was it?” “I don’t know what’s down there tonight.” “You got her message.” “Yes.” He found a key and passed it to the officer. “I said I’d deal with it.” The key turned but the lower door would not open. The officer pushed once, stopped, and asked Hari whether there was anything behind it. Hari said he didn’t know. Mr Vale went down to look. I could hear him speaking to the officer, asking for another torch. “She told you,” I said when he came back up. “Nell, I haven’t seen inside yet.” “You knew it was unsafe.” People had gathered at the end of the corridor. The girl from the costume room was there, still holding her iron by its handle, unplugged. I wanted him to stop sounding as though the important part was the wording. “You knew exactly what happened,” I said, loudly enough for the people behind me to hear, “and you carried on building the set.” Dev said my name. Mr Vale looked at me for a moment, then at the officer. “I was outside when there was a crash,” he said. “The delivery van was still here. Ask the driver. I came back in and was told somebody had dropped a panel.” One of the officers asked him for the driver’s details. He gave them straightaway. Hari came up the stairs. “We can’t get that door open. There might be something against it.” Mr Vale started to follow him down again, but the officer asked him to stay. She was arranging for help to open it safely. People in the corridor began to talk; I heard my own accusation repeated, with one word changed. Dev drew me aside. “He didn’t fix the rack,” I said. “I heard.” “And now he’s pretending—” “I don’t know what he’s doing. Tell the officer about Kit’s photograph. Her arrow had been drawn in yellow, pointing at the buckled wheel. Below it, she’d written *This was wobbling while Mo put up the flats.* I had forgotten she’d mentioned him by name. The officer thanked me when I showed her. She took the date of the message and went to speak to Hari. I stood by the wall, listening as Mr Vale gave his account again to the other officer. A few minutes later she confirmed that the driver had been with him outside when the crash was heard. He could still have known about the rack. What I’d said about him carrying on after the crash sounded less certain. Leah stood across the corridor, pressing the corner of her clipboard into her palm. She opened her mouth when the officer came past, then asked whether she should send the remaining pupils home. The officer told her to keep everyone available for now. At the foot of the stairs, Hari was explaining the layout. “There’s the lower store through this door. Then the old scenery store further back. I haven’t used that one since Christmas.” “Another way in?” the officer asked. “I think there’s access from the costume room.” He rubbed his forehead. “The inner door sticks. Kit said something about it.” I leaned closer. “She told me a door caught if you let it shut,” Hari said. “I can’t remember which side she meant.” I remembered Kit returning from the old store one Saturday, furious because a cupboard had trapped her by the hem of her coat. She had talked about the doors down there for the rest of lunch. I tried to picture where she’d been standing when she explained them. Dev saw me thinking and kept quiet. Through the closed door below, somebody called out. I couldn’t make out the word. The officer called back, and this time the answer came clearly enough for me to know the voice. “Mo?” It was Kit.

LIGHTNESS AND DARKNESS: The chapter is appropriately tense without being overwrought. FOLLOWED CHAPTER PLAN: The chapter follows the plan closely. The plan's end beat was "from the other side of its locked outer entrance, Nell hears Kit call Mo's name"—the chapter delivers this with "It was Kit," which is slightly less specific but effective. MINOR WEAKNESSES: The chapter is almost too controlled—there's little surprise in its execution. The Leah beat is somewhat muted compared to the plan's description. # Chapter 7 — Cancelled Due to Circumstances By seven in the morning, someone had printed a notice for the theatre doors. **TODAY’S PERFORMANCE IS CANCELLED DUE TO CIRCUMSTANCES.** It kept peeling away at the top. Every person who passed pressed it back down. I watched Mr Vale do it twice while speaking to a police officer, until the officer gently took his hand off the paper. Dev had driven me home for two hours of sleep. I spent most of them wondering whether Kit meant *I sent it to you because I knew you’d come* or *I sent it to you and look what you did with that*. By the time I gave up and got dressed, Mum was back from her shift. Dev had told her the short version. She asked about Kit and Mo first, then hugged me so abruptly I nearly dropped my cereal. “I’m fine,” I said into her shoulder. “You don’t have to tell me that yet.” I went back to school because Kit’s mum had said I could visit once Kit was home, and because the school had my coat. I had left it on a chair outside the costume room. On the way, Dev told me not to worry about the chemistry assessment. I hadn’t been thinking about it. Then I was. At the theatre, parents were arriving with tickets and trays of food. One woman had made eighteen iced cakes with tiny paper blood drops stuck in them. She stood in front of the cancellation notice holding the tray while a teacher tried to find her a box. The woman said the cakes could be sold at lunch. The teacher said they weren’t sure lunch was happening in the theatre. Neither wanted to mention the decoration. Mo’s sister came past with his parents. She recognised Dev from the night before and told us Mo had broken his leg. He had already asked whether missing the performance meant he could keep the service hours. His mum laughed, then covered her face. Kit had cuts on her hand and bruises from the store. She’d been checked at hospital and sent home with her mum. Mo would stay longer. Those were the facts we had; every other conversation in the theatre seemed to begin with a different version. Hari was stacking loose flats against a wall, well away from the storage stairs. He said the police had asked everyone who stayed overnight to give an account of what they saw and when. Leah had gone home with her dad. He sounded tired when he told me and didn’t ask what I thought of her. Mr Vale came in from outside and stopped by the rack of costumes. I went over because avoiding him would have required turning round in full view of three parents, and I was tired of letting other people decide where I walked. “Mo’s sister says he’s doing all right,” I said. “I heard.” Mr Vale looked at the floor between us. “Kit’s mother told me she’s home.” “The rack was meant to be cleared.” “Yes. I’ve told the police what Kit reported, and when.” He rubbed at the blue paint on his cheek; it had survived a wash. “I shouldn’t have left it.” I thought of the driver outside, the crash inside, and what I’d shouted in the corridor. “I said you knew they were down there. I was wrong.” He nodded. For once he didn’t use the silence to start talking about the show. Behind us, the cake woman finally found a box. She slid the cakes in one at a time, saving the paper drops from catching on the lid. At midday Mum drove me to Kit’s. I could have walked, but she said she needed milk and drove the long way past the shop. Kit lived over her mum’s alterations room. Through the front window I could see a wedding dress on a stand, pinned at the waist. Mrs Mercer let me in and told me Kit was on the sofa. Kit had a blanket over her legs and her hand propped on a cushion. Sophie the stuffed dog sat on the opposite chair. Kit saw me look at it. “Mum found her in a drawer,” she said. “Apparently she was worried.” I sat in the armchair without moving Sophie. Kit asked whether the show was cancelled. I told her about the notice and the cakes. She laughed at the cakes, then winced because laughing pulled at something bruised. I had thought about apologising all morning. None of the versions in my head survived having to say them aloud. “About October,” I began. “I’ve felt awful.” Kit picked at a loose thread on the blanket with her good hand. “I kept thinking I should have said something,” I went on. “Then it got too late, and you wouldn’t look at me, and I didn’t know how to—” “Nell.” I stopped. “You’re telling me how bad it was for you.” “I know.” I hadn’t known until she said it. “Sorry.” “That day, I asked if you’d seen them put the video up.” Kit kept her eyes on the thread. “You had. You were standing beside me.” I remembered the teacher asking whether anyone could say who’d started it. I remembered the backs of the pupils in front of us and how Kit had waited for me to speak. “You didn’t need to take on the whole school,” she said. “You just needed to say yes.” “I was scared they’d do it to me.” “I know.” There was nothing to argue with. Mrs Mercer came up the stairs carrying a mug of tea for Kit. I stood, though no one had asked me to leave. “Mo’s sister says he’s already asking about service hours,” I told Kit. “Of course he is.” I said I’d see her later. Kit didn’t correct me, but she didn’t promise anything either. At home, I lay on my bed fully dressed. The group chat was discussing refunds. I muted it again. That evening, my phone buzzed. *Mo says your pyjamas were the worst part of his night.*

The moment where Kit says "You're telling me how bad it was for you" and Nell admits "I hadn't known until she said it" is genuinely perceptive characterisation. Kit is appropriately direct and unforgiving without being cruel. Dev is present but peripheral, which suits his role. The cake woman is a lovely minor detail that does real tonal work. **Emotionally Engaging** The chapter earns its emotional weight. The apology scene between Nell and Kit is the centrepiece and it works because it refuses easy resolution. Kit's correction—"You're telling me how bad it was for you"—is a precise, painful observation that lands without melodrama. The ending text from Kit ("Mo says your pyjamas were the worst part of his night") is perfectly calibrated: it reopens the door without pretending the door was never closed. The hug from Mum ("You don't have to tell me that yet") is a small, effective beat. **Compelling Plot** The chapter is largely denouement, which the plan acknowledges. The plot interest here is emotional rather than narrative. The chapter handles this transition competently: the cancellation notice, Mo's family, Leah's absence, Mr Vale's accountability, and then the visit to Kit. The pacing is appropriate for a wind-down chapter that still needs to carry emotional stakes. **Coherent** The chapter is entirely coherent. The timeline (morning, midday, evening) is clear. The various threads—Mo's injury, Leah's culpability, Mr Vale's responsibility, the Nell-Kit rupture—are all addressed proportionally. **Weak Dialogue** The dialogue is one of the chapter's genuine strengths. "You're telling me how bad it was for you" is excellent. "I know" as Kit's response to Nell's fear is devastating in its brevity. The Mo's-sister exchange is natural. Mr Vale's "I shouldn't have left it" is appropriately flat. The final text message lands. There is no weak dialogue here. **Tell-Don't-Show** Mostly the chapter shows rather than tells. The apology scene is dramatised rather than summarised. However, there are a few moments of mild telling: "I had thought about apologising all morning. None of the versions in my head survived having to say them aloud" is slightly expository, though it's in Nell's voice and feels earned. The paragraph summarising Kit's injuries and Mo's situation is necessarily expository but appropriately brief. **Unsurprising or Uncreative** The chapter avoids the obvious. The apology scene doesn't resolve into reconciliation. Kit doesn't forgive Nell. The ending is a joke rather than a declaration. The cake woman with blood-drop decorations is an inspired detail. Mr Vale's scene is handled with more nuance than expected. The Sophie the stuffed dog callback (the name Kit gave a stuffed dog, used earlier as a fake name in texts) is a nice touch that rewards attentive readers. **Amateurish** There are no amateurish elements. The prose is controlled, the structure is purposeful, and the emotional beats are earned rather than announced. **Purple Prose** The prose is clean and restrained. No purple prose. **Forced Poetry or Metaphor** The chapter is largely free of metaphor, which suits the voice. The wedding dress on the stand "pinned at the waist" is a small visual detail that works without straining. Nothing feels forced. **Well-earned Lightness or Darkness** The tonal balance is excellent. The cake woman with blood-drop decorations is darkly comic without being callous. Mo's sister's laugh-then-cover-face is precisely observed. The ending joke earns its lightness because the preceding scene was genuinely difficult. The chapter doesn't let the comedy undercut the emotional seriousness. **Characters Consistent with Profile** All characters behave consistently with their profiles. Nell overcorrects in her apology and is called on it. Kit is direct and unforgiving but not cruel. Dev is present and supportive without taking over. Mr Vale is defensive but ultimately accountable. Hari is tired and doesn't editorialize about Leah. Mo is already angling for service hours, which is exactly right. **Followed Chapter Plan** The chapter follows its plan closely. The cancellation notice, the cake detail, Mo's broken leg, Hari stacking flats, Leah gone home, the apology scene with Kit, Kit's correction about the October incident, and the final text message—all present and executed. The plan's note that Nell "makes it too much about how awful she felt" and Kit stops her is dramatised precisely as described. **Faithful to Writing Prompt** The chapter is faithful to the darkly comic British YA tone established in the prompt. The voice is consistent, the comedy is present but not dominant, and the emotional stakes are maintained. **Minor criticisms:** The chapter is perhaps slightly safe in its execution—it delivers exactly what the plan promises without significant surprise or elevation beyond the plan. The prose, while clean, rarely achieves anything beyond competent clarity; there are few sentences that genuinely sing. The "I lay on my bed fully dressed" paragraph is slightly flat as a transition. # Chapter 8 — In Daylight I replied, *He was lying down when he saw them. From above, the ducks are less aggressive.* Kit’s typing dots appeared, vanished, then appeared again. *He wants to know if you’ll wear them when you visit.* *Depends. Is he charging admission?* I waited a minute before sending, *How is he?* *Bored. Hospital crisps are an insult.* Mo had eaten crisps during a rehearsal once and dropped half a packet into a painted fireplace. He still claimed somebody else had done it. I told Kit that, and she sent back a photograph of the fireplace from her camera roll. There were two yellow crumbs in one corner. We did not mention October. By the following afternoon, Mum had run out of milk. I volunteered to go to the corner shop, partly because I wanted a drink with enough sugar in it to undo the chemistry assessment I’d missed. The school had moved it to Monday. The horse would not be submitted for marking. At the shop, Mr Malik told me I looked tired, which seemed fair, and asked after Kit and Mo. He had already heard that Mo’s leg was broken. He had also heard Mr Vale had locked them underneath the stage, so I spent a minute explaining the difference between a door jamming and a person locking it. “Still a bad door,” Mr Malik said. He gave me the change, then nodded towards the window. Kit was outside reading the back of a crisp packet. She wore a coat over yesterday’s clothes, and the yellow pencil was still in her hair. She had a carrier bag looped over her uninjured wrist. I took so long putting my change away that Mr Malik asked whether I needed the receipt. Outside, Kit held up the packet. “He requested these. They’ve changed the recipe.” “Can he tell?” “He’ll tell everyone.” She was going to see Mo. I said I’d heard he was getting out tomorrow, and she said his sister had promised to bring him home in a wheelchair even if the hospital didn’t give him one. We stood beside the shop window while two younger pupils walked between us and stared openly. Kit stared back until they hurried on. “I was getting milk,” I said. Kit looked at the bottle in my hand. “Good result.” The bus stop for the hospital was down the road. She started walking, slowly enough that I could come too if I wanted. I did. At the crossing, she said, “Mum thinks I should stay home.” “She’s probably right.” “Mo made me promise the crisps.” “You could have given them to his mum.” “I’m not trusting his family with them. His sister already ate the ones I left at the hospital.” A car let us cross. Kit thanked the driver with a lift of her good hand and winced afterwards. I wanted to tell her to stop using it, but she knew it hurt. We passed the charity shop where we used to look for costumes. Its window held a mannequin in a graduation gown with a plastic tiara balanced on the cap. Kit slowed to examine it, then kept going. I had seen her stop at that window dozens of times. Usually I stopped too. “I meant what I said yesterday,” I told her. “About being scared.” “I know you were.” “I saw who posted the video. And when the teacher asked, I said I didn’t know.” I watched the pavement ahead. “You asked me before we went in. I told you I’d back you up.” Kit’s carrier bag rustled against her coat. “Yes.” I had an explanation for every part of it. The boys who made the video had been awful to me in Year Nine; the teacher looked tired and ready to call it settled; Kit could speak in front of people without her throat closing. None of that changed my answer. “I’m sorry I lied,” I said. We reached a bus stop with no shelter, only a timetable under cloudy plastic. Kit set her bag down on the bench. She looked at me properly. “The girl in the video still goes bright red when anyone mentions the trip,” she said. “I saw her last week.” “I know.” “You didn’t, actually.” She was right. I hadn’t asked. The girl had left our form group the term after it happened, and I had allowed myself to lose track of her. Kit sat down and pulled the crisp bag clear of the puddle on the bench. I stayed standing. “I don’t know what you want me to say,” I told her. “Neither do I.” A bus went past on the other side of the road. It wasn’t ours. Kit watched it until it turned the corner. “I sent the code because it was yours,” she said. “I knew you’d remember it.” “I was angry when I got it.” “I thought you might be.” “I came, though.” “I know.” She shifted along the bench to make room, then looked annoyed at herself for doing it. I sat down anyway. Her sleeve brushed my arm. There was a dark red mark near the cuff. I caught her wrist before I thought better of it, then let go at once. “Sorry. Is that blood?” Kit looked down. “Paint. From the flats.” “Are you sure?” She rubbed the mark with her thumb. Nothing came off. “It’s been there since Wednesday. Leah couldn’t find the tin of red, so I carried it down from art. I got paint all over myself before we’d even opened it.” “How?” “The lid was loose. I put it under my arm.” She held out the sleeve for me to inspect. “I’d already told Mr Vale not to keep tins on that rack. I was on my way to tell him again when Mo shouted.” I remembered the streak in the group photograph and how long I’d stared at it in Dev’s car. “You could have told me it was paint,” I said. “You hadn’t asked.” The bus appeared at the end of the road. Kit picked up the crisps, and I stood with the milk. Neither of us had asked the other to come along to the hospital. When the doors opened, Kit got on ahead of me and moved her bag off the seat beside her.

[Analysis] Chapter 8 is the closing chapter of a darkly comic British YA story, and it functions as a quiet, earned denouement rather than a dramatic resolution. The writing plan called for Nell and Kit to meet outside a corner shop, walk together, have a frank but incomplete conversation about the October incident, and end with Kit moving her bag on the bus—an open but not closed ending. The chapter delivers all of this with considerable skill. The opening text exchange is well-handled. The duck pyjama joke lands naturally, and the rhythm of the exchange—dots appearing and vanishing, the photograph of the fireplace with two yellow crumbs—establishes the tentative re-establishment of contact without sentimentalizing it. The detail of Mo's crumbs in the fireplace is a small, specific, funny thing that feels genuinely observed rather than manufactured for effect. The line "We did not mention October" is clean and does real work: it tells us what the texts were and weren't, without belaboring it. The corner shop scene with Mr Malik is economical and good. His correction of the rumor (Vale locked them in vs. the door jamming) is both funny and thematically resonant—the story has been about how narratives distort under pressure. "Still a bad door" is a perfect line. The detail of Nell taking so long with her change that Mr Malik asks about the receipt is a lovely piece of showing-not-telling about her anxiety. The walk to the bus stop is where the chapter does its most important work. The conversation about October is handled with real restraint and intelligence. Nell's apology is not clean or complete; Kit does not accept it warmly or reject it coldly. The exchange "I don't know what you want me to say" / "Neither do I" is exactly right—it refuses the false resolution of a YA lesson-speech while still moving the relationship forward. The detail that the girl from the video "still goes bright red" and that Nell "had allowed myself to lose track of her" is quietly devastating and morally precise. Kit's "You didn't, actually" is a perfect, small knife. The ending with the paint on the sleeve is beautifully constructed. Nell grabs Kit's wrist instinctively, fears blood, is told it's paint—and then Kit explains how she got it, which loops back to the night's events and to Kit's earlier safety warnings about the rack. The final image of Kit moving her bag on the bus is exactly the right note: not reconciliation, not rejection, but an opening. The plan called for this precisely, and the execution matches the intention. The dialogue throughout is strong. It sounds like real teenagers—clipped, indirect, occasionally funny, occasionally cruel in the way that honesty is cruel. "I'm not trusting his family with them. His sister already ate the ones I left at the hospital" is a perfect character beat for Kit. The voice is consistent with Nell's profile: sharp, self-aware about her own failings, not quite able to stop calculating even when she's trying to be honest. There are minor quibbles. The charity shop mannequin in the graduation gown is a slightly over-deliberate symbol of something (transition? performance? the gap between ceremony and reality?), and Kit slowing to look at it and then moving on feels like it's reaching for significance without quite earning it. It's not a serious flaw, but it's the one moment where the writing nudges toward the literary rather than trusting the scene. The line "The horse would not be submitted for marking" is a callback to the chemistry assessment horse from earlier chapters (presumably), and while it's funny, a reader encountering only this chapter might find it slightly opaque—though in context it presumably works. The chapter follows its plan faithfully and precisely. Characters are consistent with their profiles. The lightness (Mo's crisps, the duck pyjamas, Mr Malik's rumor correction) is genuinely earned against the darkness of the October incident and the night's events. There is no purple prose, no forced metaphor, no amateurish reaching. The writing is controlled, specific, and emotionally intelligent throughout. The author demonstrates consistent command of voice, character, and tone across eight chapters, maintaining a first-person narrator (Nell) whose dry, observational wit never tips into parody or self-congratulation. The relationship between Nell and Kit is the emotional core, and it's handled with appropriate ambiguity: no neat reconciliation, just a bus seat moved over. The mystery structure works well. The three blood emojis, Leah's deception, the knocking under the stage — these are parcelled out with good pacing. The paint-versus-blood ambiguity is used effectively multiple times without becoming tiresome. Dev is a minor character done right: present, useful, not over-explained. His line "Six-year-olds sometimes do" is perfectly calibrated. The darkly comic register is maintained throughout. The girl in the bloodstained dress eating a banana is a perfect image. The cancelled performance notice peeling off the door, Mr Vale pressing it back while talking to police, is quietly excellent. WEAKNESSES: The pacing in the middle chapters (3-5) occasionally slows as the search logistics accumulate. The procedural detail of who checked which room is necessary but sometimes reads as inventory rather than drama. The tension is maintained, but some passages feel like they're marking time. The metaphors are almost uniformly good, but a few reach slightly: "the sort of thing I would have seized on if I wanted to convince myself she was fine" is slightly over-explained. The piece occasionally tells us what Nell is feeling when the showing has already done the work. The resolution of the Leah subplot is somewhat underdeveloped. Her motivations (fear, not malice) are established, but she disappears from the final chapters without the story fully reckoning with what she did.
