Behind them, Rusk’s cutter kept enough distance to stay out of the ship’s wash. He had not entered the Shatter yet. Iri stood with their hand against the cockpit doorframe. “Reduce thrust. A little.” Mara did. The blue point returned. Sol started the survey recording. The Shatter looked almost empty from the forward screen. A few stars wavered, no more dramatic than heat above a road. Mara knew what an unmarked crossing could do to a ship. Eight years earlier, the two crews Adela had mentioned had gone in within an hour of each other. Neither distress beacon had lasted long enough for a position fix. “Marker confirmed,” Sol said. “Transmitting the read to Bellwether.” Rusk hailed them. Mara left it unanswered until the first data packet cleared the array. “Captain,” he said, “you have one verified marker. It won’t bring you through. Turn out now, and I can still keep your ship off the impound list.” “You’re inside the crossing?” Mara asked. “Not far enough to require your navigator.” Iri looked toward the speaker. “The bearing won’t survive a chase,” Rusk said. “You know that.” Mara ended the call. Sol did not look up from their screen. “He’s right about the chase,” they said. “He can wait at the entrance.” “Then we go farther.” Mara glanced back at Iri. “That was the first marker.” “I see it.” “We can turn out along the course we came.” Iri watched the pale light fade behind them. They had set their own terms; Mara kept her hands on the controls and waited. “There’s another ahead,” Iri said at last. “Left of the line on your map.” “Do you want to guide us there?” “I do.” Iri came forward, close enough to read the helm. “But I will not spend the rest of this crossing earning the one you already gave me.” “You aren’t.” “Then give me the course controls.” Mara checked the pilot-assist screen. From the spare console, Iri could enter headings and thrust changes directly. She released the lock, leaving herself a physical cutoff at the helm, and moved Kit out of the seat beside Sol. Iri sat. They entered a shallow turn and waited while Mara flew it. The second marker came into view against a dark band that hid the stars beyond it. The range finder gave three distances in quick succession, none of them close. Sol adjusted the array. At the door, Kit gripped the back of the now-empty chair. “Which reading?” Mara asked. “Don’t use them yet,” Iri said. They touched their fingers to the console edge. Their breathing had changed, becoming slow and deliberate. They entered a new heading: straight toward the dark band. “Sol?” Mara asked. “The marker’s in there. I can’t fix its position unless we stay on course.” The bearing temperature reached the limit. Sol opened an engine schematic on their screen and routed coolant from the reserve loop. Mara held the heading. As the band filled the screen, the ship’s aft sensor showed Rusk’s cutter crossing the threshold behind them. “He’s following our reads,” Kit said. “He has the first one,” Sol replied. “Not this.” Rusk hailed again. Mara let the call through. “The band shifts,” he said. “You won’t be able to record while evading me.” “Then don’t make me.” “I’m giving you a way out.” Mara watched his cutter edge closer on the aft display. He had been careful all the way from Bellwether, using the port’s rules and her fuel gauge. Here, he had only the distance between their ships and whatever his instruments could find. Iri entered a correction. Mara flew it. Rusk’s cutter matched the turn late, then dropped back. A metallic bang ran beneath the cockpit floor. Sol swore and unstrapped. “Bearing?” “Array coupling. Keep her steady.” Sol disappeared down the ladder. On the schematic, the survey signal flickered. Mara heard a locker slam open below, then the hammer of a tool against a fitting. “What are you taking?” she called. “The kit for the bearing.” “Sol—” “I’ve got three minutes before the coupling melts. Fly.” Iri’s hand hovered over the course controls. “There is space to our right,” they said. “If we leave now.” Mara looked at the array signal. It steadied briefly under Sol’s work, then dropped again. She kept the heading Iri had given her. The dark band opened around them. For an instant, Mara could see two versions of Rusk’s cutter on the aft screen, one above the other. The lower image disappeared. Rusk pulled away from the crossing and turned back toward Bellwether. The second marker burned blue ahead. “Got it,” Sol said. “Don’t change thrust.” Mara flew steadily until the array completed its read. Sol sent the coordinates, then a third, shorter packet mapping the safe approach between the markers. The signal left the ship before the coupling failed. Iri entered one final turn. We need the approach clear before the next tanker comes in.” “Adela—” “The transfer arm is beyond repair. I’ll send you the figures when we’ve counted the hose as well.” The channel closed. Kit unstrapped and went to bring water from the galley. They handed a cup to Iri first, then to Sol. When they reached Mara, they held on to the cup for a moment. “The worker I talked to,” Kit said. “Did anyone get hurt?” “Adela said no one was under the arm.” “That wasn’t what I meant.” “I don’t know.” Mara took the cup. “Ask when we dock.” Kit nodded and returned to the galley. Mara had wanted to tell them Bellwether would be fine. She could still see the white plume from the torn hose crossing the field. A Meridian cutter emerged from the Shatter two hours later. Rusk kept well outside the *Wayward*’s position and did not hail. He turned toward another beacon and disappeared from the scope. Mara marked his course in the log; she did not try to guess where he was going. Bellwether’s tug reached them before the bearing cooled. It caught the *Wayward* gently enough that Sol went down to check the tow fitting twice, suspicious of any noise they had not made themselves. The tug pilot asked Mara to leave the engines cold. “No argument,” Mara said. “That’s a first for this berth,” the pilot replied. At the port, the damaged loading rack lay fenced off. Workers had rigged a temporary hose across the next pad, forcing a tanker to wait while they cleared a passage for the *Wayward*. Kit watched through the cockpit window until Mara sent them to help with the tow lines. Adela met Mara at the hatch carrying a repair estimate. She had written corrections in the margin and crossed out one charge. “The swivel was due for replacement,” she said. “You owe us for the arm and the hose. Not the swivel.” Mara looked at the total. She could not pay it. “My next freight payment,” she said. “I’ll sign it over.” “You’ll need a next job.” “I know.” Adela produced a form. She had left the payment date blank. Mara signed, and Adela gave her a copy. “The port record’s filed,” Adela said. “So is Rusk’s report. He calls your survey data incomplete.” “It is.” “He’s advising ships not to use it.” Adela folded the form into her case. “They ought to listen to the warning and read the data. One of my pilots is already asking what equipment she’d need to check the next marker.” Mara glanced toward the fenced-off rack. “Can you afford to send her?” “Not today.” Adela went to speak with the tug crew. She did not thank Mara, and Mara was relieved not to have to answer. Sol spent the afternoon drawing up a list of parts. The bearing sat at the top, followed by the array coupling and two items Mara had thought were sound. She took the list without disputing it. Kit found the port worker by the temporary hose. He had passed word of their departure to Rusk, believing the recovery order would keep the tanker schedule intact. Kit came back angry, though not with anything useful to do with the anger. Sol gave them the job of clearing the hold. Mara found Iri there after dusk. Kit had unbolted the last of the restraint frame and stacked its pieces beside the crate. Iri stood in the open space, looking at the empty case. “There’s a freighter leaving tomorrow,” Mara said. “Its captain says it can take a passenger beyond Meridian territory. I haven’t told her about you.” Iri ran a thumb over a scrape in the crate’s rim. “Will she take me without papers?” “She said she’d talk to you.” “And your ship?” “Stays here until Sol gets the bearing replaced. After that, I don’t know.” Iri looked around the hold. “I would like passage when it leaves.” “On the *Wayward*?” “Yes. Farther out.” Mara considered what the repair debt would leave them. “I can tell you the fare once we have a destination.” “I guided your ship across the Shatter.” Mara took her pocket notebook out, though she had not written down a fare. “You did.” Iri watched while she put it away again. “You can come,” Mara said. “When we know where.” They moved past her toward the hatch. She thought I&#x27;d been sleeping. -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt. The scope will be a short story, written over {n_chapters} chapters. Each chapter will be approximately 1000 words so plan accordingly for this scope. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. # Brainstorming **The central question:** “I caught her staring at me again. She thought I’d been sleeping.” The stare could be predatory, frightened, protective, or an attempt to determine whether the narrator is still themselves. Its meaning could change as the story unfolds. **Possible characters and relationships** - A husband wakes to find his wife watching him after she returns from caring for her dying mother. He suspects something came home with her. - A daughter catches her mother staring at her bedside, repeating a childhood habit that stopped years ago. The daughter may be the one possessed. - Two sisters share an apartment after one survives a near-fatal accident. Each believes the other brought something back. - A hospice nurse stays with a former patient’s family and begins watching them sleep, as if waiting for someone to wake. - A partner sits awake beside the narrator because sleep is the only time the narrator speaks in a voice that isn’t their own. **Possible forms of possession** - A spirit takes control in brief intervals, leaving the host aware but unable to move. - It transfers through eye contact, making the staring both threatening and necessary. - It inhabits memories before it can inhabit a body; loved ones notice that familiar stories have changed. - It enters during sleep, so staying awake offers safety at a mounting physical and psychological cost. - It cannot imitate an ordinary human action—blinking, dreaming, recognizing a loved one—and uses the host’s knowledge to hide the lapse. **Story beats to explore** - Open in the middle of a nightly ritual: the narrator pretends to sleep and catches her staring again. - Establish a plausible explanation for her behavior before revealing a small, undeniable impossibility. - Let each character investigate the other, turning domestic intimacy into mutual surveillance. - Reveal that the watcher has been keeping records of what happens during the narrator’s sleep. - Set a deadline: an approaching funeral, a medical procedure, the last night of a vigil, or the point at which neither can safely stay awake. - End with a choice that could save one person only by trusting someone who may no longer be themselves. **Tone and pacing** - Keep the horror close to the body and home: a mattress shifting, a held breath, a familiar hand stopping just short of a face. - Give the relationship enough warmth that the possible loss of either person matters. - Use the eight-chapter structure to move from suspicion to evidence, then to conflicting explanations and a costly decision. Around 1,000 words per chapter allows each chapter one substantial development rather than several reversals. - Consider either a tragic ending, where the narrator understands the truth too late, or an uneasy survival that reinterprets the opening stare. # Reflection The strongest version seems to make the stare mean two things at different points in the story. Initially, a narrator who sees their partner watching them sleep has good reason to fear the partner. If the partner is actually checking for signs of possession *in the narrator*, the opening line gains a satisfying second meaning without relying on a twist alone. A story in which nobody can sleep has immediate tension, but eight chapters of escalating exhaustion could become repetitive. Sleep would work better as a recurring danger than as the only plot mechanism. Likewise, a fixed possession rule could generate suspense, but explaining every detail would make the haunting feel procedural. A few observable limits, with room for uncertainty, would better suit intimate horror. The marriage or long-term partnership offers the most emotional leverage for a roughly 8,000-word story. The narrator can recognize tiny deviations in a loved one’s behavior—and can also be forced to confront evidence of their own deviations. A recent death could give both characters a credible reason to be exhausted, secretive, and reluctant to call for help. The danger is that grief and possession might compete for attention; it would help if the supernatural threat exploited what each person already fears about losing the other. The ending should probably require an action, not just a revelation. Learning who is possessed would be unsettling, but choosing whether to let that person sleep, restrain them, or trust their account would turn the mystery into a climax. An ambiguous final image could work if the immediate choice has a clear consequence. Ideally, the last stare would echo the first while leaving the reader newly uncertain about who is watching over whom.
Great now let's continue with planning the short story. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention The story will be an intimate possession horror told in **first person, past tense** by Mara, who has returned home with her wife, Elise, after the funeral of Mara’s mother. It will open with the prompt’s line: “I caught her staring at me again. She thought I’d been sleeping.” Mara initially believes grief—or something brought back from her mother’s house—has changed Elise. Gradually, Elise’s watchfulness will prove less like a threat than a vigil: Mara has been doing things in her sleep that she cannot remember. The possession will have a small set of observable rules rather than a fully explained mythology. The presence can take control only while Mara sleeps; it learns from her memories and grows more capable each night. Elise’s records provide evidence, but because Mara narrates, the reader experiences that evidence through someone with a reason to doubt it. The entity’s origin will remain uncertain. Its immediate aim will not: it wants Mara to invite it to remain when she is awake. The emotional core is the marriage. Elise must risk frightening and restraining the person she loves; Mara must decide whether to trust Elise’s account over her own memory. The prose should be restrained and sensory, with dread arising from altered domestic routines rather than frequent shocks. Across eight chapters of roughly 1,000 words each, the story will move from suspicion, to evidence, to an attempted escape, to a deliberate confrontation. The ending will resolve the immediate danger at a cost, then echo the opening stare without treating ambiguity as a substitute for a climax. # Chapter Planning ## Chapter 1 — The Watcher Mara wakes—or pretends to wake—and catches Elise staring at her from a chair beside the bed. Elise gives an inadequate explanation: Mara had been talking in her sleep. Their strained conversation establishes the recent funeral, several sleepless nights, and Mara’s fear that Elise has not been herself since they returned. After Elise leaves, Mara finds dirt beneath her own fingernails and a strip of black thread caught between her teeth. The chapter closes with Mara deciding to stay awake and watch Elise instead. ## Chapter 2 — Ordinary Explanations Mara searches for explanations: grief, sleepwalking, medication, the disruption of travel. She notices precautions Elise has quietly installed—a bell on the bedroom door, a covered mirror, a chair placed where its movement would make noise. A brief, affectionate memory shows what their bedtime routine used to be, making the new arrangement feel like a loss. That night Mara catches Elise recording something on her phone. Elise refuses to play it, saying Mara asked her not to. ## Chapter 3 — The Recording Mara obtains the recording. Her sleeping voice speaks calmly with Elise, asking intimate questions it should already know the answers to. It nearly persuades Elise to remove the bell before saying something in Mara’s mother’s voice. Elise admits there have been several such nights; she concealed them because Mara becomes terrified when told, then forgets the conversation after sleeping. Mara demands that they leave the house. Elise agrees, though the recording suggests the house may not be the problem. ## Chapter 4 — Away From Home They spend the night in a roadside motel, hoping distance will help. Exhaustion briefly softens their hostility, and Mara begins to believe Elise. Then Mara wakes in the bathroom with no memory of getting there. The mirror is uncovered, and someone has written **LET ME STAY** in the condensation. Security footage shows Mara entering the bathroom alone. Elise points out that Mara was awake and speaking when she returned to bed—a troubling change from the earlier episodes. ## Chapter 5 — What It Knows Back home, they compare Elise’s notes with Mara’s gaps in memory. The presence has been practicing: first simple movements, then conversation, then waking without immediately surrendering control. Its attempts to imitate Mara are imperfect, especially when asked about feelings rather than facts. Mara recalls a moment at her mother’s bedside when, desperate for one more lucid conversation, she said aloud that she would let anything speak through her. She cannot know whether that invitation caused the possession, but the entity has begun repeating her words back to her. ## Chapter 6 — The Bargain Mara tries to stay awake while Elise searches for help, but exhaustion makes Mara’s perceptions unreliable. The presence begins speaking to her in brief lapses: it claims it can preserve her mother’s voice and memories if Mara consciously asks it to remain. It also suggests Elise has already decided to hurt her. Mara discovers Elise has prepared restraints for the next time she sleeps. Hurt and afraid, Mara confronts her. Elise admits she may have to hold Mara down, but insists she will not make the choice without telling her. ## Chapter 7 — The Vigil Mara and Elise choose a controlled confrontation. They set a camera running, leave the lights on, and agree on a phrase Elise can use to test whether Mara has returned. Mara allows herself to sleep while Elise watches. The presence wakes in Mara’s body and uses everything it has learned about their marriage to persuade Elise to release it. When persuasion fails, it imitates Mara’s genuine terror convincingly enough that Elise hesitates. Mara surfaces briefly, realizes the presence needs her willing invitation to remain awake permanently, and refuses it aloud. ## Chapter 8 — The Last Night Mara’s refusal breaks the presence’s hold long enough for Elise to keep her awake until morning. The ordeal leaves Mara with missing hours and memories she cannot cleanly separate from the entity’s; she also learns Elise was injured while stopping her. Weeks later, they are still together but no longer pretend that trust can return untouched. Mara wakes to find Elise watching her again. This time she understands why—and tells Elise she is awake. Elise asks their agreed question. Mara answers correctly, but the final beat leaves open whether the answer is proof of safety or merely something the presence has learned.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a Human Might Approach This Piece A human writer might begin with the discomfort of the prompt rather than with the mechanics of possession. Someone is awake in bed, pretending otherwise. Someone who knows them well is watching. Why does the watcher believe she must not be caught? That situation contains more than fear. There might be resentment at being observed, embarrassment at pretending to sleep, an impulse to reach for one’s partner, or the knowledge that a perfectly ordinary explanation would sound like a lie. A writer could spend time with those reactions before deciding what the supernatural threat does. They might also bring an inconvenient specificity to the story: the chair Elise chooses because the other one squeaks; the familiar way Mara knows Elise is tired; the argument they have already been having about whether to turn the hallway light off. These details need not announce themselves as clues. They make the marriage exist before the horror starts dismantling it. A human approach would likely include some resistance to the neatest version of the premise. If the apparent watcher is protecting the narrator, that reversal is satisfying—but perhaps too readily available. The writer might ask what Mara has done to deserve Elise’s mistrust, what Elise gets wrong, and what neither of them will admit even when the supernatural evidence is clear. The possession can expose an existing fault line rather than create every conflict on its own. Finally, a human writer might protect what they *don’t* know. The entity’s origin need not be explained, but its uncertainty should feel like the characters’ uncertainty, not the author withholding a prepared answer. Conversely, ambiguity about who is in control should not make the characters’ emotional choices meaningless. # Telltale LLM Approaches That Might Not Serve This Story These are tendencies, not rules. Several can be useful in moderation; they become problems when they substitute for observation or dramatic choice. ### A very orderly escalation An LLM-friendly outline can make each chapter deliver a conspicuous new clue: dirt under the nails, then a recording, then footage, then writing on a mirror, then a confrontation. That creates momentum, but it can also make a haunting feel like a sequence of scheduled reveals. Real dread often develops unevenly. A character may spend pages dealing with one piece of evidence, or discover something alarming and then have to buy groceries. ### Familiar horror shorthand Covered mirrors, bathroom condensation, inherited voices, bedsides, restraints, and ominous recordings all belong comfortably to the genre. Together, they risk producing an atmosphere assembled from recognizable parts rather than one particular marriage in one particular home. The issue is not that these devices are forbidden; it is whether each has a reason to belong *here*. “LET ME STAY” on a fogged mirror, for instance, communicates the entity’s goal efficiently. It also risks being the most expected way a supernatural presence could communicate it. Something less theatrical—and more plausibly mistaken for Mara’s own act—might be more disturbing. ### Clues that exist only for the reader A strip of black thread between Mara’s teeth is striking, but unless it connects to a meaningful object or action, it can read as a promise of significance the story hasn’t earned. The same applies to the bell, covered mirror, and security footage. Each detail asks the reader to track it. Too many such details can turn the story into a puzzle box when its strongest material is relational. ### Characters behaving to preserve the twist Elise conceals recordings because Mara “asked her not to,” and Mara forgets being told after sleeping. That gives Elise a reason for secrecy, but it needs pressure-testing. What exactly has Elise tried? Why hasn’t she involved a doctor, a friend, emergency services, or someone who can help her stay awake? Why does Mara accept the motel as the next step? If their choices seem optimized to delay the reveal, readers will feel the author’s hand. ### A love story that stays too agreeable The plan says Elise and Mara love each other and eventually choose to work together. That is a sound emotional foundation, but “trust your partner” could become an easy thematic answer. Love might coexist with annoyance, old injuries, selfishness, disbelief, or the desire to be proved right. Elise might have good reason to watch Mara and still behave badly. Mara might be possessed and still be correct about something Elise has done. ### The explained-monster problem The planned rules are clear: control during sleep, learning through memories, growing more capable, needing a willing invitation to remain awake. This gives the climax a solvable shape. But it may make the entity feel like a system to be mastered. The invitation rule, especially, risks appearing just in time to provide the solution unless earlier chapters dramatize why Mara and Elise suspect it matters. There is also a possible contradiction worth examining: if the entity can act briefly while Mara is awake in Chapter 6, what precisely distinguishes that from the permanent waking control it wants? The story need not provide a technical answer, but the characters’ understanding should be coherent enough that Mara’s refusal feels consequential. ### An ending engineered for elegant ambiguity The final agreed question has a tidy symmetry with the opening stare. It also resembles a familiar horror ending: the character passes a test, but perhaps the monster learned the answer. If the story ends solely on that note, it may undo the significance of Mara’s refusal and Elise’s effort. Ambiguity lands hardest when it grows from a specific remaining uncertainty, rather than a general suggestion that evil might still be present. ### “Beautiful” prose crowding out fear This premise invites polished sentences about grief, identity, and love. Too much of that could make Mara sound like she is composing a retrospective essay while frightened and sleep-deprived. Readability would probably benefit from a voice that can be petty, practical, funny at the wrong time, or imprecise about her feelings. Not every observation needs to carry a metaphor. # Deep Dive on the Current Intention and Plan ## The opening line and point of view First-person narration is a strong choice because Mara can report what she experiences without being able to verify what she does while asleep. Past tense, however, raises an interesting question: from what point is she telling this? If she narrates after the ending, her controlled account might imply survival and some recovered certainty. If that implication is unwanted, the prose may need to feel immediate despite the tense, or the framing may need consideration. The opening also deserves room to breathe. The plan moves quickly from Elise’s stare to grief, precautions, and disturbing physical evidence. A chapter of about 1,000 words can hold those beats, but opening with the strip of thread and dirt beneath Mara’s nails may steer readers toward “Mara is possessed” very early. That is not necessarily bad—the story need not depend on concealing the reversal—but it changes the source of suspense. If readers know before Mara does, the more interesting question becomes why Elise is unable to tell her. Mara should also have a particular reason to pretend to sleep. Is she afraid Elise will deny watching? Does she want to see what Elise does next? Has their marriage made direct questions difficult even before this? The answer could reveal character without requiring exposition. ## Mara’s mother and the funeral The funeral supplies emotional weight and a possible origin for the possession, but at present Mara’s mother is mostly a source of eerie material: her voice, a bedside invitation, and memories the entity can offer to preserve. This risks turning a dead character into an atmospheric device. What was Mara’s relationship with her mother? Did Mara desperately want another conversation, or did she dread one? Was Elise present at the bedside? Did Elise witness the “invitation” and interpret it differently? A more particular, perhaps less sentimental grief could sharpen the story. For example, Mara may not miss her mother’s voice uniformly; there may be things she is relieved never to hear again. An entity promising to preserve that voice would then be both tempting and repellent. The invitation “I would let anything speak through me” is dramatically useful but conspicuously suited to the haunting. People do say desperate things at deathbeds, though they rarely phrase them as occult bargains. If the line remains, it might gain force from being something Mara regrets for reasons other than the supernatural. ## Elise’s vigil Elise has a compelling position: she must watch someone she loves and decide what to do when that person wakes wrong. But she risks becoming a functional character—keeper of notes, operator of recording devices, preparer of restraints, deliverer of rules. Her fatigue and mistakes could make her more vivid. Why does she choose a chair by the bed rather than another room? What does she fear Mara will do if left alone? Has she slept at all? Does she secretly doubt her own evidence? The plan gives her an injury in Chapter 8, but an earlier mistake might matter more: perhaps she once responded tenderly to the presence before she knew it wasn’t Mara, or once treated the real Mara as if she were the intruder. Either could haunt their interactions without making Elise villainous. The restraints require particular care. They can make Elise’s predicament viscerally frightening, but they introduce the threat of coercion inside a marriage. The story should not treat that as automatically justified because Elise is correct about the possession. Mara’s fear of Elise can remain valid even when Elise’s fear of Mara is valid. ## The evidence trail Recordings and security footage are efficient ways to establish that something happens during Mara’s lost hours. Used together, they could become too decisive. Once Mara hears the recording and sees the footage, uncertainty may shift almost entirely from *whether* she is possessed to *how* they will stop it. That is a workable structure, but Chapters 4–6 then need more than additional proof. The footage, in particular, prompts practical questions. Who has access to it? Why does the motel have a camera showing the relevant movement? What does it prove that the recording did not? If it merely confirms Mara entered the bathroom alone, the scene might be stronger if Elise’s account and Mara’s own physical evidence are in conflict, rather than if external technology settles the matter. The plan’s details could also be sorted by function: - **Dirt and thread** are bodily evidence. - **Bell and chair** are Elise’s precautions. - **Recording and footage** are documentary evidence. - **Mirror writing** is direct communication. That is a broad range for a short story. Choosing fewer forms of evidence, then using them in surprising ways, might give the haunting a more distinct texture. ## The entity The best feature of the planned entity is that it learns from Mara’s memories and can imitate knowledge more readily than feeling. That distinction offers dramatic possibilities beyond a test question. It might remember what Mara said during a fight but not what she intended by it; or it might express a buried feeling with embarrassing accuracy while misunderstanding its consequences. The entity’s motive—“let me stay”—is clear enough to drive a climax, but fairly abstract. Stay where? In Mara, in the marriage, among the living? Does it fear returning to wherever it came from? It need not explain itself truthfully. Its desire might be more unsettling if Mara can sometimes recognize it as a desire she shares: to postpone loss, to avoid waking into grief, to be loved without having to account for what happened during the night. A danger here is giving the entity a persuasive monologue in Chapter 7. Horror antagonists often become less frightening when they finally state their case fluently. It may be stronger when its argument is inseparable from ordinary conversation—something Elise could almost have heard Mara say. ## The climax A controlled vigil with a camera, lights, and a test phrase provides a clear stage. Its weakness is that it sounds like a rational plan assembled by characters who understand the rules fairly well. The scene will need an unpredictable human failure: exhaustion, miscommunication, a private memory that becomes an accusation, or disagreement over what counts as consent. Mara’s refusal is a promising climax because it demands agency from someone whose agency has been compromised throughout the story. For it to satisfy, she should have had genuine reasons to consider agreeing—not merely because the entity offers her mother’s voice, but because agreeing solves some immediate, concrete pain or danger. Her refusal could also cost her something tangible. Otherwise the climactic choice risks becoming a straightforward rejection of the monster. ## The final chapter The aftermath has room to be one of the story’s most distinctive chapters. A couple cannot simply return to ordinary trust after one has watched, recorded, and possibly restrained the other. Nor can Mara be wholly reassured by knowing Elise was right. Practical details—how they sleep, whether Elise deletes the recordings, whether Mara wants to hear them again—could convey the lasting damage more effectively than a summary of their changed relationship. The proposed final question may be less interesting than Elise’s decision to ask it, or Mara’s decision to answer. Does the ritual comfort them? Humiliate them? Has Mara begun watching Elise, too? Ending on the marriage’s altered habits might preserve dread without implying that the preceding climax was futile. # Brainstorming Ways to Make the Story Feel More Human These are possibilities to test, **not revisions to the plan yet**. - **Give Mara an unflattering but understandable response.** She might be angry that Elise recorded her before she is frightened by what the recording contains. That ordering would feel emotionally plausible. - **Let Elise be wrong about something important.** She could misread an ordinary act as evidence, omit part of a recording, or mistake Mara’s genuine waking distress for the presence. Her vigil would remain necessary without making her an infallible guide. - **Make one precaution mundane and improvised.** A chair wedged under a handle or a mug placed where it will fall may feel more personal than a collection of classic horror measures. - **Let the first recording be boring for too long.** Breathing, a mattress creak, Elise asking tired questions. The delay could make the eventual wrongness more credible than an immediate uncanny voice. - **Use memories that do not flatter anyone.** If the entity knows Mara deeply, it knows small cruelties, unfinished arguments, and the ways Mara sometimes misrepresents herself. That knowledge could be more frightening than a perfect imitation of her mother. - **Allow humor without puncturing the horror.** Sleep-deprived partners might make one bad joke because silence has become unbearable. It could reveal their history together. - **Give the funeral aftermath a life beyond the haunting.** Unreturned calls, borrowed containers, a suitcase that still smells like Mara’s mother’s house: things that demand attention whether or not the entity exists. - **Make Mara and Elise want different kinds of proof.** Elise may trust what she saw; Mara may trust what she remembers; neither standard is adequate. Their disagreement can remain active after they accept the supernatural premise. - **Consider a less declarative form of communication.** Rather than writing its intention on a mirror, the presence might repeatedly perform an action whose meaning Mara only later understands—or alter something Mara herself meant to do. - **Keep at least one clue emotionally meaningful even if it is not supernatural.** Elise watching Mara may echo an earlier night of illness or grief. Its meaning need not be exhausted by the possession plot. - **Let time behave messily.** Not every chapter has to cover a night, and not every night needs a new incident. A skipped day or an exhausting afternoon of normal errands could deepen the effect of the next vigil. - **Give the entity an imperfect strategy.** It is learning, but it need not always escalate optimally. A mistake may be frightening precisely because it reveals a want or fear beneath its mimicry. - **Question the test phrase.** If it remains, its value could lie less in whether the entity can learn the answer and more in how Mara feels when Elise asks a question that should be ordinary between them. - **Resist a final explanatory sentence.** The last image or exchange should carry the altered relationship; the narration need not tell the reader what the stare means now. The most useful guiding question may be: **what would these two particular people do that no generic couple in a possession story would do?** Answering that in their speech, mistakes, household habits, and history would make the supernatural events feel as though they happened to people rather than to roles in a plot.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention The story will open with the prompt’s exact line: **“I caught her staring at me again. She thought I’d been sleeping.”** Mara, the first-person narrator, is in bed beside her wife, Elise. At first, the question is why Elise watches her. By the end, the harder question is what Elise sees when Mara wakes. They have recently returned from the death of Mara’s mother, with whom Mara had a difficult relationship. Mara wishes she had spoken differently during their last visit; she does not simply wish her mother back. Something now uses Mara’s body when she sleeps. It can draw on her memories but often mishandles their emotional meaning. Mara and Elise can observe its behavior, but they will not discover a complete set of supernatural rules or a certain origin. The presence wants Mara to stop resisting it while awake. The horror will grow out of a specific marriage rather than a sequence of elaborate clues. Elise’s watchfulness is protective, but she has also frightened Mara, concealed evidence, and made mistakes. Mara’s anger at being watched will remain reasonable even after she learns why it happens. Their humor, habits, and old disagreements should survive the crisis. The story will be told in **first person, past tense**, close to Mara’s perceptions and gaps in memory. The prose will be plain and precise, becoming spare rather than ornate when she is afraid. Each chapter, at roughly 1,000 words, will center on one scene or development; not every night needs a new supernatural spectacle. Evidence will be limited chiefly to what Elise witnesses, one recording, and the things Mara finds she has done. There will be no mirror message, convenient security footage, formal test phrase, or last-minute explanation of the entity. The climax will be Mara’s choice to remain herself despite an offer that addresses a real regret. The immediate outcome will be clear. The ending will return to Elise’s stare, but its unease will come from how the experience has changed their ordinary life, not from suggesting that the climax may have meant nothing. # Chapter Planning ## Chapter 1 — Awake Mara pretends to sleep and catches Elise watching her from the chair beside their bed. Elise claims she heard Mara get up, though Mara remembers no such thing. Their conversation is strained in familiar ways: Mara objects to being treated like a patient; Elise objects to being made to explain herself at three in the morning. Elise has set a ceramic mug on the floor by the door so its fall will wake her if Mara leaves. After Elise finally goes to the kitchen, Mara notices the hem of her nightshirt is damp. She cannot explain why. She stays awake, listening for Elise. ## Chapter 2 — The Things Elise Has Seen The next day brings funeral leftovers, messages Mara has not answered, and the ordinary work of being home. Mara searches for a harmless explanation for the damp shirt. When she challenges Elise about the mug, Elise admits Mara has been walking in her sleep. She describes one incident badly, then stops; Mara recognizes the expression Elise gets when she thinks telling the full truth will only start a fight. Mara demands to know what else Elise is keeping from her. Elise says she recorded the previous night, but Mara had asked her not to play it again. ## Chapter 3 — Playback Elise plays the recording. For several minutes, it contains almost nothing: breathing, the chair creaking, Elise asking Mara to come back to bed. Then Mara’s voice begins a calm conversation. It asks Elise about an old argument and repeats Mara’s side accurately, but misunderstands why Elise was hurt. When Elise realizes the speaker is learning from her answers and goes quiet, it uses the nickname Mara’s mother called her—a name Mara never liked. Mara’s first response is fury that Elise continued the conversation. She takes the phone, then asks to hear the recording once more. ## Chapter 4 — A Mistake Mara and Elise agree to take turns staying awake, though neither believes it will last long. During a tired afternoon, Elise mistakes something the waking Mara says for another imitation. Mara sees how quickly Elise becomes afraid of her; Elise sees the effect of being wrong. Later, Mara finds that, during a lapse she cannot remember, she packed her mother’s cardigan into a bag and placed it by the front door. It is an action that resembles her own wish to be rid of the thing and the presence’s wish to go somewhere. They cannot agree on which. ## Chapter 5 — Her Mother’s Voice Mara tells Elise about the last visit with her mother: an argument at the bedside, followed by Mara’s attempt to apologize after her mother could no longer answer. She admits she said she would give anything to hear what her mother thought of her, but resists treating those words as a supernatural bargain. That night, as Mara drifts off in the living room, Elise hears her speak in her mother’s voice. What it says is not a revelation. It is a familiar, cutting remark Mara remembers perfectly. Elise wakes Mara before it can continue. Mara is shaken less by the voice than by her wish to hear the next sentence. ## Chapter 6 — What Elise Did Elise confesses that on an earlier night she answered the presence as if it were Mara. It said something kind that Mara had not said in months, and Elise wanted to believe it. That is why she kept talking long enough to make the recording. Her confession complicates Mara’s assumption that Elise has only been watching for danger. They argue about the recording, about the vigil, and about the distance between them before the funeral. Afterward, they make a limited plan for the night: Elise will wake Mara if she begins speaking, and Mara will decide what to do once awake. Neither claims to know whether that will be enough. ## Chapter 7 — The Offer Mara falls asleep despite her efforts. Elise wakes her, but Mara comes to herself gradually, aware of her body speaking before she can stop it. The presence does not deliver an explanation. In Mara’s own voice, it offers to keep hold of the memories she cannot bear to lose, including the conversation with her mother that will never happen. It asks Mara to let it stay while she is awake. Elise cannot tell when Mara has regained control and nearly makes another wrong choice. Mara finally interrupts—not with a prepared phrase, but by answering Elise’s question in a way that admits an old, unflattering truth the presence had been trying to smooth over. She refuses the offer aloud. Elise helps her remain awake through the rest of the night. ## Chapter 8 — Morning By morning, the presence no longer speaks when Mara closes her eyes briefly, but neither woman can prove it is gone for good. The resolution is practical rather than triumphant: they arrange help, sleep separately for a while, and disagree over whether to keep the recording. Mara does not recover her mother’s last words or emerge with a purified understanding of their marriage. Weeks later, she wakes and sees Elise sitting nearby, watching her. Mara has been awake long enough that she could have spoken sooner. She tells Elise she is awake now. Elise sets down what she is holding and comes to sit beside her.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Mara Velez Mara is thirty-eight and works as a municipal records clerk. She likes a job with procedures, but not because she believes everything important can be filed correctly. She likes knowing which problems are hers to solve. At home, she is less orderly: she leaves a glass beside the bed until it needs washing, saves articles she never reads, and remembers where Elise put things even while insisting she hasn’t touched them. She and Elise have been married for nine years. Mara’s mother, Celia, died after a long decline. Mara handled appointments and paperwork, though their relationship had never made that care easy. Celia could be funny and attentive, then casually diminishing. Mara learned to answer criticism with a joke or to change the subject before she could be hurt. At the bedside, she wanted to apologize for their last argument and wanted her mother to apologize too. Neither happened. She is ashamed of how often she felt relieved on the drive home from a visit. Mara is observant, dryly funny, and difficult to comfort when she has not asked for it. She can recognize when Elise is withholding something but is slow to acknowledge why Elise might feel she has to. Her instinct under threat is to argue about what can be established: precisely when the mug was put by the door, whether the recording proves she was asleep, why Elise did not tell her sooner. This is useful until it becomes a way of avoiding what she fears. She does apologize, but sometimes she arrives at an apology by such a long route that the other person has given up waiting. She is short, broad-shouldered, and usually still when she speaks, except for her hands. She rolls the edge of a sleeve between finger and thumb or presses her nails into her palm while listening. Her dark hair is cut just above her shoulders; since the funeral, she has been tying it back without looking in a mirror. When frightened, she becomes particularly exact and polite. Elise knows that is a worse sign than shouting. Mara wants control of her body and the right to be believed about her own experience. She also wants Elise’s help, though being watched and recorded makes accepting it painful. She loves Elise, but they were already avoiding a difficult conversation before Celia died. Part of Mara wants the presence to be a simple intruder so that none of its words can be taken as her own. *Voice experiments:* > “I’m not saying the mug moved itself. I’m saying you’ve made a fairly elaborate accusation with a mug.” > “The worst part wasn’t that it knew her voice. I knew her voice. For one second I thought I might finally hear her say something different.” # Elise Velez Elise is forty-one and repairs musical instruments in a small workshop, mostly school-band instruments brought in with bent keys, stuck valves, and labels bearing children’s names. Her work has taught her to attend to tiny changes without announcing them as disasters. She is patient with objects and less patient with being told she is imagining what she can plainly see. She grew up in a crowded, affectionate family whose members spoke over one another and noticed immediately when anyone went quiet. Mara’s household was different. Elise does not mistake that difference for a mystery she can solve, but she sometimes wishes Mara would let a question have a direct answer. Before the funeral, they had been arguing intermittently about how much of their shared time Celia’s needs could claim. Elise had helped with those needs; she also resented them. She has not found a way to say both things without feeling cruel. Elise is practical, tender, and capable of an unnerving focus. She keeps a pencil tucked behind her ear even when she is nowhere near the workshop. She talks to stubborn mechanisms under her breath, but not to people—unless they are asleep. At night, she sits in the chair rather than lying beside Mara because she is afraid of waking to find she has been answering the presence again. Her notes are on the backs of old repair slips, mixed with ordinary reminders such as “return trumpet to Patel.” The disorder embarrasses her only when Mara sees it. Elise’s chief flaw is that she makes decisions alone when she thinks sharing the burden will hurt someone. Recording Mara without telling her, withholding what happened, and deciding how to monitor the bedroom all come from that impulse. They also deny Mara a choice. Elise has made at least one serious error: she has treated the waking Mara as though she were the presence. She cannot take back Mara’s expression when that happened. Elise is tall and narrow, with a habit of leaning close to hear people, even in a quiet room. She has a pale scar across one knuckle from a workshop accident and rough fingertips that catch on soft fabric. Ordinarily she moves easily through their home, turning sideways around familiar furniture without thought. During the vigil, she sits rigidly and watches Mara’s face instead of her own hands. When exhausted, her voice drops and she loses the warmth with which she usually softens blunt statements. Elise wants Mara alive and able to trust her. She also wants permission to sleep. Those motives can pull against each other: every hour she stays awake makes another mistake more likely, but leaving Mara unwatched feels unbearable. She has no special allegiance to a theory about what the presence is; she would gladly be proved wrong if Mara could be safe. *Voice experiments:* > “I put the mug there because it makes a noise. I didn’t have a plan after the noise.” > “I know what I heard. I also know I answered it. You can be angry about both.” # Celia Ruiz Celia is Mara’s mother and is dead before the story begins, but she should feel like a person rather than a source of sinister phrases. She worked for years at a dry cleaner’s and was good at identifying the owners of unlabelled coats from the things they left in their pockets. She disliked wasting food, mailed birthday cards early, and could hold a grudge over a slight that everyone else had forgotten. When Mara was young, Celia called her **Mita**—a nickname Mara grew to hate when Celia continued using it in front of other people. Celia was quick-witted and often generous in ways she could control: sending leftovers home, paying for a repair without being asked, remembering an offhand preference. Direct apologies were harder for her. She could make Mara feel childish with a single question, then seem genuinely surprised that Mara took offense. Her illness did not erase either her affection or her difficult habits. In Mara’s memories, Celia is compact, with closely cropped gray hair and a habit of holding her chin up when she is tired. Her hands were always busy—folding a paper napkin, smoothing a sleeve, testing a seam. Near the end of her life, she could no longer do much of that. Mara remembers the stillness as vividly as the sound of her voice. Celia wanted Mara near, but did not always make nearness pleasant. She liked Elise and was irritated by how readily Elise could decline an invitation. Mara cannot be sure what Celia understood of their final argument. That uncertainty gives the presence something to exploit: it can repeat Celia accurately without being able to provide the answer Mara wants. *Voice experiments:* > “Take the cardigan. It fits you better. No, don’t make a face; I’m giving it to you.” > “You came all this way to stand in the doorway?” # The Presence The presence has no confirmed name, history, or appearance outside Mara’s body. It should not be written as an all-knowing demon with a polished philosophy. It is an intruder learning how to remain among people. Sleep gives it access to Mara’s movements and memories. What it cannot reliably grasp is why a remembered moment matters—or why telling the truth about it may be cruel. Its early behavior is exploratory. It asks Elise questions it can partly answer for itself and watches the effect of phrasing something differently. It returns to Mara’s mother’s voice because both women react, though not in the same way. It may not understand whether it is offering comfort or using pain; the story need not settle that question. Its desire is simpler: when Mara wakes, it does not want to lose its hold. Through Mara, it has Mara’s height, hands, and familiar expressions, but its timing is wrong. It keeps still a little too long after Elise speaks. It may make eye contact when Mara would look away or offer an agreeable answer where Mara would argue. As it learns, such differences become less dependable. Its most disturbing imitation is not a theatrical change of voice but an ordinary sentence spoken with almost the right concern. The presence has no allegiance to Mara or Elise, though it learns that pleasing either of them can serve it. It uses real memories, including things Mara would rather deny, so dismissing everything it says as false will not protect them. *Voice experiments:* > “She was angry when you left. You already know that. Shall I tell you what she said after?” > “Elise, I don’t want to start again tomorrow. You know how tired she is.”

# Chapter 1 — Awake I caught her staring at me again. She thought I’d been sleeping. Elise sat in the chair on my side of the bed, wearing the gray sweatshirt she used to paint the kitchen. The sleeves were pushed up to her elbows. There was enough light from the hallway to see her face, but not enough to tell what she made of mine. I kept my eyes nearly shut. I wanted to find out what she did when she thought I couldn’t see her. After a while she leaned forward, and I had to resist the urge to turn my head. “Are you awake?” she whispered. “Yes.” She sat back so quickly the chair knocked the wall. “What are you doing?” I asked. “I heard you get up.” “I didn’t.” Elise looked toward the door. “All right.” That was worse than arguing. I sat up and reached for the lamp, but she said, “Don’t,” and I stopped with my hand on the switch. “Why?” “You’ll wake up properly.” “I am properly awake.” She rubbed her face. The shadow from the hallway cut across her mouth, making it hard to see whether she meant to say anything else. On the floor by the door sat one of our mugs. It was white, with a blue chip on the handle. Elise used it for tea because the chip caught on my thumb. “Did you bring a drink in here?” “No.” I pointed. She followed my hand and sighed. “It’s there so I’ll hear the door,” she said. “If the door opens?” “If you open it.” I switched on the lamp. Elise squinted and looked away. There were ordinary things I could have said. *You could have asked me to wake you. You could have slept beside me.* Instead I said, “You booby-trapped the bedroom with a mug.” “It was what I had.” She sounded tired, and for a moment I felt sorry for her. Then I remembered her face in the dark. I had woken twice that week to find her in the chair, watching. Both times she had given me some small explanation and come back to bed only after I asked her to. “When did I supposedly get up?” I asked. “About half an hour ago.” “Where did I go?” “I don’t know.” “You were sitting here.” “I woke up when you came back.” I swung my feet onto the floor. The boards felt cold. “So you didn’t hear me leave, and you didn’t see where I went.” “Elise,” she said, then stopped. She was trying to get my attention with her own name; she had done that once before, after three hours’ sleep and a five-hour drive. “Mara. Please. I heard you come back.” I waited for her to say more. She lifted the chipped mug from the floor and held it in both hands, although it was empty. We had come home from my mother’s funeral on Monday. It was Thursday, or the beginning of Friday. We still had two foil-covered dishes in the fridge from people who had never visited our house. I hadn’t put away my black shoes. Elise had slept badly in the chair at my mother’s place and badly in our bed since we returned. I knew all of that. I also knew she had been watching me when she believed I wasn’t looking. “Did I say anything?” I asked. She glanced at me. “There it is,” I said. “What?” “You know what I’m going to ask, so you’re getting ready to tell me I’m upset.” “I wasn’t.” “Then tell me.” She set the mug on the dresser. “You were in the hall. I heard your feet on the boards. When you came in, I asked where you’d been.” “And?” “You didn’t answer.” “That’s all?” “It’s what happened.” I could hear her being careful. Elise normally spoke while she was thinking, correcting herself aloud, sometimes asking me if a word existed. Now every sentence arrived finished. I tried to remember the last time I had seen her act that way with me. At the hospital, perhaps, when my mother was dying and there were nurses to listen. “You should go back to bed,” she said. “You’re still in the chair.” “I know.” “So you’re not.” Elise picked a loose thread from the cuff of her sweatshirt and wound it around one finger. At work, she repaired school instruments. She came home with bits of lint and brass filings on her clothes, then stood over the sink checking her hands before she touched anything clean. Now she looked down at her fingers as though they belonged to somebody else. “I don’t think I can sleep yet,” she said. That, at least, I believed. I moved over to leave her room on the mattress, but she stayed where she was. We looked at the space I had made. Before the funeral, I had sometimes complained that she took more than her half of the bed. “I’m going to make tea,” she said. “It’s three in the morning.” “I know where the kettle is.” She took the mug and went out, leaving the door partly open. I watched the strip of light widen as she passed down the hall. A cupboard opened in the kitchen, then closed. I pulled the blanket over my knees. I might have walked in my sleep. My mother had told me I did it once as a child, though she used to tell that story about several things she caught me doing awake. I tried to remember getting up tonight. I remembered brushing my teeth. Elise was already in bed when I came out of the bathroom, turned toward the wall. The blanket had twisted around my legs. As I freed it, my hand brushed the hem of my nightshirt. It was wet. I held the cotton between my fingers. Only the front hem was damp, a narrow band of cold fabric against my knees. The water glass beside the bed was full. There was no spill on the sheet. From the kitchen came the click of the kettle switching off. I could call Elise back and show her. I sat with the fabric in my hand until I heard her pour the water. Then I let go of it and pulled the blanket over my legs. I stayed awake, listening to her move around the kitchen.

# Chapter 2 — The Things Elise Has Seen By nine, the damp part of my nightshirt had dried. I put it in the laundry basket without showing Elise. She was asleep at the kitchen table when I came down, her head on her folded arms. A full cup of tea stood beside her. She had put a saucer over it to keep it warm. The mug from our bedroom was on the counter. I left her alone and opened the fridge. The two dishes from the funeral were stacked beneath a plastic container of olives that had been there since before we left. One dish was macaroni and cheese. The other had a note taped to the foil: *Just put it in the oven. Love, Janice.* I did not know Janice well enough to remember which side of the family she belonged to. I ate three forkfuls of macaroni cold. When I shut the fridge, Elise lifted her head. “Good morning,” she said. “It’s nearly ten.” “Then I got some sleep.” She had a crease on her cheek from her sleeve. I wanted to tell her to go upstairs, where she could sleep lying down. Instead I said, “Your tea’s cold.” She lifted the saucer and felt the cup. “It is.” The week after someone dies, people ask whether you’re taking care of yourself, then give you food in quantities that make it difficult to find anything else. I moved Janice’s dish aside and found the milk. Elise watched me take it out. I had decided to tell her about my shirt. I had also decided, while she was sleeping, that the hem could have got wet when I washed my face. Both things remained possible until I opened my mouth. “Did you use the bathroom last night?” I asked. “Yes.” “After you got up?” “I think so.” I poured milk into a glass. “Was there water on the floor?” “Not that I noticed.” I drank the milk standing up. Elise’s eyes went to my feet, then back to my face. I was barefoot, as I had been during the night. Whatever she had hoped to learn from them, I couldn’t tell. My phone buzzed on the table. A message from my cousin Nico asked if I had found the photo albums. The albums were in a box by our front door, which he had helped carry in on Monday. I typed *yes* and put the phone facedown. “Can we talk about the mug?” I asked. Elise put the saucer back on her tea. “You can admit it was a strange thing to do.” “It was a strange thing to do.” “Then why did you do it?” “So I’d hear you.” “Going to the bathroom?” “Leaving the bedroom.” “You could sleep with the door open.” “I did.” She ran a hand through her hair. It was still flattened on one side. For a moment she looked as if she might ask me to let it go, and I would have refused. Instead she said, “You’ve been walking in your sleep.” “I know what you said last night.” “It wasn’t the first time.” Outside, a truck reversed somewhere down the street, three dull beeps followed by silence. “How many?” “I’m not sure.” “Elise.” “Four that I saw. There might have been others.” I sat opposite her. “What did you see?” “The first night we got back, you went downstairs. I woke up when the front door shut.” “Did I go outside?” “You were on the step. I asked what you were doing, and you came in.” “That sounds like sleepwalking.” “Yes.” “You didn’t tell me.” “I did. In the morning. You said your mother used to find you asleep in the hall.” I remembered that conversation. We had been unpacking, and I had told Elise the story to make her laugh. She hadn’t laughed much. “The next night,” Elise said, “you were in the kitchen.” “Doing what?” She rubbed the pale scar across her knuckle. “You’d taken all the teaspoons out of the drawer. They were lined up on the counter.” I looked over at the counter, which was clear except for her mug and the kettle. “Why?” “I don’t know. When I asked, you said you were counting them.” “We have six.” “You said we had seven.” I pictured her awake in the kitchen, having that conversation with me, then putting the spoons away by herself. I had no memory of it. “Why didn’t you wake me?” “I tried to. You looked at me.” “And?” “That was all.” Her hand moved toward mine, then stopped on the table. I remembered her face in the chair and drew my hand into my lap. She saw me do it. The front door was visible from where we sat. Nico’s box blocked part of it; someone would have to step around the albums to get out. I wondered whether I had done that on the first night. “Was there anything else?” I asked. Elise stared at the worn place on the tabletop. It was a ring left by a hot pan in our first year here. She had apologized for it at the time, though neither of us had liked the table much. “You’ve been talking,” she said. “In my sleep?” “Sometimes.” “What do I say?” She stood, carried her tea to the sink, and poured it away. I felt the old, familiar irritation of waiting while Elise found a careful way to tell me something. Before she could turn around, I said, “If I’m frightening you, I need to know what I’ve done.” “You haven’t done anything on purpose.” “That isn’t what I asked.” She braced her hands on the edge of the sink. “Last night I recorded some of it.” The forks and plates in the drying rack were still there from the day before. I counted them while I worked out what she meant. “On your phone.” “Yes.” “You could have told me that when I asked what happened.” “I was going to.” “You let me sit there and argue about a mug.” “You asked me not to play it again.” “Again?” Elise turned to face me. Her eyes were red from sleeping with her face pressed into her arms. “I played it for you yesterday afternoon,” she said. “You listened to part of it. Then you told me to stop and not to let you hear it again.” I remembered yesterday afternoon. Nico had called. I had unpacked a towel from my mother’s house and found a peppermint wrapped inside it. Elise had gone out for bread. I could not remember her playing a recording. “Where’s your phone?” I asked. “In my pocket.” She kept it there. I stayed at the table, looking at her, until she took it out.

[Analysis] This chapter is a remarkably controlled piece of domestic horror writing. The author executes the chapter plan with precision and intelligence, delivering the promised revelations—the sleepwalking incidents, the teaspoons, the recording—while maintaining the specific texture of a marriage under strain. Instead, the horror accumulates through mundane details: the saucer over the cold tea, the crease on Elise's cheek, the six teaspoons that Mara counted in her sleep and called seven. These are not decorative details but load-bearing ones. The teaspoon scene is particularly effective—the wrongness of it is quiet and specific, and Elise's account of Mara looking at her ("When I asked, you looked at me. And? Mara's interrogative style—short questions, waiting out silences, refusing to let Elise redirect—feels authentic to the character profile. Elise's withholding is rendered without making her seem simply secretive; we understand the impulse even as Mara's frustration is justified. The exchange about the mug ("You let me sit there and argue about a mug") lands with real force because it's both petty and completely fair. The chapter's most impressive achievement is the final revelation: Mara cannot remember Elise playing the recording the previous afternoon. This is delivered without fanfare, embedded in a list of things Mara does remember (Nico's call, the peppermint in the towel, Elise going for bread), which makes the gap more disturbing than any explicit statement of horror could. The author trusts the reader. Character consistency is strong throughout. Mara's instinct to argue about what can be established (the mug, the bathroom, the water on the floor) is exactly as described in her profile. Her decision to hide the damp shirt in the laundry basket without showing Elise is a small but telling detail—she is already managing information herself, which complicates her later frustration at Elise doing the same. Elise's behavior—the saucer over the tea, the notes on repair slips, the decision to record rather than wake Mara—is consistent with her profile's description of someone who makes decisions alone to protect others. The Janice detail (the funeral dish, not knowing which side of the family she belongs to) is a nice touch of social texture that grounds the story in a recognizable world without slowing it down. If there are weaknesses, they are minor. The observation about the worn ring on the table—"It was a ring left by a hot pan in our first year here. She had apologized for it at the time, though neither of us had liked the table much"—is the one moment where the prose reaches slightly for significance in a way that feels a touch deliberate. It's not a failure, but it's the closest the chapter comes to announcing its own symbolism. Similarly, the truck reversing outside is a competent atmospheric beat but not a particularly original one. The chapter follows its plan faithfully: the funeral leftovers, the search for harmless explanations, the confrontation about the mug, Elise's admission of the sleepwalking incidents (described badly, then stopped), the revelation of the recording, and the crucial detail that Mara had already heard it and asked Elise not to play it again. All of this is present and handled with skill. The darkness is well-earned because it emerges from character rather than contrivance. # Chapter 3 — Playback Elise set her phone on the table between us. The recording was twenty-six minutes long. “Was I asleep the whole time?” I asked. “I thought you were at first.” She sat across from me. I pressed play. For almost a minute there was nothing but the soft hiss of the microphone. Then a chair creaked. Elise, sounding far away, said, “Mara, come back to bed.” A cupboard door closed. I could hear myself breathing near the phone. “Please,” Elise said. I glanced at her. She was watching the table, not me. On the recording, my voice said, “All right.” I recognized it as my voice, but I could not place the moment. There was a scrape that might have been the chair. Elise had left nearly half a minute of it playing before she spoke again. “You’re standing there,” she said. “I know.” “Come and sit down.” I stopped the recording. “Were you in the kitchen?” “Bedroom. You went to the dresser. My phone was on the chair arm.” “You didn’t turn on the light?” “I’d just woken up.” I pictured the room as it had been at three in the morning: the hallway light, the dresser, the chair on my side of the bed. “What was I doing at the dresser?” “Opening the bottom drawer.” There were winter clothes in that drawer and an old canvas bag we used for holidays. I pressed play again. My voice came through clearly now. “Do you remember the drive back from your sister’s?” Elise made a small sound beside me. On the recording, she said, “Which time?” “The time we stopped for petrol and Mara wouldn’t get out of the car.” I looked up. Elise kept her eyes on the phone. That had been two years ago, on the way home from a weekend at her sister Ruth’s place. Ruth had announced her engagement over lunch. Elise was delighted; I had spent most of the meal fielding questions about whether we wanted children. At the petrol station, I stayed in the car and told Elise I was tired. Later we fought because I thought she had left me alone with Ruth’s questions, and she thought I had been rude to her family. “I remember,” the recorded Elise said. “She was right to be angry.” “What?” “Ruth kept asking. You knew she didn’t want to answer.” There was a long pause. Elise had wanted me to say exactly that, once. I had said something close to it after we got home, but only after reminding her how her sister could be. “You talked about this yesterday,” I said. “Listen.” On the phone, Elise said, “Mara?” “She was right to be angry,” my voice repeated. “So you can stop being angry too.” I felt my face heat. I remembered that argument; Elise had not been angry about the questions. She had been angry because, on the drive home, I asked why she hadn’t stopped them and then refused to believe she’d tried. I had not noticed her doing it. Saying I’d been right to be angry disposed of the easier half of what happened. The recording continued. Elise asked, “What do you mean?” “I said what she should have said. Is it better now?” “No.” “What should I say?” Elise reached over and stopped the playback. “I’m sorry. I answered a few more questions before I realized.” “What did you think was happening?” “I thought you were talking in your sleep. Then you started asking me things.” “Why that argument?” “I don’t know.” I looked at the phone. “Play the rest.” Elise hesitated, then touched the screen. I heard her voice say, “Where are you now?” “In the bedroom.” “Where’s Mara?” Another pause. The recording picked up fabric moving close to the phone. When my voice returned, it sounded amused. “You’re looking at her.” “Go back to bed.” “Did she tell you about Mita?” I put my hand on the table. I had not heard that name since my mother became too ill to remember it. On the recording, Elise said, “Who?” “Mita. She hated it in front of people.” My mother had used the name in shops, at school, once while handing me a certificate onstage. I had asked her to stop long before she did. Elise knew the name because I had told her the story, but I had not heard her say it aloud. Elise asked, “Where did you learn that?” There was a dull knock, as though I had closed the drawer. My voice said, “She keeps things.” Elise drew in a breath. Then she said, more firmly, “Mara, I’m going to turn on the light.” The recording ended a few seconds later. I replayed the last part. Elise did not stop me. On the second listen, I could hear how tired she sounded when she asked where I was. I tried to imagine seeing my own wife standing at the dresser and asking her that. “Why did you stop recording?” I asked. “I turned on the light. You were crying.” “I don’t remember crying.” “I know. You let me take you back to bed.” I slid the phone away. It was warm from lying between our hands. Elise said, “Yesterday, when I played it, you got as far as your mother’s name. You asked me to switch it off.” “And then we went on with the afternoon?” “You went upstairs. A while later you asked if I wanted bread.” I remembered her going out for bread. I could not remember telling her to. “Did you try a doctor?” I asked. “I looked up sleepwalking. I was going to call today, with you.” “You should have woken me before now.” “I tried. Sometimes you woke up.” “Sometimes?” She touched the phone but did not take it. “I don’t think staying here tonight is helping either of us.” I wanted to argue that we had no reason to go anywhere. I also wanted to get out of the room before she asked me another question I could not answer. “All right,” I said. “We’ll go somewhere tonight.” Elise nodded. I looked once more at the phone, then pushed it back across the table to her.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter executes its plan with considerable skill. The central conceit—playing back a recording of something that wore Mara's body while she slept—is handled with restraint and intelligence. The author avoids the obvious horror-movie approach of making the recording lurid or theatrical; instead, the presence's wrongness is revealed through a subtle misreading of an old argument. It gets the facts right (Mara was right to be angry) but misses the emotional architecture (Elise wasn't angry about the questions themselves, but about Mara's refusal to believe she'd tried to help). This is exactly the kind of precise, character-grounded horror the plan called for. The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. Lines like "I said what she should have said. Is it better now?" are genuinely unsettling because they reveal the presence's fundamental incomprehension—it treats emotional repair as a transaction, a correct phrase to be delivered. The exchange about the petrol station argument is economical and revealing: we understand the marriage's texture, the specific shape of their old wound, and the presence's failure to grasp it, all simultaneously. Elise's "No" in response to "Is it better now?" is perfectly placed. The character work is consistent with the profiles. Mara's instinct to argue about what can be established ("Why did you stop recording?") is present throughout. Her replaying the last section twice is psychologically true—she needs to hear it again, to process it through procedure. Elise's withholding, her decision to stop the playback at the name, her admission that she answered more questions than she should have—all track with her established character flaw of making decisions alone to protect others. Elise repeated the advice to me without adding anything. We were not sure what to do with Friday night. The motel Elise had suggested was twenty minutes away, and neither of us wanted to pack a bag.
