She slept for an hour on the sofa while I sat at the kitchen table with my mother’s photo albums. Nico wanted the pictures from a camping trip when we were children. He remembered us both smiling in them. I found one of him holding a fish with his eyes closed, and three of my mother making us stand together in front of the car. I put those in an envelope. When Elise came downstairs, she had pillow marks on both cheeks. “Did I snore?” “Enough to reassure me you were alive.” She smiled, and for a few minutes we sorted photographs together. Elise picked up a picture of my mother in a yellow raincoat. “She took that coat to the hospital,” Elise said. “I know. I brought it home.” “It’s in the hall cupboard?” I nodded. It had rained through most of my last visit, and my mother had insisted I take the coat to walk to the pharmacy. I had left it hanging by her front door when I got back. Later, someone had put it among the things for us to collect. Elise laid the picture aside and took out another. “You look exactly like Nico in this one.” “No, he looks like me. I’m older.” I reached for the envelope. Elise held on to it. “Mara,” she said. “What?” “Why did you ask where the coat was?” “I didn’t.” “You asked me if it was in the cupboard.” “You asked me.” She let go of the envelope. I could see her trying to reconstruct the last few seconds, the way I was. “I did,” she said. “I’m sorry.” “You looked at me like you did last night.” “I know.” “Was it the coat?” “I don’t know what it was. I haven’t slept enough.” I slid the photograph back into the album. Elise reached for it, then stopped when she saw my hand was still there. “You were right about the coat,” I said. “It’s in the cupboard. If you need to check.” “I believe you.” “It didn’t look like you did.” She stood up and took our cups to the sink. I watched her run water over a spoon that was already clean. When she came back, I had closed the album. By early evening we were both too tired to keep making decisions. I called the motel and asked if they had a room. They did. I told Elise, and we agreed to leave after dinner. She heated Janice’s macaroni and cheese. I took a shower, partly to wake myself. Afterward I stood at the top of the stairs in my clean nightshirt, listening to Elise move plates around below. I meant to go into the bedroom for socks. The next thing I remember, I was kneeling by the front door. The hall was dark. The kitchen light showed beneath its door, and Elise was still handling plates. A canvas bag sat open beside me. I had taken it from the bottom drawer of the dresser. My mother’s cardigan was folded inside it, with the sleeves laid across the front. I was holding one of my own shoes by its heel. I set the shoe down. My knees hurt from the floorboards. I could not remember coming down the stairs or fetching the cardigan from the spare room. “Elise?” She opened the kitchen door at once. Her gaze moved from me to the bag. “I think I went to sleep,” I said. She stayed where she was. “Can you stand?” “Yes.” I stood, using the wall. I wanted her to come closer. I was also afraid she would ask me something and decide the answer was wrong. “What happened?” she asked. “I came down here, I suppose.” “I didn’t hear you.” “I know. You were in the kitchen.” I pointed to the cardigan. It was brown, with one stretched pocket. My mother used to keep tissues in it and forget to take them out before washing it. I had put it in the spare room because I didn’t want to decide whether to keep it. “Did you pack that?” Elise asked. “I must have.” “Were you taking it somewhere?” “I don’t remember.” She looked at the front door. Nico’s box had been moved to one side, clearing the way. I could have done that before kneeling down; I had no memory of it either. “I wanted to get rid of it,” I said. “When we came home. Maybe I still do.” Elise touched the strap of the bag. “Maybe.” Her answer irritated me. She was trying to leave room for what I thought, and I could tell she did not agree. “Go ahead,” I said. “Tell me what you think I was doing.” “I don’t know. I came out when you called.” “I know you don’t know.” My voice rose. “But you’re looking at the door.” “Because it’s open.” I turned. The front door stood ajar, held by the edge of the doormat. Cold air came through the gap. We both crossed to it, Elise reaching it first. She shut it and turned the lock. “I didn’t see it,” I said. “I believe you.” This time I could not tell whether she did. I didn’t question why you’d brought it up.” “What did you say?” “I said I was angry because you’d told me I should have rescued you, then wouldn’t believe I’d tried.” It was what she had told me after the trip. I had believed her eventually, but that word—*rescued*—still made me uncomfortable. I took another piece of toast. “You must have noticed something was wrong,” I said. “Not at first. You listened. Then you said I could be angry.” “You’d wanted me to say that.” “Yes.” She folded the repair slip, opened it again, and looked at the writing. “How long did you talk?” I asked. “A few minutes. I told you I’d felt stupid, trying to explain myself in the car while you stared out the window.” She glanced up. “You said you were sorry I’d been alone in that.” I couldn’t remember ever putting it that way. Elise had, often enough. She might have remembered the words from an argument I’d forgotten. “Were you glad?” I asked. “I was. Then you asked me what else you could say to make it better.” That was when she sat up and reached for her phone. She had not expected to make the recording she later played for me; she wanted to hear our conversation in the morning, when we were both less tired. “You were talking to it before you knew,” I said. “Yes.” “And after you knew, you kept answering.” “I thought if it was asking questions, it might answer one.” “You let it ask about us.” “I know. I answered.” I left the burned crust on my plate. For two days I had imagined Elise listening from the chair, certain that whatever spoke in my voice was dangerous. She had wanted something from it too. I was angry with her for talking and angrier that I understood why. She reached for the plate. I held on to it. “You could have told me this when I listened to the recording.” “I should have.” “Did you think I’d blame you?” “I did.” “I do.” I let her take the plate. “I’m trying not to make that all I do.” Elise carried it to the sink. I asked her to turn on the lamp first and say my name where I could hear it. “What if you don’t wake?” she asked. “Keep trying. Call for help.” She nodded. I could see she had another question, so I waited. “What if you wake up and I can’t tell?” I thought of her in the kitchen, mistaking me over the coat. “Tell me what you’re seeing. Let me answer.” “I did that before. It answered.” “Then we may have to talk for a while.” Neither of us liked the plan. She had heard my voice turn away from her. “I won’t make you lose any of it,” it said. “You can wake up and let me stay.” I could feel the pressure of the mattress under my legs. My hand still lay palm up. I could not make it close. “Who are you talking to?” Elise asked. “Mara.” “Then let her speak.” “She is listening.” Elise reached for my hand and held it. Her fingers were warm. I tried to squeeze them. My thumb moved against her skin. “Mara?” she said. My mouth opened, and the words came out too easily. “I’m here.” Elise’s grip loosened. She leaned toward me, and I saw that she wanted to believe I had returned. I wanted to believe it too. I gathered everything I had into moving my thumb again, but my hand slid out of hers. “What happened in the car?” Elise asked. “She was hurt,” my voice said. “Ruth asked about children and you didn’t stop her. She wanted you to understand.” It was close enough to what I had told myself for two years. I had been hurt. I had also seen Elise try to draw Ruth away, and afterward I acted as though I hadn’t. I could feel the memory under the words the presence chose. “Elise,” I tried to say. I made a sound. My jaw clenched. She drew back, alarmed. “Mara, if you can hear me—” “I can,” it said. “She wouldn’t say it like that,” Elise replied. I forced my hand against the blanket. My fingers curled. Elise took hold of them again, harder this time. “I saw you try,” I said. The words scraped my throat. I held on to Elise’s hand before anything else could come out. “At the petrol station,” I managed. “And at the table. I was angry, so I told you I hadn’t.” Elise stared at me. My mother’s room was still there if I let myself turn toward it. I wanted to know what she would have said. I wanted Elise to keep holding my hand. “I don’t want you here,” I said. My head jerked back. The bed frame struck the wall, and Elise grabbed me before I fell sideways. I tried to speak again, but all I could do was cough. She helped me sit forward. When I could breathe, I told her not to let me go back to sleep. We spent the remaining hours in the kitchen. Elise put water on for tea, forgot it, and had to fill the kettle again. Whenever I closed my eyes, she said my name. Sometimes I answered angrily. Once I cried because I wanted her to stop. She apologized and kept waking me. By morning, light came through the window behind her. She was sitting across the table, holding my hand. When I told her the kettle had boiled, my voice was mine. We made the tea and called the clinic.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] Chapter 7 is the climactic chapter of this possession horror story, and it largely succeeds at what it sets out to do. Let me examine it carefully across multiple dimensions. STRENGTHS: The chapter's greatest achievement is its restraint. The possession horror is rendered through precise, mundane details rather than theatrical spectacle: the missing button on Elise's nightshirt, the single sock on the floor, the kettle forgotten and refilled. These details ground the supernatural in the domestic, which is exactly what the story's plan calls for. The horror of hearing yourself speak before you can stop it is conveyed with clinical precision: "I could feel my tongue against my teeth." This is genuinely effective body horror without any purple prose. The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. The presence's speech is subtly wrong in exactly the right ways — it answers questions correctly but with slightly off emotional calibration. "You woke her. Give her a minute" sounds plausible but has that quality of someone performing concern rather than feeling it. The verification exchange ("What happened in the car?") is tense and well-constructed. Elise's "She wouldn't say it like that" is a perfect line — it shows her intimate knowledge of Mara while also being the kind of thing a frightened person would say to reassure themselves. The climax — Mara's refusal — is handled with admirable specificity. Rather than a grand declaration, she admits an unflattering truth: "I saw you try. At the petrol station. And at the table. I was angry, so I told you I hadn't." This is exactly what the plan called for: "answering Elise's question in a way that admits an old, unflattering truth the presence had been trying to smooth over." The presence had been offering a smoothed-over version of the Ruth's lunch incident, and Mara's refusal is to acknowledge the messier truth. This is psychologically sophisticated and earns its emotional weight. The offer itself — keeping the memories she can't bear to lose, including the conversation with her mother that will never happen — is genuinely poignant. The mother's room intrusion ("I could see my mother looking at me, though I had not looked at her long enough that day to remember her expression") is a quietly devastating detail. The presence can reconstruct the scene but not the face, because Mara didn't look long enough. This is the kind of precise, earned detail that elevates the writing. The ending of the chapter — the kitchen vigil, Elise forgetting the kettle, Mara crying and telling her to stop, Elise apologizing and continuing anyway — is beautifully rendered. It's exhausted and human and doesn't reach for false comfort. WEAKNESSES: The chapter is very strong but not without issues. The transition into the mother's room memory ("My mother's room came back to me") is slightly abrupt — it works, but the shift from the present scene to the memory-space could be smoother. The reader has to do a small amount of work to understand that this is the presence showing Mara what it's offering. "The words scraped my throat" is the one moment that edges toward cliché, though it's not egregious. The physical struggle — "My head jerked back. The bed frame struck the wall" — is the most conventionally horror-movie moment in the chapter, and it feels slightly out of register with the quieter, more psychological horror that precedes it. It's not badly written, but it's the chapter's least original beat. The verification game (asking about Ruth's lunch) is effective but the reader might wonder why Elise doesn't have a better verification question prepared after all these nights — something the presence couldn't have heard on the recording. This is a minor logical quibble, but it's there. CONSISTENCY WITH PLAN AND PROFILES: The chapter follows its plan closely and faithfully. The presence makes its offer, Elise nearly makes another wrong choice, Mara refuses by admitting an unflattering truth, and they survive the night in the kitchen. Mara's voice is consistent with her profile — exact, controlled, becoming spare when frightened. Elise's exhaustion and her continued watchfulness despite her mistakes are both present. The presence's behavior — learning, slightly off in timing and emotional calibration — matches the character profile precisely. The chapter is faithful to the writing prompt's spirit: the possession horror grows from the specific marriage, the characters' humor and habits survive (the forgotten kettle), and the resolution is practical rather than triumphant. Overall, this is accomplished literary horror writing — restrained, precise, emotionally intelligent, and consistent with its own established world and characters. Its flaws are minor. # Chapter 8 — Morning The woman at the clinic asked whether I was in immediate danger. I looked at Elise across the table. She had fallen asleep sitting up, though she was still holding my hand. “I don’t know,” I said. The woman was quiet for a moment. Then she told me to bring someone with me and come in as soon as they opened. Elise woke when I put down the phone. She had slept for less than a minute and was embarrassed by it. She went upstairs to dress while I watched the kettle cool. At the clinic, I told the doctor I had been walking and speaking in my sleep. I told her there were periods I could not account for. Elise described the nights she had witnessed. We did not play the recording. The doctor asked about the tablets I had taken, the funeral, and how much either of us had slept. She asked whether I felt safe at home. I said yes. Then I looked at Elise and said I wasn’t sure what I had been doing there. The doctor listened to both answers. She arranged tests and advised us not to spend another night managing this alone. She said it would help if someone else could stay with us. In the car, Elise asked if I wanted to call Nico. I said no too quickly. At the next set of traffic lights, I asked her to call Ruth. Ruth arrived that afternoon with a bag of clean clothes, a loaf of bread, and no attempt to make us explain ourselves over the phone. She listened when we told her what we could. Then she put the bread in the kitchen and asked which of us had slept. Elise said she was fine. Ruth took one look at her and told her to lie down. I stayed downstairs with Ruth. She showed me a photograph of her dog, who had eaten the corner of her sofa, and talked about how much the repair would cost. I could hear Elise moving above us before the bedroom went quiet. The tests gave us no answer that day. I slept on the sofa that night, with Ruth in the armchair and Elise upstairs. When I woke, Ruth was reading. She had heard me turn over once. I went to the kitchen for water and came back without finding anything moved or missing. In the morning Ruth told Elise I had slept. For several nights after that, one of them stayed with me. I disliked hearing them arrange their shifts. I disliked needing them. I also slept, and each morning I could remember lying down and waking up. When Ruth went home, Elise and I kept the bedroom door open. We argued about the recording. I wanted her to delete it. Elise said she might need it for the doctor if I had another episode. “You already told her what happened,” I said. “She didn’t hear it.” “I did.” Elise put her phone away without deleting anything. I was angry enough to sleep in the spare room that night. In the morning, I came downstairs and told her I could live with her keeping it until after the tests, but I wanted to know when she listened to it. She agreed. Neither of us apologized for the argument. My mother’s cardigan stayed folded on the spare-room bed. One afternoon I put it on and found that the sleeves reached farther down my hands than I remembered. I wore it while I sorted the remaining photographs for Nico. I found one of my mother laughing with her head turned away from the camera. I could not remember what had amused her. I put the picture in an album and kept the cardigan. Elise went back to work. She came home one evening with a trumpet case and spent an hour freeing a valve at the kitchen table. She told me the child who owned it had tried cooking oil before bringing it in. I laughed, and she looked up to see whether I was making fun of him. I was. She laughed too, then went back to the valve. A few weeks later I woke in the night and saw her sitting in the chair. She wore her work trousers and an old T-shirt. A repair slip rested against her knee. She must have come home late; I had gone to bed before she arrived. I lay still. Elise was watching my face, waiting to see whether my eyes would open. I could have said something at once. Instead I watched her rub her thumb over the rough edge of the slip. She looked as though she needed sleep. “I’m awake,” I said. “I can see that.” “How long have you been there?” “Not long. I heard you talking.” I tried to remember a dream, but nothing came. “What did I say?” “You said you were cold.” I pulled the blanket up around my shoulders. “I am.” Elise leaned forward. For an instant I thought she was going to ask what I meant by it. Instead she set the slip on the floor and came to sit beside me. Her hand found mine under the blanket. “What’s on the slip?” I asked. “Ruth’s birthday. I wrote it down so I wouldn’t forget.” “It’s next month.” “I know.” She rested her head against mine. “Go back to sleep, Mara.” I did not want to yet. We sat together until I heard her breathing slow. Then I switched off the lamp.

[Analysis] This is a sophisticated piece of possession horror that operates almost entirely through domestic realism and psychological ambiguity. The author has made a deliberate and largely successful choice to keep the supernatural element understated—the "possession" manifests through sleepwalking, recorded conversations, and a voice that speaks in the protagonist's name but with uncanny knowledge. This restraint is both the story's greatest strength and, occasionally, its limitation. CHARACTER AND DIALOGUE The two central characters, Mara and Elise, are rendered with genuine nuance. Their relationship has texture: the argument about Ruth's lunch, the petrol station incident, the way Mara waited for her turn to speak rather than truly listening. These details accumulate into a portrait of a marriage under strain from grief and old resentments. The dialogue is notably strong throughout—it captures how people speak when they're exhausted and frightened, with sentences that arrive "finished" (as Mara observes), careful and guarded. The line "You booby-trapped the bedroom with a mug" is perfectly calibrated: wry, specific, and character-revealing. Elise's admission that she kept answering the entity because she wanted something from it is the story's most psychologically honest moment. The characters' actions are consistently believable. Mara's decision to hide the wet nightshirt hem, Elise's recording, the canceled motel room—all feel like choices real people would make under these circumstances. The introduction of Ruth in the final chapters is handled economically and well. PACING AND STRUCTURE The pacing is generally strong, with each chapter advancing both the supernatural plot and the emotional subplot. The story builds tension effectively through accumulation rather than escalation. However, the middle chapters (3-5) occasionally feel slightly repetitive in their rhythm: revelation, Mara's disbelief, Elise's careful explanation, another revelation. The climactic Chapter 7 is the most dramatically intense and earns its place, though the resolution in Chapter 8 moves perhaps too quickly from crisis to tentative normalcy. HORROR ELEMENTS The possession horror is handled with admirable restraint. The entity's strategy—using intimate knowledge of the couple's arguments to offer emotional resolution—is genuinely unsettling and original. The line "I can keep the things she wakes up missing" is the story's most chilling moment, and it works because it's been earned by the preceding chapters. The entity's offer is seductive precisely because it addresses real wounds in the relationship. This is sophisticated horror writing. WEAKNESSES The story's restraint occasionally tips into understatement that diffuses tension. The ending, while tonally appropriate, resolves too neatly—Mara simply wakes up one night saying she's cold, Elise comes to sit beside her, and the story closes on a note of quiet domesticity. The final image is lovely but the transformation from crisis to this equilibrium feels slightly compressed. We don't fully understand what happened or why it stopped, which is a legitimate artistic choice but may frustrate readers expecting more resolution. There are occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly over-worked: "The shadow from the hallway cut across her mouth" is fine, but some of the observational details accumulate to the point of slight preciousness. The story is not purple, but it occasionally strains toward a literary register that doesn't quite fit the domestic horror mode. The "Mita" detail—the childhood nickname—is effectively deployed, but the mechanics of how the entity knows it (heard it on the recording, or found it in Mara's head) is left deliberately vague in a way that works thematically but slightly undermines the horror logic. ORIGINALITY The story is genuinely creative in its approach. Using grief and marital strain as the vector for possession, and making the entity's power lie in its ability to offer emotional resolution, is fresh. The recording as a plot device is well-handled. The story avoids most possession horror clichés. OVERALL This is accomplished literary horror fiction. Its strengths—character, dialogue, restraint, thematic coherence—outweigh its weaknesses. It is not a masterpiece, but it is a very good story. # Brainstorming **Possible babysitters** - A retired stunt driver takes a quiet sitting job for extra cash. When intruders target the child, she turns an ordinary suburban house—and eventually a getaway car—into an obstacle course. - A former getaway driver is trying to stay out of trouble. She knows the crew that comes for the child and understands exactly how far they will go. - A nursing student has no combat skills but is resourceful, stubborn, and excellent under pressure. Her advantage is knowing the family’s routines and the neighborhood better than the intruders do. - A woman once betrayed by the child’s powerful parent accepts the babysitting job under a false name. The attack forces her to choose between revenge and protecting someone innocent. **Possible threats and motives** - A criminal crew mistakes the family home for an easy place to recover stolen evidence. - The parents’ employer sends men to retrieve a drive they believe the child has unknowingly brought home. - A local developer wants the family frightened into silence before they can expose a fatal cover-up. - The attack is personal: someone from the sitter’s past has found her, and the child is caught in the middle. **Possible pulp flavors** - **One-night siege:** fast, claustrophobic action, with each room presenting a new problem. - **Neighborhood chase:** the sitter and child escape the house, only to discover the crew has people watching the streets. - **Crime-noir revenge:** rain, neon, crooked cops, double-crosses, and a sitter whose past makes her more dangerous than anyone expects. - **Darkly comic action:** improvised defenses, criminals arguing over a botched plan, and a babysitter who stays dryly unimpressed by their threats. **Story beats to explore** - Open with the sitter handling an ordinary childcare crisis, establishing competence before any violence begins. - Give the child a distinct personality and a useful skill—perhaps a love of maps, amateur radio, or magic tricks—without making them implausibly fearless. - Let the first intrusion look like a burglary, then reveal a more deliberate objective. - Put the sitter at a disadvantage: no phone, a compromised escape route, and a reason not to trust the police. - Reveal her past in stages, through choices and consequences rather than an explanatory monologue. - Make “revenge” more than retaliation for tonight’s attack: the crew’s leader helped ruin someone’s life years ago. - End with a choice between catching the villain and keeping the child safe. The sitter should earn the revenge by refusing to sacrifice the child for it. **Eight-chapter pacing possibilities** - Chapters 1–2: establish sitter and child; spring the attack; end with the realization that escape will not be simple. - Chapters 3–4: improvised resistance and flight; uncover what the intruders want. - Chapters 5–6: a betrayal or apparent rescue turns dangerous; reveal the sitter’s connection to the villain. - Chapters 7–8: counterattack, reckoning, and an aftermath that acknowledges the cost. # Reflection The strongest version seems to combine the **one-night siege** with a **crime-noir chase**. A whole story confined to one house could become repetitive over roughly 8,000 words, while moving into the neighborhood halfway through would let the danger escalate and give each chapter a different physical objective. A former professional—particularly a getaway driver—fits the pulp promise of “the wrong babysitter.” She can be formidable without being invincible: driving expertise helps during an escape, but it cannot solve a locked door, a frightened child, or a corrupt officer. The nursing student offers a more surprising underdog story, though it may pull the tone away from the larger-than-life revenge implied by the title. A false-name sitter seeking revenge has intrigue, but risks making her decision to babysit feel contrived unless her interest in the family is carefully grounded. The child should matter to the plot rather than function as luggage. A modest, believable contribution—remembering a route, recognizing a voice, or hiding an object—would work better than turning them into a miniature action hero. Their fear can also keep the story honest when the action becomes flamboyant. For a satisfying revenge tale, the antagonists need a concrete wrongdoing beyond choosing the wrong house. A past betrayal tied to the present attack would give the climax emotional weight and make the sitter’s history pay off. That connection should be planted early but explained late enough to preserve momentum. Likewise, a corrupt-police angle creates useful pressure, though too many conspirators could crowd a short story; one compromised officer and one recognizable crew leader would be plenty. At approximately 1,000 words per chapter, each chapter needs one main turn rather than several elaborate set pieces. A useful rhythm would be: **ordinary night disrupted; house breached; escape attempt; discovery; false safety; personal revelation; confrontation; aftermath**. The central promise remains clear throughout: the attackers assume the sitter is an obstacle they can dismiss, and every chapter shows the cost of that mistake.

# Intention **Working title: *The Wrong Babysitter*** This will be a fast, rain-soaked pulp revenge story unfolding over one night in a small industrial city. Its voice will be close third-person, anchored to **Mara Voss**, a former getaway driver who now keeps a low profile and occasionally babysits for her neighbor. The prose will be lean and vivid, with dry humor under pressure. Action will be easy to follow and consequential rather than a string of effortless victories. Mara is watching **nine-year-old Kit Bell** while Kit’s mother works a late shift. A crew breaks in looking for a flash drive Kit’s mother took from her employer, a freight company used to launder money. Their leader, **Dane Rusk**, once abandoned Mara’s younger brother during a botched job and let him take the blame. Mara has wanted to make Rusk answer for years, but she has never gone looking for him. Tonight he brings the fight to her. Kit will be frightened, observant, and resourceful—not an action hero. A local police officer on Rusk’s payroll will close off the obvious route to safety, forcing Mara and Kit out of the house and across the city. The story’s driving question is whether Mara can protect Kit without becoming the reckless person she used to be. Her final victory will come from putting Kit’s safety ahead of a chance to chase Rusk, then using what she has learned to bring him down. At roughly **1,000 words per chapter**, each chapter will have one principal action or revelation and end on a turn that drives the next. I’ll avoid a sprawling conspiracy, extensive backstory, and an ending that treats the violence as cost-free. # Chapter Planning ## Chapter 1 — The Sitter Mara arrives at the Bells’ house for what should be an ordinary evening. Kit tests her with small tricks and questions; Mara wins trust by being candid rather than sweet. Kit’s mother, Elena, leaves for work distracted and asks Mara not to open the door for anyone. After bedtime, a car idles across the street. The lights go out. Someone tries the back door with a key. ## Chapter 2 — Not a Burglary Mara hides Kit and confronts the intruders indirectly, buying time with noise, darkness, and the house’s cramped layout. She realizes they are searching for something specific. A voice on one intruder’s radio says the name “Rusk,” and Mara recognizes it. Her attempt to call for help fails when a responding officer quietly signals to the crew instead. Mara and Kit escape into the rain through the adjoining garage. ## Chapter 3 — The Long Way Out Mara tries to reach a trusted all-night mechanic who owes her a favor. The crew pursues them through residential streets, pushing Mara into a driving maneuver she hoped never to use again. Kit spots a familiar delivery logo on one pursuer’s vehicle and connects it to Elena’s workplace. They reach the mechanic’s shop—but find its doors chained and a message waiting for Mara. ## Chapter 4 — What Elena Took Mara learns that Elena copied freight records tying Rusk’s crew to a fatal warehouse fire and hid the drive inside one of Kit’s belongings before leaving home. Kit remembers which one. Mara also learns Rusk is holding Elena, making simply disappearing impossible. She secures Kit a temporary hiding place with the mechanic and arranges a trade, intending to get Elena back without surrendering the only evidence. ## Chapter 5 — Bad Trade At a shuttered roadside diner, Mara meets Rusk and the compromised officer. The exchange is a trap: Rusk wants the drive, Elena, and Mara silenced. Mara has prepared for deceit, but not for Kit to be found at the mechanic’s shop. The resulting scramble gets Elena free while leaving Mara in Rusk’s hands. Rusk tells her how her brother really died, confirming that he chose to leave him behind. ## Chapter 6 — No Second Passenger Mara escapes custody at a cost, then reunites with Elena and Kit. She has a narrow chance to go after Rusk immediately, but Kit is hurt and terrified, and the corrupt officer still knows where they are. Mara chooses to get them somewhere secure first. In doing so, she notices that the freight records point to a final shipment Rusk cannot afford to lose. Instead of following his trail, she decides to get ahead of him. ## Chapter 7 — Last Run At the freight yard, Mara turns Rusk’s expected getaway route against him. Elena uses her knowledge of the shipping system to expose the records, while the mechanic contacts people outside the compromised officer’s reach. Mara faces Rusk during his attempt to flee. She has the opportunity to kill him, but doing so would jeopardize the evidence and leave Kit waiting for her again. She stops him and keeps him alive to answer for both the warehouse fire and her brother. ## Chapter 8 — Morning Shift Daylight brings investigators, statements, and consequences. The corrupt officer’s involvement is exposed; Elena and Kit are safe but shaken. Mara’s own history cannot stay buried now that she has stepped into the open, and she accepts that uncertainty rather than running. Kit returns a small object Mara lent them on the first night, giving the ending a quiet echo of the opening. Mara has her revenge—not by becoming Rusk, but by making sure he cannot abandon anyone else to take his place.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a Human Writer Might Approach This Prompt “They fucked with the wrong babysitter” is a **pulp promise**, not just a premise. A reader expects bad people to underestimate someone, suffer for it, and discover—preferably in an entertaining, specific way—why they made a terrible choice. A human writer might begin with that emotional transaction rather than with the mechanics of an eight-chapter plot: *What would make me cheer? What would make the babysitter memorable? What kind of revenge would feel nasty, funny, or satisfying enough to justify this title?* They might also be less concerned with making every component “balanced.” The story could be vicious, absurd, sentimental in one unexpected place, or oddly preoccupied with babysitting itself. The best particulars might come from an image or irritation: a child who will only sleep if the hallway light is on; a sitter trying to keep her voice calm while telling an armed man to wipe his shoes; an attacker who thinks “babysitter” means “teenager” and never updates his assessment quickly enough. For roughly 8,000 words, a human writer might anchor the piece around a handful of scenes they *want* to write, then build enough plot to connect them. They may leave some logistics untidy if the emotional and action logic hold. They may also resist explaining the sitter’s entire past. What matters is that her behavior feels particular: what she notices, what angers her, what she will not do in front of a child, and what she does anyway. That does not mean “make it messy” on principle. Pulp needs clean cause and effect so the reader can enjoy each reversal. The useful distinction is between **clarity of action** and **neatness of design**. The first helps this story; too much of the second could make it feel assembled. # Common LLM Approaches That May Not Serve This Story - **Turning the premise into a generic competence reveal.** An LLM may make the babysitter a former soldier, assassin, or getaway driver, then have her execute increasingly perfect maneuvers. That fulfills “wrong babysitter” literally but can drain the premise of surprise. Competence is more satisfying when it has a peculiar shape and real limitations. - **Making every character primarily serve a function.** The child supplies clues, the mother supplies the evidence, the mechanic supplies shelter, the officer supplies a betrayal, and the villain supplies backstory. If their personalities do not create friction beyond those functions, readers can feel the outline underneath the scenes. - **Planting and paying off everything too tidily.** The delivery logo, hidden drive, trusted mechanic, fatal fire, brother’s death, final shipment, and returning keepsake could form a flawless chain. A flawless chain is not automatically gripping. It can make the world seem designed for the protagonist’s arc rather than inhabited by other people. - **Replacing pulp pleasure with moral reassurance.** “She could kill him, but chooses not to” is a familiar resolution that can sound like the story apologizing for its own revenge premise. Restraint might be the right ending, but it should arise from a hard, immediate circumstance or a distinctive choice—not from a generic lesson that revenge is bad. - **Softening consequences without making them specific.** “Safe but shaken,” “at a cost,” and “accepts uncertainty” sound responsible in an outline. On the page, they may become a vague gesture toward realism before everyone receives closure. One concrete consequence is worth more than several abstract ones. - **Writing action as polished trailer copy.** Rain, neon, a freight yard, a shuttered diner, and a last run all belong to pulp, but they can become familiar visual shorthand. The prose could also lean too hard on clipped one-liners, ominous chapter endings, and declarations of what a character “really” is. Readers still need to know where people are standing, what they want, and why the next move works. - **Explaining emotion at the moment it should be felt.** An LLM might follow a sharp action beat with a sentence spelling out its meaning: Mara realizes she is no longer running from her past; Kit understands she can trust her; revenge means protecting the innocent. Those interpretations may be true, but stating them repeatedly would blunt the scenes. # Deep Dive on the Current Intention and Plan ## What Is Already Promising The plan has a strong central pressure: Mara wants an old enemy, but she is responsible for a child *right now*. That gives the revenge plot something to collide with. The one-night structure suits the title’s urgency, and moving from house to streets to freight yard offers a useful escalation of scale. Keeping Kit frightened rather than improbably capable is a good instinct. So is giving Mara a skill—driving—that becomes useful only in certain circumstances. Rusk’s connection to her brother creates a reason the attack is more than a random home invasion. The corrupt officer also prevents the easiest solution from ending the story in chapter two. Those elements provide a workable spine. The main danger is not that the plan lacks plot; it may have **too much well-behaved plot**. ## The Babysitter Could Get Swallowed by the Getaway Driver The title promises *the wrong babysitter*. The outline presently promises *a former getaway driver who happens to be babysitting*. By chapter three, the distinctive setting and relationship risk becoming a vehicle for a familiar criminal-past thriller. Questions worth exploring, without committing to answers yet: - What does Mara do that a capable getaway driver **who is not a babysitter** would fail to do? - Does caring for Kit change her tactics in surprising ways, beyond delaying revenge? - Is she an experienced sitter, or is she awkwardly doing a favor for a neighbor? Both offer different kinds of specificity. - Could ordinary childcare knowledge become tactically important without turning the story into a gimmick? - Does Kit know a version of Mara that Rusk does not—and can that difference influence the confrontation? The strongest version may keep the babysitting relationship active through the final chapters. Otherwise the story’s hook becomes an inciting-job description rather than its central engine. ## Mara Risks Being Familiar Before She Is Particular “Former getaway driver keeping a low profile, with a brother lost to a villain’s betrayal” is serviceable pulp architecture. It is also recognizable. Her dry humor, hidden past, reluctance to become her old self, and eventual choice not to kill Rusk could make her feel like a composite of established action protagonists. Specificity could come from choices less grand than her backstory. How is she at bedtime? What lie does she tell to keep Kit calm, and is she ashamed of it? Does she enjoy driving fast, fear it, or resent that it remains the one thing people value about her? What petty trait survives the crisis—impatience with waste, an inability to remember names, a reflexive insistence on returning borrowed property? Her history matters, but her present-tense habits may do more to make her human. It is also worth asking whether the brother’s death is the most interesting source of revenge. It is a conventional emotional credential for a hard protagonist. Perhaps the plan can complicate it, make Mara partly culpable, or let Rusk’s account be self-serving rather than a neat revelation of “how he really died.” ## Rusk Is Currently More of an Answer Than a Person Rusk orchestrates the attack, betrayed Mara’s brother, holds Elena, springs a trap, supplies the revelation, and tries to flee at the end. Those are useful jobs, but they risk making him an all-purpose villain. If every piece of the night traces cleanly back to him, he can seem omniscient until the plot requires him to lose. His *manner* of underestimating Mara may matter as much as his crimes. Does he recognize her immediately and assume she has gone soft? Does he genuinely fail to recognize her at first? Does he remember their shared history differently? A revenge story benefits when the target can wound the protagonist through his worldview, not just through information he has saved for chapter five. The crew could also have a personality beyond “Rusk’s men.” One impatient intruder, one who realizes this job is going badly, or one who keeps interpreting Mara’s actions incorrectly might make the premise more fun. ## Kit and Elena Need Lives Outside Their Plot Tasks Kit currently tests Mara, recognizes a logo, remembers a hiding place, gets found, gets hurt, and receives a final keepsake. That is a coherent role but a conspicuously useful one. Children are often inconsistent: brave about one thing and distraught over another, observant about something adults dismiss and wrong about something they swear they saw. Giving Kit wants unrelated to the crime might keep them from feeling engineered to unlock plot stages. Elena’s situation deserves scrutiny too. She has copied dangerous records, hidden evidence in her child’s belongings, and gone to work while a crew is after her. What did she believe would happen? If she knowingly exposed Kit, the story should not quietly excuse it because she is the mother who needs rescuing. If she did not know the danger was imminent, the sequence should make that clear. Her choices might put her in meaningful conflict with Mara rather than making her chiefly a hostage and freight-system expert. The mechanic presents a similar opportunity. “Trusted all-night mechanic who owes her a favor” is efficient, perhaps *too* efficient. A human-feeling relationship usually has an inconvenience attached: the favor has expired in the mechanic’s mind, the shop is not a safe place for a child, or Mara has misunderstood what the mechanic can afford to risk. ## The Plot’s Logistics May Be Both Too Busy and Too Convenient The plan includes a break-in, corrupt police response, garage escape, car pursuit, mechanic’s shop, intercepted message, hidden drive, hostage trade, trap, capture, escape, reunion, final shipment, evidence exposure, and freight-yard confrontation. That is a lot of turns for eight chapters of about 1,000 words each. A fast pace is desirable, but each major reversal needs enough room to register. In particular: - **The chapter-three message** could feel like a device for moving Mara toward the next plot station unless its delivery and sender are compelling. - **Kit being found at the shop** risks making Mara’s precautions feel pointless simply because the story needs a new crisis. - **Mara escaping custody** is a major beat currently covered by a few words. If it is easy, Rusk looks inept; if it is hard, it may deserve more room. - **The final shipment** arrives late as a way to furnish a climax. It may need earlier presence in the story’s physical world, even if its importance remains unclear. - **The evidence exposure** could sound simpler than it is. Who receives it, why will they act, and what stops the compromised officer or Rusk from interfering? The story does not need a procedural explanation for every mechanism. It does need the reader to feel that victories result from choices rather than newly revealed infrastructure. ## The Moral Arc Is Coherent but Predictable Mara chooses Kit over immediate revenge; later she chooses to keep Rusk alive. Both choices point to the same conclusion. That clarity may be satisfying, but it could also make the final two chapters feel predetermined. Readers might anticipate the “true revenge is not becoming him” idea long before the confrontation. One possibility to consider is separating the two decisions. Protecting Kit need not automatically make Mara merciful. Keeping Rusk alive might be hateful rather than noble: she wants him identified, convicted, and forced to answer questions. Or she might make a costly choice for Kit earlier, then do something morally uncomfortable later. Pulp can withstand a protagonist whose victory is not a perfectly clean demonstration of growth. The phrase “making sure he cannot abandon anyone else to take his place” gives the ending a polished thematic finish. It may be worth resisting that kind of summary in the eventual prose and trusting a concrete final interaction to carry the meaning. ## The Setting Could Be More Than Pulp Atmosphere “Rain-soaked small industrial city,” “shuttered diner,” and “freight yard” establish genre quickly. They also risk making the location feel like a backdrop assembled from noir components. A human writer might choose one or two unglamorous local realities to puncture the mood: a badly timed road closure, a nearly empty twenty-four-hour pharmacy, a yard whose workers are more worried about losing shifts than criminal intrigue, a diner that closed only last month and still has a handwritten sign on the door. Such details should affect decisions rather than decorate paragraphs. The most convincing city is one that obstructs Mara in its own particular ways. # Ideas to Make the Eventual Story Feel More Human These are possibilities for later consideration, **not revisions to the plan yet**: 1. **Start with a genuine babysitting problem.** Let Mara mishandle some small, ordinary need before proving herself under threat. Being good in a chase should not automatically mean she knows how to comfort a child. 2. **Give the attackers a specific mistaken assumption.** Rather than generally underestimating “a babysitter,” they might think Mara is a teenager, believe she will hand over Kit to save herself, or recognize her and assume her old injury still limits her. The story can then exploit that precise mistake. 3. **Let an improvised tactic fail.** Mara’s first clever move need not work perfectly. Failure creates texture and forces a less elegant decision. 4. **Allow Kit to be inconvenient.** A frightened child might refuse the safest route, tell someone the truth at the wrong moment, or insist on going back for something important only to them. Mara’s responsibility becomes real when she cannot treat Kit like a cooperative piece of equipment. 5. **Make one secondary character refuse their assigned role.** The mechanic may decline the favor; Elena may disagree with Mara’s plan; an intruder may walk away rather than fight. The plot can still progress, but not everyone needs to behave as Mara expects. 6. **Keep some history contested.** Rusk’s account of Mara’s brother could contain a truth Mara hates, a lie she wants to believe, or both. A perfectly clarifying villain confession may be less powerful than an answer that leaves her with something to live with. 7. **Vary the pleasure of each action sequence.** The house intrusion can be tense and quiet; the drive exhilarating but frightening; the trade humiliating; the freight-yard climax ugly and short. If every encounter is a showcase for Mara’s coolness, they will blur. 8. **Find one strange, memorable object.** Pulp often lodges in memory through tangible specifics: a child’s prize from a fair, an enormous raincoat, a cracked rearview mirror, a bag of melting ice. An object can become meaningful through use without announcing itself as a symbol. 9. **Let humor come from people under strain.** Mara’s dry lines will land better if they are occasional and situational. Kit might find something funny that Mara does not, or Rusk might be irritated by a banal inconvenience in the middle of his grand plan. 10. **Make the ending narrower.** The entire criminal enterprise need not be conclusively dismantled by morning. The central wrong can be answered, Kit can survive, and Mara can face a specific consequence without a full institutional cleanup. 11. **Permit an uncomfortable aftertaste.** Revenge may be satisfying while leaving Elena furious, Kit less trusting, or Mara unsure whether she protected her charge as well as she claims. An emotional loose end can give the victory weight. 12. **Protect readability over verbal flourish.** In the eventual draft, short, concrete sentences can carry the action; longer ones can slow down for dread or aftermath. Distinctive prose need not call attention to itself in every paragraph. The central question for a later revision is: **What could happen in this story because Mara is *this particular person babysitting this particular child*, rather than because a skilled action protagonist happened to be in the house?** Answering that through behavior and scene design would do more than any amount of grit, rain, or backstory to fulfill the prompt.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Working title: *The Wrong Babysitter*** This is a compact, one-night pulp revenge story about criminals who assume the woman watching a child will either panic or step aside. **Mara Voss**, a former getaway driver, has been babysitting **nine-year-old Kit Bell** often enough to know the house’s stubborn locks, Kit’s bedtime bargains, and the shortcut through the neighboring yards. She is much less sure how to comfort a frightened child. Her old skill will help, but the reason the intruders have picked the wrong sitter is that Mara knows **this child** and refuses to leave them behind. Mara’s enemy, **Dane Rusk**, leads a small crew seeking freight records copied by Kit’s mother, **Elena**. Years ago, Rusk abandoned Mara’s younger brother during a job and let him take the blame. Mara has avoided him since; this is not a revenge mission she arranged. Rusk recognizes her and assumes the woman who ran then will run again. His mistake is the story’s engine. The revenge should be forceful and satisfying, not an excuse for Mara to deliver a tidy lesson about forgiveness. The story will move through a few clear locations—the Bell house, nearby streets, an all-night mechanic’s shop, and the freight yard—rather than piling on traps and revelations. Elena’s records concern a fatal warehouse fire; the proof exists, but getting it to someone trustworthy is difficult because **one local officer** is working for Rusk. Elena made a dangerous choice in hiding a copy at home, and Mara will not pretend otherwise. Kit is observant but frightened, sometimes helpful and sometimes inconvenient. In roughly **1,000 words per chapter**, each chapter will center on one immediate problem and end with a consequential turn. The voice will be close third-person, plainspoken and sharp, with humor arising from character rather than constant quips. Violence will be swift, spatially clear, and costly. The ending will settle Mara’s confrontation with Rusk and Kit’s immediate safety without claiming that one night cleans up every crime or repairs every relationship. # Chapter Planning ## Chapter 1 — House Rules Elena leaves for a late shift at the freight yard, distracted but unwilling to explain why. Mara’s immediate challenge is getting Kit to bed: Kit wants the hallway light left on and an elaborate promise about what Mara will do if they hear a noise. Mara makes the promise carelessly, then has to decide whether she means it. After Kit falls asleep, Mara notices a man outside who appears to be watching the house. He uses a key on the back door. ## Chapter 2 — The Wrong Woman Mara hides Kit and tries to slip out without a fight. The first intruder assumes she is a disposable witness; Mara injures him but fails to stop him calling for help. Rusk arrives, recognizes Mara, and offers her a chance to walk away. She recognizes him too. When a patrol car pulls up, Mara nearly leads Kit to it—until she sees the officer speak familiarly to Rusk. Using the shortcut Kit showed her weeks earlier, she gets them out through the neighboring yards. ## Chapter 3 — No Good Shortcut Mara reaches her parked car, but the escape is ugly rather than effortless: she loses a pursuer only after damaging the car and frightening Kit badly. They make it to the all-night shop run by **Sol**, a mechanic from Mara’s driving days. Sol will let them in but refuses to hide a child while armed men are searching. Mara calls Elena from Sol’s phone. Elena admits she copied records linking Rusk to a warehouse fire and put the only copy she has in Kit’s schoolbag. Before she can say more, the call cuts off. ## Chapter 4 — The Bag Kit admits the bag is still at home: they took it off to show Mara a drawing before Elena left. Mara wants to go back alone, but Kit insists the bag is not where Mara thinks it is. Their disagreement exposes how much Mara has been treating Kit as cargo. Together they recover it from the Bell house while the crew searches elsewhere. The drive is inside—but so is a note from Elena explaining that Rusk has a shipment leaving the yard before dawn. Mara arranges to pass the evidence to a reporter Elena trusts. Then Rusk calls: he has Elena. ## Chapter 5 — Terms Mara agrees to meet Rusk at a closed roadside diner, with Sol holding the drive and Kit at his shop. She offers herself in exchange for Elena, expecting Rusk to cheat. He does: the corrupt officer has followed her trail to Sol. Mara’s preparation is enough to get Elena clear of the diner, but not enough to keep Kit safe at the shop. When Rusk threatens to have the officer take Kit, Mara gives herself up. Alone with Rusk, she hears his version of her brother’s last night: Rusk left him, but Mara’s brother stayed behind to give her time to escape. Mara cannot tell whether that final detail is true. ## Chapter 6 — One Thing First On the way to the yard, Mara exploits an argument between Rusk and the officer and escapes. She gets back to Sol’s shop expecting it to be empty or worse. Sol and Elena have delayed the officer; Kit is alive, frightened, and furious that Mara promised not to leave them. Mara could pursue Rusk now, but first helps Elena and Sol get Kit to a staffed emergency department, beyond the lone officer’s control. Kit will not accept another sweeping promise. Mara gives a smaller, honest one: she is going to stop the people who came to their house. ## Chapter 7 — Last Run Elena knows which truck carries the shipment; Sol knows a service entrance Mara can reach before it leaves. Elena sends copies of the records to the reporter and a state investigator, but the physical shipment is still Rusk’s way out. At the yard, Mara uses her driving skill to block his escape—not in a flawless chase, but by making a risky move that wrecks her car and leaves her exposed. Rusk tries to blame Mara’s brother for the old job and Elena for the fire. Mara beats him, takes his keys, and leaves him trapped beside the evidence as the yard workers and investigators arrive. She does not spare him to prove a point; she wants him present when people start asking questions. ## Chapter 8 — After the Noise By morning, Rusk is in custody, the officer’s involvement is exposed, and the warehouse records are no longer held by one frightened family. Mara must give a statement that brings her own criminal past into view. Elena thanks her for saving Kit, then demands to know why Mara took Kit back to the house; Mara has no answer that makes it a good decision. Kit, exhausted and guarded, asks whether Mara will babysit again. Mara says Elena gets to decide. The story ends on the battered Bell doorstep, with the hallway light still burning: the child is home, the threat is over for now, and nobody mistakes Mara for an easy target.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Mara Voss Mara, thirty-eight, drove for thieves for most of her twenties. She was good at routes, timing, and keeping her head while everyone else shouted. After her younger brother **Nicky** died on a job with Dane Rusk, she left town for a few years, then came back under her own name, to the annoyance of people who assumed she must be hiding. She now delivers parts for an appliance repair company. The money is ordinary; the fixed hours still feel strange. She began watching Kit when Elena’s childcare arrangement fell through. She was meant to cover one evening. Kit liked that Mara spoke to them as though they could understand bad news, and Elena liked that Mara showed up when she said she would. Neither of them knows much about her old work. Mara knows Kit wants the hall light left on but tells Elena it is because the switch sticks; she thinks Kit would dislike having a fear reported. Mara is reliable in ways that are easy to miss. She checks the car’s fuel level before going inside anywhere, puts a glass of water beside Kit’s bed without being asked, and remembers which houses on the block have dogs. She is also impatient with people who explain things twice. When frightened, she becomes curt enough to sound angry. She finds apologies difficult because she tends to follow them with an explanation of why she did what she did. She is lean, dark-haired, and usually dressed in work trousers and a jacket with one cuff going shiny. She has a small gap between her front teeth. When she listens, she turns her head slightly, as if trying to pick out a sound behind the speaker. Kit has noticed that she drums two fingers against her leg at red lights, then stops when the light changes. Mara wants Kit alive and out of Rusk’s reach. She also wants, with an intensity she has kept quiet for years, to see Rusk unable to talk his way out of what he did to Nicky. Sol is an old friend who knows the ugliest version of her; Elena is a neighbor who trusts the version she sees now. Mara cares what both of them think, though she would deny it. > “I said we’d go if there was trouble. I didn’t say we’d take the front door.” > > *Nicky would have laughed at this car. Then he would have told her exactly how to fix it.* # Kit Bell Kit is nine. They like drawing floor plans of places they know: their house, the school, a grocery store where the frozen-food aisles make no sense to them. The plans include things adults rarely mark, such as the loose board in the Bell porch or the place behind the sofa where a dropped pencil can disappear. Their schoolbag contains folded drawings, pencil stubs, and, because Elena put it there, a flash drive Kit knows nothing about. Kit negotiates at bedtime. They ask for the hall light, then for the door to stay open, then for Mara to say what she will do if someone comes in. Once given an answer, they remember its exact wording. They can be helpful when told a concrete task—count the houses to the corner, hold this, stay where I can see you—but a vague “be brave” irritates them. Under pressure they sometimes go quiet and refuse to move. They hate being picked up without warning. They are small for their age, with a fringe they cut themselves two weeks ago and have defended ever since. Their expressions are frank until they are scared; then they watch people without looking straight at them. They collect elastic bands on one wrist and leave pencil shavings in their pockets. Kit loves Elena and worries when she is late, though they pretend to be interested only in whether she brought food home. They trust Mara because she does not invent cheerful answers. After Mara leaves them at Sol’s shop, that trust is damaged. Kit’s anger is not a lesson for Mara; it is a child remembering what they were promised. > “That isn’t what you said. You said if there was trouble, we’d go *together*.” > > “The bag’s not by the door. Mum moved it because I kept tripping over it.” # Elena Bell Elena is thirty-four and works dispatch at the freight yard. She knows which supervisors actually answer their phones, which drivers swap shifts unofficially, and how often a container number gets copied into the wrong box on a form. That familiarity led her to records that did not add up after a warehouse fire killed two workers. At first she thought someone was covering up negligence. When she found Rusk’s name attached to repeated off-books movements, she made a copy. She hid the drive in Kit’s schoolbag because it was the one thing she was certain would come home. She intended to collect it after her shift and take it to a reporter she had contacted. She did not believe Rusk knew about her yet. She was wrong, and she will not find it comforting when people point that out. Elena is capable and tired. She makes lists on envelopes, loses the envelopes, and can usually recall the lists anyway. She saves the last serving of something Kit likes and eats standing over the sink when she gets home. She is kind to Mara but has not asked many questions about her past; she has had enough of people who treat help as an opening for intimacy. When afraid, she gets practical first and angry later. She has broad shoulders, close-cropped curls, and a work badge whose plastic sleeve has cracked at one corner. She moves quickly until she must make a decision, when she goes still. She often keeps a hand on Kit’s shoulder in crowds; Kit shrugs it off and then walks close beside her. Elena’s first allegiance is to Kit. She also feels responsible to the families of the workers who died, one of whom she knew. She trusts Mara with childcare, not with deciding how much risk Kit should take for the evidence. That distinction remains important even after Mara saves them. > “I thought I had until morning. I know how that sounds now.” > > “You got them out. Thank you. And then you took them back into that house.” # Dane Rusk Rusk is in his mid-forties. He built his freight operation by being useful to people who did not want to know precisely how a shipment got moved. He can make a delayed truck arrive, a missing form appear, or an inconvenient witness feel very alone. He prefers arrangements to threats because arrangements leave fewer people thinking of themselves as his enemies. Years ago, Rusk and Mara drove jobs together. During a botched pickup, he left Nicky behind. Rusk tells the story as though everyone made a choice that night; he uses the same language for the warehouse fire. He may believe parts of his own account. He knows Mara’s driving skill and remembers her leaving after Nicky died, but he has not imagined that staying with a neighbor’s child might make her harder to move than she was for herself. Rusk is tidy without being stylish. He wears a good coat over cheap shirts and keeps a handkerchief in his pocket because the yard leaves grit on every surface. He does not raise his voice when he first grows angry; he starts calling people by their full names. When a plan slips, he checks who is watching before he reacts. He wants Elena’s records and the departing shipment secured. He would rather Mara accept a deal and vanish than force a confrontation, but he will hurt Kit if that is what works. His crew’s loyalty depends on getting paid and believing he has control. The officer is a purchased convenience, not a confidant. > “Mara Voss. I’d heard you were driving washing-machine parts. I hoped somebody was being funny.” > > “I didn’t leave your brother to die. I left a bad job. You know the difference, even if you don’t like saying it.” # Sol Mercado Sol is forty-one and runs an all-night repair shop near the freight district. “All-night” mostly means truck drivers know they can knock on the side door and find him asleep in the office. He met Mara when both worked around stolen cars: she drove them, and he made them look less recently stolen. He stopped before she did, partly because he wanted the shop to survive an inspection and partly because he had grown tired of wondering who was in the boot. Sol knows Mara will keep driving a damaged car long after anyone sensible would pull over. He is fond of her, but his shop is not a safe house, and he resents being treated as though a shared past obliges him to risk his livelihood whenever hers catches up with her. He lets Mara and Kit in because Kit is standing there wet and shaking. He still tells Mara no when she asks him to keep the child while she goes after Rusk. Sol is solidly built, with a stiff left knee and a grease mark he habitually makes worse by trying to rub it away. He wears reading glasses on a cord and has to put them on to see a phone screen, even when someone is threatening him over it. He talks while working but falls silent when he is deciding whether to trust someone. He wants his business intact, Mara alive, and Kit nowhere near the danger. Those wants stop fitting together. He will help, though not always in the way Mara asks, and he will expect her to remember that he had a choice. > “I’ll fix your car. I’ll make a call. I am not a fort with a tire sign on it.” > > “You used to ask before you brought trouble through my door.” # Officer Cal Hearn Cal Hearn is a local patrol officer in his early fifties. Rusk first paid him for information about inspections and complaints near the yard. Hearn told himself that was different from helping anyone get hurt; by the time he had reason to reconsider, Rusk knew enough to ruin his career. The money still helps with bills, and Hearn no longer bothers pretending he takes none of it. He likes being regarded as the reasonable person in a room. He speaks gently to frightened people and expects that tone to count in his favor, even while he blocks the door they need. He is not eager to fight Mara. He would prefer to make her believe cooperating is the safest choice, then tell himself whatever follows was out of his hands. Hearn is heavy around the middle, with a careful haircut and boots polished more often than his patrol car is cleaned. He rests his thumbs on his belt when he talks. # Chapter 1 — House Rules The first thing Kit asked was whether Mara had brought the good bread. “The bread’s bread,” Mara said. “That means no.” “It means I forgot.” Kit stepped back from the doorway to let her in. “Mum bought it.” “That’s different.” “It’s in the cupboard.” Elena came out of the kitchen wearing her work coat, one arm caught in its lining. She had been called in two hours early and looked as though she’d spent both of them trying to locate something important. Her badge was clipped upside down. “Sorry,” she said to Mara. “I’ll be back after six.” “You said five,” Kit told her. “I know. I’m sorry.” Mara took her boots off. The Bell house had pale carpet in the hall and a back door that stuck unless you lifted the handle before turning the key. She knew this because she’d been coming here most Thursdays for nine months, and because Elena always forgot to tell new people. “There’s pasta in the fridge,” Elena said. “Kit ate already, but—” “I can find food.” Elena nodded without hearing her. She checked her phone, then patted her coat pockets. “Keys,” Kit said. “Fruit bowl.” “I know where they are.” Kit led Mara into the kitchen while Elena went to retrieve them. On the table lay a drawing of the house in colored pencil. Kit had included the narrow space between the garage and the neighbors’ fence, marked with an arrow. “What’s that for?” Mara asked. “Mr. Alden put his bins there. You can’t get through now unless you go sideways.” “Useful information.” “You always say that.” Elena returned with her keys and looked at the drawing. “Have you done your spelling?” “Nearly.” “That means no,” Mara said. Kit gave her a look of betrayal. Elena’s mouth twitched, but she was already reaching for the door. “Don’t open up for anyone,” she said to Mara. “I don’t usually.” “I mean it.” Mara glanced at her. Elena held the keys so tightly their teeth had marked her palm. “Okay,” Mara said. Elena crouched to kiss Kit’s forehead. Kit tolerated it, then watched from the hall as she walked to her car. Elena stopped halfway down the path and looked back at the house. She raised a hand. Kit raised one too. When her car was gone, Kit said, “She’s being weird.” “She’s late for work.” “She’s late for work all the time.” Mara had no answer to that. She went into the kitchen and opened the fridge. Two containers of pasta, half a pepper, and a bottle of milk with a date she didn’t trust. She took the pasta. Kit finished the spelling at the table while Mara ate standing up. At eight-thirty they argued about washing, at nine about teeth, and at nine-fifteen about the hall light. “It stays on,” Kit said. “Your mother said lights out.” “She means my light.” “Convenient distinction.” “That’s what she means.” Mara left the hall light on. Kit got into bed with a folded drawing tucked under the pillow. There were pencil shavings caught in the cuff of their pajama top. “Your bag for tomorrow?” Mara asked. “Done.” “Spelling sheet in it?” Kit stared at her. Mara held out a hand. Kit surrendered the sheet, and Mara put it by the bedroom door. She was nearly out when Kit said, “If somebody comes in, what do we do?” “Somebody like who?” “I don’t know. Somebody.” “We go.” “Where?” “Out the back, if we can. Through Mr. Alden’s bins.” “You’re too big to fit.” “I’ll turn sideways.” Kit considered this. “Together?” “Together.” “You promise?” Mara had promised things before to make the next ten minutes easier. She knew Kit would remember every word. “Yes,” she said. From downstairs came the small settling click of a cooling radiator. Kit pulled the blanket to their chin. Mara went down to rinse her fork. She locked the back door, lifting the handle until the bolt caught, and checked the front. In the living room she found a remote, turned the television on low, and watched half a program about people repairing a fishing boat. She couldn’t have said what needed fixing. At ten-thirty, headlights washed across the ceiling. They paused, moved on, then came back. Mara got up and looked through the front curtain. A dark car had stopped across the street, three houses down. Its engine was running. She could make out one person in the driver’s seat. She let the curtain fall. Cars stopped there. People got lost, checked addresses, waited for somebody to come out. She carried her glass into the kitchen. The car was still there five minutes later. Mara switched off the television. Upstairs, Kit’s bedroom door was open the agreed few inches, hall light shining through. She took her phone from her pocket and checked the screen. Two bars. At the back of the house, something scraped against brick. Mara stood in the kitchen with her glass in her hand. The noise came again: metal against metal, quiet and deliberate. She set the glass on the counter and went to the doorway, where she could see the back door without standing in front of it. A man filled the frosted pane. His face was only a blur. He had one hand at the lock. Mara looked toward the stairs. Kit had finally gone to sleep. She could hear nothing from their room. The man inserted a key. It turned halfway and stopped. He tried again, harder. The handle dropped, but Mara had lifted it when she locked up; the bolt stayed in its frame. For a moment the man did not move. Then he raised his head toward the dark kitchen. Mara stepped back before he could make her out through the glass. Upstairs, a floorboard creaked. Kit was awake. The key began to turn again.

He was young, with rain flattened against his hair and a cut on his palm from the window. “Where’s the kid’s bag?” Mara tightened her grip on the rail. He noticed. “You the sitter? He caught the end before she could swing again and yanked. She let go; when he came forward, she shoved the table at him. He shouted into the radio clipped to his coat. “She’s here. Mara ran to the stairs. Behind her, the man shoved the table away, limping after her. She reached the landing, grabbed Kit’s hand as they crawled out from beneath the bed, and pulled them toward the bathroom. “You said stay there,” she whispered. “He was yelling.” Fair enough. The bathroom window opened over the garage. Its latch was stiff; Mara forced it with both hands. She looked down. A rain barrel stood under the sill, beside the lower roof. She climbed out first, crouching on the slippery tiles, and reached back for Kit. They were halfway through when a car door slammed out front. A man called from the street, “Mara.” Kit froze. “Keep coming,” Mara said. The voice rose again. “I know you’re in there.” She got Kit onto the roof and shut the window behind them. Kit’s trainers slid on the wet surface. Mara caught their coat and guided them along the wall, away from the edge. Downstairs, the front door opened.
