# Chapter 2 — The First Bite By morning the rags beneath the shutter had gone gray. Ivo crouched beside them without touching. “They’ve caught powder. That’s something.” “Something good?” Mara asked. “Something we can see.” Ruth had wedged the delivery shutter shut with two lengths of shelving. The dead mutant remained on the other side. Mara could smell it through the gap whenever the stove went out. At breakfast they drank hot water. Nell carried her cup into the front room, where Ruth was fitting a new pin to the window shutter. The sharp taps of metal on metal continued after Mara had finished hers. She went to the back door. The piece of foreleg still lay on the tile where the shutter had severed it. Its dark outer plate had curled away overnight, exposing a pale, dense interior. Mara fetched an empty tin and eased it over the piece. Ivo looked up from his notes. “What are you doing?” “Keeping flies off.” “There aren’t any flies yet.” “Then it’ll be ready for them.” He watched her. Mara left the tin in place. She had been hungry often these past months. Usually hunger made her thoughts smaller: water, fuel, the next place they might search. This morning she kept returning to the smell. She knew the difference between meat going bad and meat on a hot griddle. She knew as well that this flesh was unlike anything she had cooked. “We could try it,” she said. Ivo took his pencil from behind his ear. “You haven’t even seen what’s under that plate.” “That’s why I said ‘could.’” They took the tin into the old washroom, where there was a drain and a narrow window that opened onto a blank brick wall. Mara found a bent boning knife she had once used to trim ham for sandwiches. Ruth came when she heard them gathering things and stood in the doorway. “No,” she said. Mara laid the knife on the sink. “We’re looking at it.” “You’ve got a pan.” “I’ve got a pan because the kitchen has one pan we can spare.” Ruth looked at Ivo. “I can’t tell her it’s safe,” he said. “I also can’t tell her the flesh will do what the spores do.” “That ought to settle it.” Mara turned the tin over and let the foreleg fall into the sink with a heavy slap. Ruth flinched. A ridge of small dark nodules ran along its outer plate. Mara could not tell whether they were spore sacs, joints, or simply the way the creature grew. “We leave anything near those,” Ivo said. “And anything from the end that touched the passage floor.” “How much does that leave?” “We’ll find out.” Ruth stayed. When Mara had difficulty holding the slippery limb steady, Ruth pinned it with a pair of tongs. Her grip was firm; she looked past Mara’s shoulder while Mara cut. Beneath the plate the flesh came apart in fibrous layers. It bled a thin, clear liquid. Mara cut a cube no larger than her thumbnail from the center, away from the nodules and the severed end. She set it in a chipped saucer. “We should throw the rest away,” Ruth said. “We might,” Mara replied. Ruth released the tongs. “You might.” They carried the saucer to the kitchen. Nell appeared from the front room before Mara had lit the stove. “I want to watch,” she said. “You can.” “Am I allowed to say what I think?” “You’re unlikely to ask permission either way.” Nell folded her arms and stayed beside the door. Mara heated the pan until a drop of water skated across it. There was no oil. She added a little saved drippings from the bottom of a jar, then the cube of flesh. It hissed. The smell rose at once, rich and earthy, like the panfuls of mushrooms she had cooked for autumn pies. Mara pressed it flat with a spoon so the center would heat through. She turned it three times. By the time she slid it onto the saucer, its edges had browned. Ivo placed his pencil on the table. “Let it cool.” “It won’t take long.” “I know.” Mara waited until she could pick it up. Everyone was looking at her. Ruth stood nearest the back door, her hands still marked where the tongs had pressed into them. “If you’re ill,” Ivo said, “tell me when you first notice anything. Even if it seems minor.” Mara nodded. She put the piece in her mouth. The browned edge cracked between her teeth. Inside, it was tender and substantial, with a deep, nutty flavor that the little dab of drippings could not account for. She had meant to chew once and swallow quickly. Instead she kept it on her tongue. “Well?” Nell asked. Mara swallowed. Her empty stomach clenched around the mouthful, then settled. “It tastes good.” “Good for something you found under a door,” Nell said, “or good?” Mara looked at the saucer. A spot of juice had cooled on its rim. “Good,” she said. Ruth went to the sink and washed her hands, though she had never touched the flesh. Nell asked what it tasted like and rejected each comparison Mara tried. Ivo wrote down the time. Then he moved the remaining foreleg, still under its tin, onto the cold ledge outside the washroom window. They agreed to wait until morning before anyone ate more. Ivo checked Mara’s eyes and temperature that afternoon. Ruth took the first watch at the rear shutter. Nell, assigned the front, came back twice to ask whether Mara felt strange. By evening Mara was tired, hungry, and impatient with being examined. She washed the pan herself. A thin browned patch remained where the little cube had rested. She loosened it with water and tipped it down the drain before she could taste it.

# Chapter 3 — The Plate At dawn, Ivo woke Mara by putting the back of his hand against her forehead. She opened her eyes. “You could ask.” “You were asleep.” “I’m awake now.” “No fever.” He sat back on his heels. “Any headache? Nausea? Tingling?” “Hungry.” “I expected that.” Mara pushed herself up from the folded blankets. Ruth had already lit the stove. Nell sat nearby with her oversized coat on, holding a cup in both hands. When Mara came in, Nell looked her over before saying good morning. “Well?” she asked. “Still me.” “That’s what you’d say if you weren’t.” “You can test me on the bread prices.” “We haven’t had bread prices in months.” “Then it’s a poor test.” Nell smiled, briefly. On the table lay the boning knife, wrapped in a rag, and the tin that held the rest of the foreleg. Ruth set down her cup. “I thought we agreed to wait until morning.” “We did,” Mara said. “Morning isn’t a medical finding.” “No,” Ivo said. “She could still get sick. We all know that.” Ruth looked at each of them in turn. Nell held her cup to her mouth without drinking. “I’m not stopping you,” Ruth said. “I want to know how much you mean to cook.” Mara lifted the tin. “Only what we can take from the middle without touching those nodules.” “There’s hardly any middle.” “There’s enough for four tastes.” Nell put down her cup. “You had a taste. I want a piece I can chew.” They took the foreleg back to the washroom. Ivo tied on his cloth mask, then checked that Mara’s covered her nose. He drew a rough outline of the limb on the back of an old flour order and shaded the areas they would not use. He left a generous margin around the dark nodules. It was more meat than Mara wanted to discard; she cut where he marked. Ruth held the tongs again. This time she watched the knife. Nell waited in the doorway with a clean plate, shifting her weight from foot to foot. When Mara had cut three pieces, Nell took the plate without being asked and carried it to the stove. “We should wash this room before we eat,” Ivo said. “We will,” Mara replied. He looked at the knife in her hand. She laid it in the tin beside the scraps. He picked up a rag and started with the sink while she washed her hands. Mara heated a spoonful of drippings in the pan. She had saved salt in a paper packet at the bottom of a flour jar. She used half of what remained, rubbing it into the meat before it went over the heat. Three pieces made the kitchen smell full of dinner. Nell came to stand at Mara’s elbow until she was asked to set the table. “I know how to do this,” Nell said. “I know you do.” “You keep telling me anyway.” Mara turned the first piece. Its surface had browned, but the thick center needed longer. She lowered the heat and put a lid over the pan. They ate from the chipped blue plate Ada had given Mara years ago. Its crack ran through a painted pear near the rim, and Mara always set it down gently. Today she cut each cooked piece into smaller portions on the board, then brought the plate to the table. Nell counted them. Mara waited while she chose first. Ivo took one bite and reached for the salt packet. “I used it,” Mara said. “I noticed. I’d like more.” “That’s the last of it.” He set the packet down. “Then I’ll manage.” The meat was softer than the sample Mara had tried, its juices caught under the lid. It tasted even better with salt. Nell ate her portion quickly, then used a crust of yesterday’s bread to collect what had run onto the plate. She caught Mara watching and pushed the plate toward Ruth. Ruth cut her piece in half. She ate one half, looking down. After a long while she picked up the other. “Well?” Nell asked. “It’s meat.” “You know what I mean.” Ruth chewed and swallowed. “Yes, I do.” Ivo asked whether anyone objected to his taking a remaining piece. Nell pointed out that he had already reached for it. He took the piece and, after eating it, wrote down the time beside each of their names. Mara knew he would check them all in the night. There was a little laughter when Ivo tried to describe the flavor for his notes and came up with “rather good.” Mara laughed too. She had coaxed something worth eating from a scrap nobody had wanted to touch. For a few minutes, she sat back and let herself enjoy their empty plates. Then Ruth carried the blue plate to the sink. Mara heard her scrub the pear with more force than it needed. They cleaned the washroom together. The noduled scraps went into two tins with tight lids. Ruth insisted they keep them outside the window until they could dispose of them away from the bakery. The safe-looking meat left in the foreleg amounted to less than Mara had hoped; she cooked it that evening and divided it without argument. After supper, Nell found a place for Ivo’s notes inside the old recipe ledger. “Don’t put them near the food pages,” Mara said. “There aren’t any clean pages left.” “Use the back.” Nell turned the ledger over and tucked the paper inside its cover. Mara considered asking her to take it out, then went to help Ruth check the shutters instead. At the front window, Ruth raised one board a finger’s width. Rain shone on the street. A low shape moved past the corner, followed by another. Both stopped beside the drain where Mara had poured away the pan water. Ruth lowered the board slowly. “How many?” Mara whispered. “Two that I saw.” Behind them, Ivo was putting the pan away. Nell asked whether they could cook another piece tomorrow. Mara looked at the dark gap beneath the shutter until the second shape moved on.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter demonstrates considerable craft and restraint. The model has executed the chapter plan faithfully and with genuine skill, producing a piece that earns its tonal register through specific, concrete detail rather than declaration. The chapter opens with Ivo's medical check—a practical, character-revealing gesture that immediately establishes the stakes without belaboring them. The exchange between Mara and Nell about testing her identity ("That's what you'd say if you weren't") is sharp, economical, and genuinely funny in a way that feels earned rather than inserted for levity. This is the kind of dialogue that reveals character through texture rather than exposition. The characters are handled with notable fidelity to their profiles. Ivo's caution is present but not paralyzing—he draws the margin on the flour order, he writes down the times, and then he asks for seconds. This is exactly the character described: someone who cannot stand apart from the decision he won't fully endorse. Nell's counting of portions, her impatience, her use of the bread crust to collect the juices—all of this is specific and consistent. Ruth's behavior is the most nuanced: she eats both halves of her piece, refuses to call it good when Nell does, and then scrubs the blue plate's painted pear "with more force than it needed." That last detail is the chapter's best moment—it shows Ruth's conflict without naming it, and the choice of the blue plate (Ada's gift) as the vessel for this meal is quietly devastating. The blue plate detail is particularly well-handled. The crack through the painted pear, the gentleness with which Mara always sets it down, and then Ruth scrubbing it hard—this is the kind of layered, earned symbolism that doesn't announce itself. It works because it's grounded in the physical world of the story. The ending is effective: the shapes at the drain where Mara poured the pan water, the implication that the smell of their cooking has drawn attention, Nell asking about tomorrow's meal while Mara watches the dark gap. This closes the chapter on exactly the right note of cozy-horror tension—warmth and threat coexisting without melodrama. Some minor weaknesses: the washroom cleaning sequence is slightly procedural and loses a little momentum. The line "Three pieces made the kitchen smell full of dinner" is a nice construction but sits slightly awkwardly in the sentence rhythm. The chapter is perhaps slightly thin on Mara's internal conflict—the plan called for her to feel "absurdly pleased that they like her cooking" while also being troubled, and while this is present, it could be slightly more developed. The moment where she "sat back and let herself enjoy their empty plates" is good but brief. The dialogue throughout is strong—it reveals character, advances the scene, and avoids the twin pitfalls of being either too on-the-nose or too oblique. Ruth's "It's meat" followed by "Yes, I do" is exactly right. Ivo's "rather good" for his notes is a small, perfect comic beat. The prose is clean and controlled. There is no purple prose, no forced metaphor, no poetic riffing that doesn't land. The writing is confident in its restraint. The cozy-horror register is maintained throughout: the warmth of the meal, the ordinary complaints about salt, the laughter—all set against the shapes moving past the window at the end. The chapter follows its plan closely: Mara remains well, Ruth eats but objects when Nell calls it good, Ivo asks for more salt, Nell reaches for seconds, and the smell of cooking draws movement to the street. All plan elements are executed. # Chapter 4 — The Price of Seconds Nell had found the route in January, when the drains were frozen and the creatures kept to their cellars. It took them through the barber’s shop, up a stairwell, across two roofs, and down into the loading yard behind Fenwick Street. “You went there alone?” Mara asked. “I came back.” “That’s an answer to a different question.” Nell tightened a length of cord around her coat cuff. Ruth, sitting by the stove, snorted. “I told her not to go,” she said. “She didn’t tell me where she’d been until afterward.” Mara looked from one to the other. Nell kept working on the cuff. They had spent the morning making a snare from laundry line, a bent length of shelving, and the pulley Ruth had taken off a flour hoist. The plan was to catch one mutant by a hind leg and pull the line from the upper loading dock. If it stopped moving, they would go down to it. If it did not, they would leave. Ivo said they should wait another day after eating the meat. Nell asked what they would eat while they waited. He packed his notes away. Ruth refused to leave the bakery undefended. She helped them test the pulley twice, then handed Mara a pack lined with an old raincoat. “Don’t fill it just because there’s room,” she said. “I won’t.” Ruth looked at her for another moment. “If something comes after you, drop it.” Outside, Nell led them through the barber’s shop. The mirrors had cracked in the cold; Mara saw three hunched figures pass through them before they reached the stairs. On the roof, she could see the front of her bakery two blocks away. She had never looked at it from above. One shutter sat crooked where Ruth’s new pin held it in place. They crossed to the loading yard over a plank Nell had found and hidden beneath loose roofing felt. At the far end of the yard, a mutant scraped along the wall where rainwater ran from a broken pipe. It was smaller than the one at the bakery, though its back plates stood higher. It stopped to rub its flank against the bricks. Nell pointed to a narrow strip of ground between two broken pallets. Mara and Ivo lowered the snare there. The mutant eventually circled toward it, head low, nosing through a drift of wet paper. Its hind foot caught. Nell pulled the line taut from the dock while Mara hauled on the pulley. The creature fell sideways and thrashed. “Keep it off the pallets,” Ivo said. Mara pulled harder. A plate on the creature’s back opened, and a low sigh came out of it. Nell’s hands slipped an inch along the cord. Ivo brought the bent shelving down on the creature’s head. He had to strike twice. Afterward he stood looking at the shelving in his hands, rain dripping from its end. They waited. The mutant did not move again. Up close, its outer plates smelled of wet bark and something sharp. Ivo pointed out three spore sacs along its underside. All appeared intact. Mara held the pack open while Nell cut a thick section from a hind leg, working from where the snare had torn the outer plate. It took longer than Mara expected. Nell’s knife kept meeting tough fibers, and they had to shift the body to reach them. As they lifted the cut piece, Nell stopped. A pale streak of powder marked its underside. “That one’s split,” she said. Ivo knelt. Beneath a fold of plate, one small sac had been crushed by the fall. He held his hand over the meat without touching it. “Leave the piece.” “We can cut higher,” Mara said. “Perhaps. Not here.” “There’s clean flesh above it.” “There might be.” Nell was still holding the weight of the leg. “I can cut another section.” “We’ve spent half an hour on this one,” Mara said. “Give me the knife.” She took it and cut well above the streak. Ivo asked her to move farther back. She did, though it left only a narrow strip worth packing. By then Nell had begun looking toward the alley entrance. “Mara,” she said. A reply came from beyond the yard: a low breathy sound, then claws against the paving stones. They gathered the tools. Mara put the strip in Ruth’s pack and folded the raincoat lining over it. She could smell the cut flesh through the cloth. The living mutant entered the yard as they reached the dock stairs. It went straight to the carcass, its plates lifting. “Go,” Ivo said. Nell led them up, across the plank, and through the stairwell. Mara’s pack struck every other step. In the barber’s shop Ivo shoved an old chair under the outside door handle. It broke as something hit the door from the street. They ran the remaining block. By the time they reached the bakery, Mara’s breath rasped against her damp mask. Ruth opened the front shutter a crack, saw them, and pulled the door wide enough to let them through. She dropped the bar into place behind Ivo. “What happened?” she asked. “Another one followed us.” “From the yard?” Mara nodded. She set the pack on the floor, careful not to let it touch the counter. A sound came from the street. Claws clicked on the pavement, paused, then moved along the wall toward the front window. Ruth reached for the bent pin she had replaced that morning and checked that the new one held. “You brought meat?” she asked. “A little.” Ruth looked at the pack. Mara caught the savory smell from its lining and wished, too late, that she had left it in the yard.

[Analysis] Chapter 4 of this cozy-horror post-apocalyptic story demonstrates considerable craft and discipline. Let me assess it across multiple dimensions. **Narrative Execution and Plot** The chapter follows its plan closely: Nell reveals the route, the group hunts, they encounter a damaged spore sac, Mara insists on cutting around it (her moment of dangerous desire for a larger haul), and a living mutant pursues them back to the bakery. The plan specified that "their delay lets a living mutant follow the scent of the injured one" and that "they escape with meat, but the pursuer reaches the bakery before they can secure the entrance." The chapter delivers this faithfully, though the mutant doesn't quite breach the bakery in this chapter—that's reserved for Chapter 5, which is appropriate pacing. **Character Consistency** The characters are rendered with precision against their profiles. Ivo's cautious hedging ("Perhaps. Not here." / "There might be.") is perfectly calibrated to his profile's flaw of making caution sound like judgment. Nell's competence and practicality shine through her route-finding and her calm observation of the approaching mutant. Ruth's brief appearance—handing over the pack, her warning "If something comes after you, drop it"—is economical but characterful. **Dialogue** The dialogue is one of the chapter's strongest elements. "I came back." / "That's an answer to a different question." is sharp and reveals character efficiently. Ruth's "Don't fill it just because there's room" is exactly her voice. The mirror image—"three hunched figures pass through them"—is the one moment that edges toward the poetic, but it earns its place as a genuinely unsettling image that doesn't overstay its welcome. **Tension and Pacing** The hunt sequence is well-paced. The final image—Mara catching the savory smell from the pack's lining and wishing "too late, that she had left it in the yard"—is an excellent closing beat that captures the story's central horror: the appetite that persists even when it's dangerous. **Weaknesses** The chapter is competent to excellent throughout, but it rarely surprises. The beats unfold as expected: hunt goes mostly well, complication arises, they escape with consequences. The mutant's behavior (going straight to the carcass, plates lifting) is described efficiently but the creatures remain somewhat abstract. The emotional texture, while present, doesn't quite reach the depth the character profiles promise—Ruth's grief, Nell's fear of being sent away, Mara's complicated pride—these are gestured at rather than fully inhabited. The chapter is doing necessary plot work, which limits its emotional range somewhat. The line "She had never looked at it from above. One shutter sat crooked where Ruth's new pin held it in place" is a nice grounding detail, but the roof crossing generally feels slightly rushed compared to the careful attention given to the hunt itself. **Overall** This is skilled, disciplined genre writing. It executes its plan faithfully, maintains character consistency, avoids the common pitfalls of purple prose and forced metaphor, and delivers genuine tension. Its limitations are those of a middle chapter doing necessary work rather than failures of craft. # Chapter 5 — The Front Room The creature touched the shutter with the tips of its claws. Ruth lifted one finger to her lips. Ivo stood by the barred door, still holding the iron shelving from the yard. Nell had stopped just inside the front room. Rain ran off her coat onto the floor. Something dragged across the boards. Then the creature struck hard enough to knock the new pin loose. Ruth caught it before it hit the tiles. “Back kitchen,” she whispered. Mara lifted the pack. Its lining had folded open, and the meat lay close to the top. She tucked the raincoat around it and followed Nell between the display counters. Behind her, Ruth pushed the pin into place again. The next blow drove it out of her hand. A gap appeared between two shutter boards. Through it Mara saw a strip of dark plate, then a pale sac pressed against the wood. “Ruth!” “I see it.” Ruth jammed the shelving end against the board. Ivo came to help her. The creature pushed inward, slowly at first. Mara pulled Nell toward the kitchen door, but Nell caught the corner of the pack. “Don’t let it touch the counter,” Nell said. “I’m trying not to.” A claw punched through the shutter. Ivo struck it with the shelving. The creature recoiled, wrenching the board outward, and the shelving flew from his hands. Ruth hauled on the inside brace, trying to bring the loose board back against the frame. Mara turned to help her. The pack slid off her shoulder and hit the old display counter. Nell grabbed for the strap. It tore from the side seam. The meat and several loose scraps spilled over the wood. Mara saw a puff of pale dust rise from one of the scraps—the piece she had thought she’d left behind when she cut above the damaged sac. Nell reached toward it. “Hands off,” Ivo said. Nell stopped. The claw came through the gap again, opening and closing. Ruth got the brace across the shutter. “Mara, the door.” Mara ran to the bakery entrance. She drew back its bolt a fraction, enough to lift the iron latch from inside, then slammed it. The noise drew the creature away from the window. Its weight landed against the door instead. Ruth used the moment to ram the pin home while Ivo wedged the broken shelving across the two loose boards. The creature struck the door twice. The bar bowed but held. From the back of the room, Nell called, “It’s going.” Mara listened. Claws scraped along the threshold, moved toward the drain, and dwindled down the street. They stayed where they were until Ruth’s arm began to shake from holding the brace. Ivo took it from her. A thin line of daylight showed beside the damaged board. “Kitchen,” Ruth said. “All of us.” “We have to deal with that,” Mara said, pointing to the counter. “From the kitchen. With cloths over our faces.” They shut the kitchen door and packed its lower gap with damp rags. Ruth rolled the stool against it. Mara had last used the front counter to sort fuel scraps. She could see it through the door’s glass pane, with Nell’s torn pack hanging from one corner and the meat scattered across the surface where she once put loaves to cool. Ivo checked their hands. Nell had a shallow scrape on one knuckle from the pack buckle. He washed it while she complained that it had not even bled. “That piece was clean when I packed it,” Mara said. “The dusty one?” Ivo asked. “I thought I’d cut past the sac.” Nell pulled her hand away as soon as Ivo was finished. “We could have had all of that.” “No,” Ruth said. “We had it. Then it came through the window.” “We can wash the counter.” “We will wash the counter.” “And the meat?” Ivo looked toward the glass. “I wouldn’t eat anything that fell out of the pack.” “You didn’t see where every piece landed.” “I saw enough.” Nell turned to Mara. Mara remembered the pale puff above the display wood. “We leave it,” she said. Nell’s mouth tightened. “I carried that from the yard.” “I know.” “You told me to keep hold of it.” “I know.” Ruth drew a chair up to the kitchen door and sat down. “You could have left it at the yard.” Mara looked at the floor. Mud from their boots had dried in small half-moons beside the stove. “I cut away from the sac.” “You stayed to cut. That thing got here because you stayed.” “We didn’t know it would follow.” “You heard another one come into the yard.” “I thought we’d lose it on the roofs.” Ruth leaned forward. “You thought a lot of things for all of us.” No one answered her. Ivo covered the water barrel, though its lid was already on. Nell picked up a chipped cup and put it down again. They ate nothing that evening. Ivo said they could clean the front room once the street had been quiet long enough; Ruth said the loose shutter needed repair first. After dark, he fetched their blankets from the upper landing and they spread them on the kitchen floor. Nell curled up beside the stove without taking off her coat. Mara sat with her back against the pantry door. Through the glass pane she could make out the old counter, pale where years of customers’ elbows had worn the wood. The meat was still there. She wanted to retrieve it badly enough to stand up once. Ruth, sitting in the chair, watched her until she sat down again.

# Chapter 6 — A Name for Dinner By morning, the meat on the display counter had darkened at the edges. Mara could see it through the kitchen door whenever someone passed the glass. Ivo made a list on the back of a flour order: water, fuel, intact jars, rags. Nell read it over his shoulder. “You forgot food,” she said. “There isn’t any to count.” “Then put a zero.” He wrote *food: 0*. Nell went to sit beside the stove. They waited until the street had been quiet for an hour before opening the kitchen door. Ruth had shown them how to remove the brace from the damaged shutter without letting the loose board swing in. She fixed the board while the others cleaned, keeping her knee braced against the wall. None of them crossed the strip of floor below the broken pane until she said it would hold. Mara put on a damp cloth mask and went to the counter. The largest piece of meat had fallen where she used to set out the breakfast buns. She scraped it into a tin without touching it. Nell held the tin steady. Neither of them spoke until all the scraps were inside. “Where does it go?” Nell asked. “Out the front,” Mara said. “Not near the drain,” Ruth called. They carried it down the block in the afternoon, when the rain eased. Ivo tipped the scraps into a deep rubbish pit behind the barber’s shop. Mara stood back and watched him cover the tin’s contents with rubble. She had spent most of the morning wanting to save them. Seeing them on the ground did not change that. Back at the bakery, they scrubbed the counter with hot water and the last of the harsh soap Ruth had found in the laundry. Mara made Nell wash the seams of the torn pack. Nell did it thoroughly, then held it up by its loose strap. “This can be sewn.” “After it’s dry,” Mara said. “After we have something worth carrying in it,” Nell replied. The front room smelled of soap and wet wood. Mara opened the little hatch in the kitchen wall to let steam escape. Once, she had passed cups of tea through it to customers who sat at the counter. Now it faced the room they were still reluctant to use. At the table, Ivo laid out his notes. He had recorded the first bite, every meal, and every complaint of headache or stomach pain. There were none. “We’ve been lucky,” he said. “Have we?” Nell asked. “Or can we eat it?” “We’ve eaten part of one creature. We left the sacs alone as best we could. Cooking it may have helped. I can’t say which of those mattered, or whether we’ll find out something else later.” “So we do what we did,” Mara said. “As carefully as we can.” Ruth sat on her stool, rubbing dried soap from a knuckle. “And where do we get the next one?” No one answered at once. “Not Fenwick,” Nell said. “The thing followed the scent from the cut one. We’d never make it home carrying a full pack.” “We could catch one closer,” Mara said. Ruth looked at her. “It was close yesterday.” “I mean without going out after it.” She gestured toward the delivery passage. Ruth had driven a creature off that morning while they worked at the front. The shutter and shelving had held; the passage beyond it remained sealed and filthy. They had not gone in to clean the burst sac. Nell stood and examined the hatch. “We could work the shutter from here.” “Through the serving hatch?” Mara asked. “Run a rope above it. The pulley’s still here. We’d pull from the kitchen.” Ruth came over despite herself. She tested the hatch frame with a thumb. “This wood won’t take the weight.” “The beam might,” Nell said. Ruth looked up. “Maybe.” They measured the distance to the beam with a length of string. Ivo checked the back shutter twice while they worked. When Nell proposed opening it to clear the passage, he shook his head. “Not while there are spores on the wall.” “We’d have to clear it eventually.” “Yes. With a way to close it again if something comes in.” Ruth fetched another piece of string. “We’d rig that first.” Mara stood at the kitchen table, listening to them discuss where to put the pulley. Ruth had not asked her to help measure. At the yard Mara had insisted on bringing meat home, and Ruth had been left to hold the front shutter against the creature that came with it. Mara picked up the ruler and walked over. “I should have dropped the pack,” she said. Nell kept one end of the string against the beam. Ruth looked at Mara, then back at the wall. “You should have come when Nell said there was another one,” Ruth said. “I know.” Mara held the ruler where Ruth pointed. Nell called out the distance, and Ivo wrote it down. After a while Ruth said, “Ada used to say she could tell how much meat was on a chicken just by looking.” Mara glanced at her. “I thought of it yesterday,” Ruth said. “Looking at the one on the shutter. How much we could cut off.” “We were all hungry,” Mara said. “I know. That doesn’t make me like having thought it.” She took the ruler from Mara and checked the measurement herself. They worked until the light went. They found two usable lengths of cord, a pulley that needed cleaning, and enough fuel for perhaps three more fires. Before they stopped, Ruth drew a chalk line on the kitchen floor beneath the serving hatch. “If we rig it,” she said, “nobody steps past there while the shutter’s raised. Not for a larger piece. # Chapter 7 — The Delivery Hatch Ruth made the trap twice before she would let them bait it. The first version put too much strain on the beam. When Nell pulled the cord, the pulley tore a splinter from the wood and dropped at her feet. The second held, but the shutter fell crooked and left a gap wide enough for a mutant’s head. They spent their last sound length of cord correcting it. Mara held the ladder while Ruth fixed a metal guide to the wall. Nell went back and forth to the kitchen, pulling the rope whenever Ruth asked. Ivo watched the rear passage through the wired-glass pane and called out whenever something moved beyond the outer door. By late afternoon, the shutter dropped cleanly. It made a terrific noise. Mara felt it through the ladder beneath her hands. “That’ll bring them from every drain on the block,” Ivo said. “Then we’d better close the outer door after we catch one,” Ruth said. The outer door was the part Mara disliked. One of them would have to open it far enough for a creature to enter the passage. Ruth had run another cord to its handle so they could pull it shut from the kitchen, but it was an old wooden door, swollen at the bottom and scarred by claws. They cleared the passage first. With the inner shutter wedged down, Ruth and Ivo scraped dried spore dust from the accessible wall into a lidded tin. Mara heated water for the tools. Nell kept watch through the front boards. Every time they opened the inner shutter a few inches to reach farther, Mara heard Ruth say, “Slowly.” For bait, Mara had only the browned scrap she had saved in the bottom of the drippings jar. She had meant to spread it over their next supper, whatever supper turned out to be. She put the scrap in a tin lid, and Ruth slid it along the passage floor with a pole. The smell of it reached the kitchen when they raised the shutter. Nell sniffed. “We should have eaten that.” “We may yet wish we had,” Ivo said. At first nothing came. They waited behind the chalk line, taking turns looking through the wired glass. Ruth sat to spare her knee, though she kept one hand on the outer-door cord. Mara held the shutter rope. Nell had the pole ready to pull the bait farther in if a creature stopped at the threshold. Light faded from the passage. Then something scraped at the outer door. Ruth pulled the cord until it opened a hand’s width. A dark plate appeared in the gap. The creature pushed through sideways, its foreclaws testing the tile ahead of it. Ruth gave the cord slack and let it come farther. The creature found the lid and nosed it across the floor. “Now?” Nell whispered. “Wait until its back legs clear the door,” Ruth said. The creature drew in a breath, plates lifting. Mara pulled the shutter release. Steel dropped, struck something with a clang, and stopped halfway. The shutter rope jerked in her hands. The creature twisted under the gap and shoved one foreleg toward the kitchen side. “Pull the outer door,” Ivo said. Ruth heaved. The wooden door moved an inch and stuck. The mutant pushed against the shutter, raising it farther. Ruth looked up at the metal guide. “The left side’s caught. Nell, the pole. Push the guide outward.” “From where?” “Here. Stay behind the chalk.” Nell braced the pole against the guide. It slid off. She tried again, reaching as far as she could without crossing the line. Mara held the rope tight; the creature’s weight made the cord bite into her palms. “I can get a better angle from the passage,” Nell said. “No,” Ruth and Mara said together. Ruth got off the stool and wedged her shoulder beneath Nell’s arms, taking some of the pole’s weight. “There’s a notch in the iron. Below your hand.” Nell shifted the pole into it. The guide gave with a sharp crack, and the shutter dropped onto the mutant’s back. It thrashed, striking the outer door. Ruth hauled the door cord again, but the bottom still would not move. “Put your foot against the frame,” Mara said. “I am.” “Higher. Where the wood’s sound.” Ruth changed her footing and pulled. The door shut. Ivo dropped its wooden locking bar from a cord they had rigged above it. It clattered into place. Inside the passage, the creature struck the shutter once, then went still. Mara held the rope until Ruth told her she could let go. When she opened her fingers, red grooves crossed both palms. They waited a long time. Ivo checked the outer door through the pane. Nell examined the guide without touching it and said she thought she could bend it back. Ruth told her she could try tomorrow. A second creature came along the alley. Its claws clicked outside the wooden door. It pushed against the boards and gave a low sigh. Mara looked at Ruth’s cord, hanging loose now that the bar had fallen into place. “Will it hold?” she asked. “For tonight,” Ruth said. They left the catch where it lay and took turns watching the passage while Mara got the stove going. Fuel burned quickly under the pot. Before they ate anything, there would be water to heat, tools to wash, and a carcass to cut while the outer door kept what had followed it outside.

Ivo's lines are minimal but appropriate—he watches, he calls out, he gives the one decisive instruction ("Pull the outer door") at the right moment. The dialogue never explains itself or reaches for significance. Character consistency is strong. Ruth sits to spare her knee but keeps her hand on the cord—a detail that honors her profile without calling attention to itself. Mara's impulse to hold the rope until told she can let go, and then the physical consequence of that (the grooves in her palms), is exactly the kind of concrete action-before-mouth detail her profile describes. Nell's attempt to cross the chalk line and the dual refusal is consistent with her profile's tension between capability and the group's protectiveness. Ivo's watchfulness and his single moment of decisive instruction fit his character. The tension is well-managed. The second creature arriving at the outer door after the catch is a smart, low-key escalation that reinforces the plan's limitations without melodrama. The chapter is not uncreative, but it is doing something deliberately modest: it's a procedural chapter in a story that earns its weight through accumulation. The trap-building sequence is specific enough to feel real without becoming tedious. The "chalk line" as a safety boundary is a nice concrete detail. The wooden door swollen at the bottom is the kind of specific obstacle that makes fictional mechanics feel grounded. There is no purple prose, no forced metaphor, no tell-don't-show failures of note. # Chapter 8 — Supper, For Now By morning, the creature outside the delivery door had gone. Nell checked twice before Ruth let anyone near the shutter. They raised it only far enough to see the catch. The steel had broken its back plates, but the pale sacs beneath its belly looked whole. Ivo made Mara lower the shutter while he fetched the flour order with his notes. “We could start with the hind leg,” she said. “We could look first.” They looked. Ruth held a lamp through the serving hatch while Ivo marked the position of each sac on his drawing. Nell pointed out one he had missed beneath a folded plate. Mara tied cloth around her mouth and nose and waited for them to finish. Cutting the creature took most of the morning. The shutter remained low enough that no one could crawl through. They used the hooked pole to draw each section within reach, and threw out anything too close to a sac. Twice Mara looked at a clean-looking strip and thought they might keep it. Twice Ivo said he could not see where it had come from, and she put it in the discard tin. “We’re wasting half of it,” Nell said. “More,” Mara replied. Nell carried the tin to the washroom window. She did not argue further. Mara watched her go, remembering the pack torn open on the front counter. Ruth worked the pole from her stool. She hated the weight of the creature dragging at its end, but her hands were steadier than Mara’s. When they finished, she helped wash the tools and checked the outer door for damage. The lower hinge had pulled away from the wood. She wedged it shut with a length of shelving. “We won’t set the trap again until that’s fixed,” she said. “Can you fix it?” Nell asked. “Yes. If nobody needs me to do it today.” Mara set aside enough of the meat for supper and sliced the rest thin. She could hang some in the cool washroom for a day; beyond that, she did not trust it. They had no salt to spare for preserving, and the stove could not stay lit all night. She told Ivo so when he asked how long their catch would last. “Tomorrow,” she said. “Perhaps the day after, if it keeps.” “That’s not much.” “It’s more than yesterday.” As the pan heated, Ruth brought the blue plate from the shelf. Its painted pear still had a faint line of soap caught in the crack. Mara rinsed it and dried it with a clean corner of her apron. They had a handful of dried onions left in a jar. Mara soaked them in hot water, then tipped them into the pan beside the meat. The onions caught on the browned edges, and soon the smell filled the kitchen. Nell stood by the stove until Mara gave her the spoon. “Keep them moving,” Mara said. “I know.” “Then keep them moving.” Nell did, scraping carefully where the meat stuck. Ivo set out cups of water. Ruth stayed at the kitchen door, looking through the glass at the cleaned counter and the shutter boards beyond it. “You can sit down,” Mara told her. “I can see from here.” Mara put a little water in the hot pan to loosen its browned juices. Steam rose around Nell’s hand. She stepped back and let Mara finish. For supper they had four portions and a little broth. Mara chose the smallest before Nell could inspect the plate. Nell inspected it anyway. “You’ve done it again.” “There’s plenty here.” “Then take more.” Mara looked at the others. Ivo was already cutting into his portion. Ruth had wrapped her hands around her cup, waiting for the meat to cool. Mara took another piece. Nell nodded and began eating. The onions were scorched in places. The meat was better for it. Ruth ate half her serving and went to check the rear door. When she returned, her plate was still where she had left it. She sat down and finished the rest. Ivo reached toward the plate. “Is anyone keeping the crisp piece?” “I thought you’d taken it,” Nell said. “I took one.” “There were two?” “There were three,” Mara said, and divided the last one with the spoon. Ruth accepted her share without looking up. They talked about the hinge while they ate. Ruth needed two screws long enough to reach sound wood. Nell thought there might be some in Barlow’s workshop, if its drawers had not been emptied. Ivo wanted to repair the guide as well, though Ruth said it would serve for another drop. They would decide in the morning whether the outer door was worth opening for a hunt. The broth was thin, but Nell drank hers to the bottom. Mara poured her a little more. A weight pressed against the delivery shutter. All four stopped. Mara could hear claws finding the steel, then the slow breath of something in the passage. Ruth set down her cup and listened. “Outer door’s still shut. It’s in the alley.” “Testing it?” Nell asked. “Maybe.” The pressure eased. After a few minutes, Ivo went to check the pane. He came back and sat down. The outer bar was in place. Mara gathered the empty plates. At the sink, Nell picked a browned shred from the pan and ate it. “What did you put on it?” she asked. “Besides the onions.” “Nothing.” “It didn’t taste like nothing.” “The onions burned a little.” “Then next time, burn them the same way.” Mara began to tell her how long to leave the pan before adding water. Halfway through, she realized she was describing a recipe. She kept going, and Nell listened with the spoon in her hand.

# Brainstorming The prompt suggests someone who has become accustomed to entering a manor by a route meant to be inaccessible. That habit could be romantic, comic, dangerous, or all three. The upper windows might offer a way around a stern guardian, a means of reaching a sickroom, an escape from an unwanted engagement, or access to a room whose owner has vanished. **Possible protagonists and romantic pairings** - A governess climbs into her former employer’s manor to retrieve letters that could ruin a young woman’s prospects. The reclusive heir catches her and helps her search. - A botanical illustrator visits an elderly patron through the conservatory roof after the household refuses her entry. The patron’s nephew initially mistakes her for a thief. - A lady’s companion uses the upper windows to help her mistress evade a controlling guardian. She falls for the guardian’s principled but unsuspecting steward. - A widowed locksmith’s daughter is hired to repair the manor’s old casements. Her skill brings her into the path of an aristocrat trapped by family obligations. - A young woman returns secretly to the house where she was raised, looking for proof that her late mother was wronged. The new master has his own reasons to distrust the family’s official history. **Ways to use the manor** The building could feel almost like a character: ivy against stone, a conservatory with a convenient roofline, narrow servants’ stairs, a locked east wing, and windows offering different views of the estate. Its upstairs rooms could hold more private truths than its formal ground floor. Repeated climbs might trace a change in the lovers’ relationship: trespass, uneasy cooperation, trust, then a final arrival by invitation. **Possible tensions and tone** The story could be a light comedy of mistaken identities and narrow escapes. Alternatively, the windows could conceal a dangerous secret and give the romance a Gothic edge. A middle course may suit eight chapters best: sparkling exchanges and growing intimacy set against a real threat to someone’s reputation or independence. Victorian class rules would make a woman’s secret visits consequential, without requiring a melodramatic villain. **Possible eight-chapter rhythm** 1. Open with an attempted upper-window entry and an immediate interruption. 2. Establish why the visitor cannot simply use the front door. 3. Force the visitor and the manor’s occupant into a reluctant alliance. 4. Let shared work reveal competence, attraction, and a misleading clue. 5. Raise the social risk at a gathering where one slip could expose them. 6. Give them a private moment of honesty, followed by a damaging discovery. 7. Bring the secret into the open; make each choose what they will risk. 8. Resolve the practical conflict and let the romantic resolution answer the opening image. # Reflection A mystery about inheritance could provide momentum, but a complicated legal puzzle would consume too much of an approximately 8,000-word story. The central question should be simple enough to grasp early and resolve through a few concrete discoveries. Likewise, too many family members or servants with competing secrets would crowd the romance. The governess or companion offers a strong reason to be overlooked at the front door, while the illustrator or locksmith’s daughter would have a distinctive practical skill that makes her climbs convincing. Combining an outsider’s useful expertise with a personal stake in the house could give the protagonist agency beyond stumbling into a mystery. The person who catches her should have the power to stop her, but a reason to listen; that imbalance offers tension if he earns her trust rather than merely granting permission. The upper windows work best as more than a clever entrance. They can embody the difference between public propriety and private truth. If the opening climb is furtive and the last approach is openly welcomed, the image gives the short story a satisfying shape. Repeating the climb in every chapter might turn it into a gimmick, though; using it at key turning points would preserve its force. For the romance, attraction can grow through specific acts of trust: one person steadies a ladder, the other shares a compromising letter, and each resists an easy chance to protect themselves at the other’s expense. A genuine disagreement near the end would make their eventual union more persuasive than a simple misunderstanding would. The strongest direction seems to be a warm Victorian romance with a contained household secret, light Gothic atmosphere, and a heroine whose familiarity with the upper windows comes from both skill and necessity. An eight-chapter plan could devote the first two chapters to the secret entry and stakes, the middle four to cooperation and deepening feeling, and the final two to public choice and resolution.
