# Intention I’ll write a warm Victorian romance with a contained mystery, a touch of Gothic atmosphere, and a lightly witty third-person voice close to the heroine. The story will take place at Briarcombe Hall, a manor whose upper windows offer both a practical route inside and a way of reaching the private truths concealed behind its respectable front door. The heroine, **Clara Vale**, is a botanical illustrator. As a girl, she often visited Briarcombe with her mother, a gifted gardener, and learned to reach the conservatory’s upper windows by way of its adjoining roof. She returns after her mother’s death to recover a portfolio of drawings and correspondence left in the keeping of Briarcombe’s elderly mistress. When Clara is refused entry, she takes the route she remembers—and is caught by **Edward Ashcombe**, the mistress’s nephew and the manor’s new master. Clara fears the portfolio will be claimed as part of the estate and used without acknowledgment. Edward, trying to settle his aunt’s affairs responsibly, assumes at first that Clara is taking property to which she has no right. Their search for the portfolio becomes a narrow, character-driven mystery rather than an elaborate inheritance plot. As they uncover his aunt’s intentions, each must decide whether to trust the other with something that matters: Clara’s chance at independent work, and Edward’s duty to a family whose conduct he cannot wholly defend. The romance will grow through conversation, shared work, and consequential choices, not instant certainty. Class and reputation will create real obstacles, but neither Clara nor Edward will be rescued by a last-minute change of fortune. The ending should resolve the ownership question clearly and allow them to choose one another without asking Clara to give up her profession. At approximately 1,000 words per chapter, each chapter will center on one encounter or turn. I’ll use the windows at pivotal moments rather than inventing a climb for every chapter. The prose will aim for period flavor without dense imitation, historical exposition, or a villainous household full of competing secrets. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — The Upper Window** Clara returns to Briarcombe and is turned away at the front door: the late Mrs. Ashcombe’s rooms are closed while the estate is inventoried. She climbs from the conservatory roof to the window she knew as a girl. Edward catches her entering. Their sharp exchange ends when she names the portfolio she has come to find—and describes a drawing he has recently seen among his aunt’s papers. **Chapter 2 — Terms of Entry** Edward agrees to let Clara identify the drawing, under his supervision. It proves to be her mother’s work, though the portfolio itself is missing. Clara explains its importance: a publisher is willing to consider her illustrations if she can supply the botanical studies made with her mother. Edward offers a brief, private search rather than allowing her to wander the house. Neither is satisfied with the arrangement, but both accept it. **Chapter 3 — Mrs. Ashcombe’s Garden** Their search takes them through the conservatory and the late mistress’s upstairs sitting room. Clara’s knowledge of the plants and Edward’s familiarity with his aunt’s habits complement one another. They find a note suggesting Mrs. Ashcombe meant to give the portfolio to Clara, but no signed document. Edward begins to believe Clara; Clara sees that his caution is not simply disdain. **Chapter 4 — A Narrow Escape** A visit from Edward’s aunt Lady Beatrice interrupts their work. Clara must leave by the upper window rather than be found alone in Edward’s company. Edward helps her across the roof, turning an undignified escape into their first unguarded moment together. Afterwards, Lady Beatrice presses him to sell the conservatory’s contents, including anything left in its locked cabinet. **Chapter 5 — The Locked Cabinet** Edward and Clara open the cabinet before the sale. Inside are letters showing that Mrs. Ashcombe intended to sponsor their joint botanical volume, with Clara credited as its illustrator, but the drawings are still absent. Clara suspects Edward delayed telling her about the sale; he admits he hoped to settle matters quietly before alarming her. The lapse strains their new trust just as their attraction becomes difficult to ignore. **Chapter 6 — What the Window Conceals** Clara discovers that her mother hid the portfolio above the conservatory’s interior windows to protect the drawings from damp during repairs. She and Edward recover it together. Among its pages is Mrs. Ashcombe’s signed letter stating that the drawings belong to Clara and outlining the proposed volume. Relief gives way to a harder question: whether Edward will oppose Lady Beatrice’s sale openly, and whether Clara can bear another private arrangement dependent on his goodwill. **Chapter 7 — The Front Door** Clara refuses to continue visiting in secret. When Lady Beatrice arrives with the prospective buyer, Edward presents the letter, withdraws the portfolio from the sale, and acknowledges Clara’s work before the household. His choice costs him an easy peace with his family. He asks Clara to stay, but she leaves to meet the publisher on her own terms; he does not ask her to choose between that opportunity and him. **Chapter 8 — An Open Invitation** Some weeks later, Clara returns with a commission for the botanical volume and plans to finish its studies at Briarcombe. She comes to the front door, where Edward receives her openly. They speak plainly about affection, work, and the life they might build together. Their engagement is a shared decision, not a reward for solving the mystery. The story closes with Clara looking up at the familiar upper windows: still a possible entrance, but no longer the only one available to her.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a human writer might approach this piece A human writer might begin less with the plot than with the odd pleasure of the prompt: *“One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows.”* Who says this, and why does it sound so matter-of-fact? The sentence promises repetition, physical ingenuity, and a faint disregard for rules. It also implies that the manor is a place the speaker has reason to visit often but cannot enter normally. That could lead a writer toward questions less orderly than “What mystery will drive eight chapters?”: - What does climbing into this house feel like? Is the stone wet? Is one window painted shut? Has somebody left a stool in exactly the wrong place? - Who first taught the protagonist this route? Did she discover it herself? - What does she want badly enough to risk a fall, arrest, or gossip? - Why *upper windows*, plural? Does she know several entrances, each with its own drawback? - Is the habit funny to her, humiliating, frightening, or so familiar she hardly thinks about it? - What might she overhear or misunderstand because she is entering rooms in the wrong order? A human approach might also preserve an awkward discovery that a tidier outline would eliminate. Perhaps Clara has come for the portfolio but finds that her mother made an ugly compromise to get the work done. Perhaps Edward is kind yet genuinely obstructive. Perhaps Mrs. Ashcombe, despite her generosity, never learned to treat Clara’s mother as an equal. Those complications need not turn the romance bleak; they can make affection and trust feel earned. For an 8,000-word story, a human writer would likely choose a few scenes they especially want to write—the first confrontation at the window, a climb that goes wrong, an encounter with one of the drawings—and build the structure around those scenes. The outline should support the life of the story, not make every chapter perform an equally neat function. # Telltale LLM approaches—and why they may not serve this story These are tendencies, not rules. The current plan has useful clarity, but it is worth watching for them as the piece develops. ### Treating the prompt as a symbol too soon An LLM might decide immediately that the windows represent exclusion and the front door represents belonging, then arrange the entire story to prove it. That reading is sound, but if every appearance of a window carries the same meaning, the image may feel assigned rather than discovered. The windows should first be *windows*: inconvenient sizes, unreliable latches, risks of being seen, surprising views. Their significance can change. One entry might be liberating; another might make Clara furious that she still has to sneak about. ### Designing a frictionless moral universe The plan currently makes both leads reasonable. Clara has a legitimate claim; Edward has a reasonable initial doubt; an explicit letter settles ownership; Edward then does the right thing publicly. This is pleasant, but it could become too safe. If Edward’s choice costs him only “an easy peace with his family,” or if Clara is always justified in exactly the right way, the obstacles may feel procedural rather than painful. A more human story might let someone be wrong in a way that cannot be explained away at once. Clara might trespass and take something she had no right to take. Edward might have signed a sale agreement without checking what it covered. They can remain sympathetic while doing harm that requires more than a conversation to repair. ### Solving emotional conflict with paperwork Letters and documents suit a Victorian story, but this plan leans heavily on them: a note establishes intention, letters reveal the book project, and a signed letter resolves ownership. If every uncertainty is answered by the next piece of paper, Clara and Edward’s choices may matter less than their filing skills. A document can establish what Mrs. Ashcombe intended. It cannot make Edward credit Clara, undo a slight, or determine whether they can trust each other. The story could use the portfolio itself—its annotations, erasures, or evidence of collaboration—to carry some of the discovery. ### Making every chapter end on a clean “turn” An outline benefits from clear turns, but prose can become mechanical if each chapter follows the same pattern: search a room, find a clue, share a charged moment, suffer an interruption. A human story may linger somewhere unexpected or allow a scene to end unresolved. Variation in chapter texture would help: an active climb, a quiet afternoon working, a social confrontation, an argument that happens while both characters are doing something else. ### Writing “period” as polished generality LLM-generated historical romance can drift toward universally elegant dialogue: everyone is articulate, everyone trades perfectly shaped barbs, and nobody sounds distracted, repetitive, embarrassed, or occupied with practical problems. The language can be graceful without making every sentence quotable. Likewise, “Victorian” should not be reduced to propriety, inheritance, stern aunts, and a publisher. Small material specifics—what Clara carries her drawings in, how a conservatory is heated, what happens to paper stored near plants—may do more work than declarations about society’s rules. ### Wrapping the ending with a bow The front-door ending is satisfying in outline, perhaps *too* satisfying if it implies all barriers have fallen. Edward’s public acknowledgment would not erase class differences, money concerns, or the question of where and how Clara will work after marriage. The story can end happily without pretending those matters no longer exist. A small unresolved practical discussion might make the promise between them more believable. ### Mistaking competence for personality Clara knows plants, draws well, climbs skillfully, and insists on her independence. Edward is responsible, cautious, and capable of growth. These are good foundations, but they risk reading as a list of admirable qualities. More particular habits and flaws would make them memorable. What is Clara vain about? When is Edward unexpectedly funny? What does each find tiresome in the other even after attraction begins? # Deep dive on the current intention and plan ## The central premise Clara’s childhood familiarity with the manor gives her a credible reason to know its upper windows. That is one of the plan’s strengths: the prompt is rooted in her history rather than added as a stunt. Yet the wording—“One quickly learns the art…”—suggests more than an old route used once again. It hints at a skill acquired under pressure, perhaps through repeated attempts during the present story. At present, Clara climbs in during Chapter 1, escapes by a window in Chapter 4, and retrieves the portfolio near the conservatory windows in Chapter 6. That may be enough, but the *art* of entry has little chance to evolve. Could Clara’s knowledge be imperfect because the house has changed? Could Edward learn the route badly? Could a climb expose something about the manor that searching its rooms would not? Those are possibilities to explore, not requirements to force into each chapter. The proposed final contrast—upper window versus front door—is strong and legible. The risk is that it announces the ending from the first chapter. If Clara eventually decides that the front door is not always a victory, or uses an upper window later by choice rather than necessity, the motif might retain more playfulness. ## Clara’s reason for coming A portfolio of botanical studies is concrete, visual, and well suited to a botanical illustrator. It gives her a professional stake beyond the romance. The weakness is that her goal is currently quite easy to approve of. She wants what is hers, and her claim is eventually proved. What would make her need more urgent and specific? Perhaps she has promised finished plates by a date she cannot meet without her mother’s studies. Perhaps her own recent work is better than the old portfolio, but she cannot bear to leave her mother’s drawings behind. Perhaps she has exaggerated her access to the work when writing to the publisher. Any such pressure could make her decisions less pristine and more revealing. There is also a question about her mother. The plan describes her as a gifted gardener whose work is at risk of going uncredited, but at present she functions chiefly as Clara’s inheritance and motivation. A few personal traces could make her feel like a person: contradictory instructions in the margins, an unfinished drawing Clara dislikes, a private joke attached to one specimen. Clara’s feelings toward her could include admiration and irritation rather than reverence alone. ## Edward’s role and power Edward’s position creates an effective obstacle: he can keep Clara out, permit the search, stop the sale, or recognize her claim. The plan rightly says he must earn trust. But because so many practical outcomes pass through him, the story risks becoming one in which Clara’s independence exists only once a good man validates it. His eventual public acknowledgment should matter, but Clara could also take action he has not authorized and could not have devised. She might contact the buyer, retrieve evidence herself, or insist on terms for the proposed volume. Edward’s growth may be more compelling if he learns that helping Clara is not the same as directing her. His own desires could be sharper as well. “Settle his aunt’s affairs responsibly” is plausible, but rather neutral. Does he want to sell the conservatory because it is costly, because it reminds him of an unhappy childhood, or because he has already promised money elsewhere? If keeping Clara’s work out of the sale jeopardizes something he sincerely values, his choice becomes more than a test of decency. ## Mrs. Ashcombe’s convenient intentions Mrs. Ashcombe’s notes and signed letter currently supply the moral and legal answers after her death. This makes her a useful plot engine, but perhaps too useful. Why did she leave the portfolio hidden or unreturned? Why were her wishes insufficiently clear before the sale? Those questions invite either an interesting character answer or an implausibility. She could have been generous in one respect and careless in another. She might have intended to sponsor the book but postponed an uncomfortable conversation about credit. That would complicate the neat idea that the truth, once recovered, absolves the household. Alternatively, her letter could be clear while the practical problem remains: possession, a buyer’s claim, or the cost of publication. ## The mystery’s shape The contained mystery fits the scope. Readers can follow “Where is the portfolio, and who may use it?” without a family tree or legal subplot. The sequence of clues, though, may feel repetitive: 1. They find a drawing. 2. They find a note. 3. They find letters. 4. They find the portfolio. 5. They find a signed letter inside it. Each discovery confirms the same general trajectory. The middle chapters could become more engaging if at least one find *changes the nature of the problem* rather than merely moving the pair closer to proof. A drawing could reveal that Clara’s mother did not make it alone. A letter could imply an obligation Clara does not want to inherit. The portfolio might be found earlier, leaving them to confront what it contains. The present hiding place also deserves scrutiny. Clara’s mother hid paper above conservatory windows “to protect the drawings from damp during repairs.” In a humid conservatory, that may raise practical questions. If its physical circumstances are convincing and specific, the location could be delightful; if not, it will feel chosen because the plot requires another window scene. ## The romance The best romantic element in the plan is that Clara and Edward have work to do together. They can admire one another through attention and action, not simply through appearances. The risk is a familiar rhythm of “reluctant allies become attracted while solving a mystery,” with the attraction signposted but not individualized. What draws them to each other besides competence and kindness? Perhaps Clara enjoys that Edward knows nothing of botany yet asks precise questions. Perhaps he is first attracted not to her boldness but to her complete impatience with a cherished family myth. They might have incompatible senses of humor, then develop a private one. Specificity will do more than repeated moments of charged proximity on roofs. Their conflict in Chapters 5–7 also needs care. Edward delaying news of the sale gives Clara a reason to distrust him, but it resembles a standard romance misunderstanding if he could have mentioned it in one sentence. If he withholds something, the reason should be credible and the consequences substantial. Or their disagreement could be openly philosophical: he believes he can manage the matter discreetly; she knows discretion has always benefited his family more than hers. ## Class, reputation, and the “stern aunt” Lady Beatrice currently enters as the person who presses for a sale and threatens exposure. She is useful structurally but risks becoming a stock disapproving aunt. What does she stand to lose? She might genuinely believe the sale necessary to pay debts, maintain servants’ wages, or fund another dependent. If her position has force, Edward cannot dismiss her as merely snobbish, and Clara must engage with a real competing need. The household also exists mostly as a source of potential discovery. Servants would notice ladders, open windows, dust disturbed in closed rooms, and two people repeatedly searching together. One or two individuals with ordinary motives—not secret plots—could make the manor feel inhabited. A housemaid who knows exactly what Clara is doing but chooses not to say so could be more interesting than a succession of near-misses. Reputation should have a clear scale. What precisely is at stake if Clara is found alone with Edward? A lost commission? Gossip affecting her lodging or employment? Pressure to accept a proposal? The story need not explain Victorian society at length, but it should know which consequences its characters fear. ## The ending Clara meeting the publisher independently before returning is a good choice. It gives her an achievement that is not bestowed by Edward. Their engagement can be happy if they have addressed how her work will continue. The final image may need a touch of surprise. “She comes to the front door” completes the motif neatly, but readers may see it coming. A human writer might retain the satisfaction and undercut its solemnity: Clara finds Edward at an upstairs window because the front door is temporarily blocked by furniture; or she enters properly, then tells him the conservatory latch still needs fixing. Such details could allow the ending to breathe rather than delivering a single perfected symbol. # Ideas to explore before rewriting the plan These are possibilities, not decisions. Several pull in different directions. **Make the first climb less assured.** Clara remembers herself as someone who knew every foothold, but years away have changed the route—and her confidence is partly performance. Or she is genuinely expert yet has made one foolish assumption about who now occupies the room. **Give the house a practical reason to resist her.** Repairs have altered the roofline; a window sticks in damp weather; a room has been repurposed. The manor should not remain a convenient map of clues. **Let Clara’s goal shift.** She may begin by wanting the portfolio back, then discover that publication requires choosing which of her mother’s work to show—or whether to include something her mother wanted kept private. **Bring the portfolio forward.** If it appears halfway through, the second half can ask what Clara and Edward will *do* with it. That may be richer than extending the search until Chapter 6. **Give Edward a consequential error.** He might have included the portfolio in a preliminary inventory or promised the conservatory contents to a buyer. Repairing the mistake would require action, not simply admitting he should have told Clara sooner. **Make Mrs. Ashcombe imperfect.** Her patronage may have been heartfelt but patronizing. Clara can be grateful to her without owing her silence or unquestioning praise. **Complicate the credit question.** The drawings could bear both women’s marks. Clara might have improved some plates and resented being treated as the keeper of her mother’s legacy rather than an artist in her own right. **Make the romantic disagreement specific.** Edward may think public credit solves the problem; Clara may know that the contract, fee, and ownership of the plates matter more. Their argument can expose different understandings of security. **Give Lady Beatrice a defensible priority.** If the estate needs money, stopping a sale has a cost. Clara should not have to surrender her work to meet it, but the cost can remain real. **Vary the meaning of secrecy.** At first it protects Clara; later it may protect Edward’s reputation or spare him a family quarrel. Their interests need not align just because they are hiding together. **Allow comedy from inconvenience.** A boot left behind, a housemaid unimpressed by a supposedly dramatic escape, or Edward proving dreadful at climbing can make the story feel less prearranged. The humor should arise from character and circumstance, not constant polished banter. **Let a scene exceed its plot function.** Clara and Edward might spend time identifying a mislabeled plant, only for the exchange to reveal how they think. It need not produce a clue. The most useful principle for the eventual rewrite may be this: **keep the outline’s clear romantic and narrative shape, but remove some of its certainty**. The story will feel more human if the characters’ choices create problems as well as solve them, the manor remains a stubborn physical place, and the ending promises a shared life without claiming to have settled every difficulty in it.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Working title: *The Art of Entering Briarcombe Hall*** The story will take the prompt literally. Clara Vale has learned to enter Briarcombe Hall through its upper windows because the house has never been equally open to everyone who worked in it. As a girl, she followed her mother, the estate’s gardener, across the conservatory roof on errands for Mrs. Ashcombe. Years later, refused at the front door, Clara discovers that she still knows the route—though the roof is slipperier, a familiar window has been replaced, and she is no longer young enough to mistake a climb for an adventure. Clara is now a botanical illustrator. She has an offer to submit plates for publication, but the original studies she made with her late mother remain at Briarcombe. The manor’s new master, **Edward Ashcombe**, has already included the conservatory’s contents in a proposed sale to pay estate debts. He catches Clara at an upstairs window. He has good reason to object to a trespasser; she has good reason not to trust his promise to sort matters out quietly. Their search will reveal the portfolio by the midpoint, leaving the second half for the harder question of ownership, credit, and what each is willing to do in public. The romance will grow from their differing ways of paying attention. Clara knows the plants, the building’s awkward routes, and the value of her work. Edward understands the estate’s finances but has failed to ask whose labor its possessions contain. He will make a consequential mistake, not merely suffer a misunderstanding; Clara will act for herself rather than wait for his permission. Their affection should survive an honest disagreement about whether discretion protects anyone but Edward. The narration will be close third person, chiefly through Clara, with dry humor and room for embarrassment, irritation, and desire. Period detail will appear through objects and actions—drawing paper, damp glass, ledgers, latches, contracts—rather than explanatory passages or ornate imitation-Victorian prose. The manor will feel inhabited: a housemaid notices more than either lead supposes, and Edward’s aunt has a defensible reason to press for the sale. No one will produce a document that settles every moral question. Each chapter, at roughly 1,000 words, will have one main encounter or decision. The windows will recur because Clara uses them, not because every scene must illustrate a symbol. The ending will be romantic and hopeful without suggesting that an engagement erases money, class, or Clara’s need to keep working. # Chapter Planning ### Chapter 1 — A Familiar Route Clara arrives at Briarcombe expecting to collect the studies Mrs. Ashcombe kept for her. A servant, following Edward’s instructions during the estate inventory, cannot admit her to the closed rooms. Pressed by a publisher’s approaching deadline, Clara climbs from the conservatory roof toward an upper window she knew as a girl. The old foothold crumbles; the replacement window opens into the wrong room. Edward finds her halfway through it, muddy, angry, and plainly not a practiced burglar. She names the portfolio. He recognizes it from the sale inventory. ### Chapter 2 — What Is in the Inventory Edward shows Clara the entry: a cabinet and its contents have been offered to a buyer as part of the conservatory sale. He made the agreement without examining every item, believing they belonged to his aunt. Clara cannot prove which studies are hers, and Edward cannot simply take goods out of a signed agreement. He allows her to look through the conservatory with him that afternoon. Their search reveals her mother’s handwriting on plant labels—and how much of the place Edward has inherited without understanding it. ### Chapter 3 — The People Who Remember Mrs. Finch, a housemaid who knew Clara as a child, points them toward the former workroom without pretending she failed to see Clara climb in. There they find loose drawings: Clara’s, her mother’s, and several bearing corrections from both. Clara is unsettled to discover her mother revised one of her plates without telling her; she had imagined their work as more neatly divided. Edward learns that his aunt spoke of the proposed botanical book but never settled its terms. Clara leaves with copies of her own drawings, made under Mrs. Finch’s watchful eye, and refuses Edward’s suggestion that they keep the matter secret until he has spoken to the buyer. ### Chapter 4 — The Portfolio Clara returns by appointment, through the front door, to search a storage room with Edward. She spots signs that a cabinet was moved during conservatory repairs and remembers where her mother used to store work safely away from the damp: in a dry upstairs workroom reached by a narrow window from the roof. The window sticks; Edward’s attempt to help is less graceful than hers. They find the portfolio. Its contents could meet Clara’s deadline, but they also include notes for a book that Mrs. Ashcombe discussed as though she alone would decide its publication. Clara and Edward share a moment of pleasure in the discovery before the disagreement it raises catches up with them. ### Chapter 5 — A Quiet Solution Edward proposes asking the buyer to release the portfolio without making a public dispute of it. He explains the estate debts and his aunt Lady Beatrice’s concern for the servants whose wages depend on the sale. Clara understands the difficulty but will not let her and her mother’s work remain an uncredited part of the bargain. When she learns Edward has already written to the buyer describing the drawings as his aunt’s “botanical materials,” she is furious. He meant to gain time; his description has strengthened the buyer’s claim. Their attraction is unmistakable, but Clara leaves rather than accept an apology that changes nothing. ### Chapter 6 — Clara’s Name Clara takes the drawings she copied to her publisher and receives a concrete offer: a commission for plates in her own name, provided she can deliver the originals for reproduction. She also writes directly to the buyer, explaining the competing claim and asking him to suspend the transfer. At Briarcombe, Edward finds correspondence showing that his aunt admired the women’s work while repeatedly postponing payment and credit. He does not hide it. Clara comes back to examine the letters, and they speak more frankly about her mother, his aunt, and Edward’s mistake. Their intimacy grows from that candor, but Clara will not ask him to choose her over an obligation she has not tried to understand. ### Chapter 7 — The Sale The buyer and Lady Beatrice arrive to finalize the conservatory purchase. The buyer has received Clara’s letter; he wants a clear account, not a quarrel over disputed plates. Before them, Edward corrects his inventory and acknowledges that the drawings were made by Clara and her mother. He offers to renegotiate the sale without the portfolio, accepting a lower price and the work of finding another way to cover the shortfall. Lady Beatrice objects because the shortfall is real. Clara proposes paid botanical studies of the conservatory before it changes hands—not a miraculous solution to the debt, but work that earns her a fee and gives Edward a useful record. Afterward, he tells Clara he loves her. She believes him, but says she must first deliver the commission she has won. ### Chapter 8 — An Open Window Several weeks later, Clara returns to Briarcombe to finish the conservatory studies. She enters through the front door carrying her drawing case; Mrs. Finch, unsurprised, lets her in. Clara and Edward discuss the practical matters their affection cannot solve by itself: her deadlines, the money he still owes, and where she would work if they married. They cannot promise an effortless life, but they can make promises they intend to keep. Clara accepts his proposal. Later she notices the troublesome upstairs window standing open while rain threatens her drying drawings. Without ceremony, she takes the familiar short route to close it. Edward follows by the stairs, arriving in time to help.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Clara Vale Clara, twenty-six, grew up in the lodge beside Briarcombe’s kitchen gardens. Her mother, Ruth Vale, was employed as a gardener but became an informal collaborator on Mrs. Ashcombe’s proposed botanical book. Clara learned to draw by sharpening Ruth’s pencils, then by being allowed to sketch specimens Ruth had finished with. She learned the upper-window routes because Mrs. Ashcombe disliked having muddy plants carried through her formal rooms, yet often wanted fresh specimens in her upstairs workroom. What the household called an ingenious arrangement spared its carpets at the expense of Ruth’s and Clara’s dignity. Clara now takes illustration work wherever she can find it. She is observant, quick to act, and more patient with a difficult plant than with an evasive person. She labels drawings with exact dates and locations, but repeatedly loses the pins she uses to fasten her hair. When she is anxious, she cleans her nib instead of beginning. She has kept one of Ruth’s badly drawn early studies because it makes her laugh. She dislikes being called fearless: she is afraid of falling, of failing her publisher, and of discovering that some work she thought of as hers was mostly her mother’s. Her pride can make help feel like an insult. She sometimes answers the slight she expects before a person has offered one. When Edward suggests a quiet solution, she hears the old household assumption that a Vale can be grateful for whatever an Ashcombe arranges—even though his concern about the debts is genuine. She must learn to distinguish accepting help from surrendering judgment, without losing the instinct that has protected her. Clara is medium height and wiry from walking, carrying equipment, and climbing when she ought not to. Her dark hair rarely stays pinned through a day’s work; there is often graphite along the side of one finger. She studies things directly but can avoid a person’s eyes when she is hurt. In Edward’s formal rooms, she initially stands as though prepared to be asked to leave. In the conservatory, she moves without thinking about where she is permitted to put her feet. She wants the portfolio for the commission, but also wants to know where her work ends and Ruth’s begins. She loves her mother without wishing to spend her life as her custodian. She trusts Mrs. Finch, who has known her since childhood, though she does not like being fussed over. Her feelings toward Mrs. Ashcombe remain mixed: fondness for a woman who encouraged her drawing, anger at the ease with which that woman postponed questions of payment. Clara is drawn to Edward’s willingness to listen carefully; she watches for the moment listening becomes deciding on her behalf. > “That is a fine distinction, Mr. Ashcombe. It is also one I cannot afford.” > > *She could climb the roof with a portfolio under one arm. It was the descent, watched by everyone, that troubled her.* # Edward Ashcombe Edward, thirty-one, inherited Briarcombe from his aunt after several years spent managing the financial affairs of another branch of the family. He knows what a debt costs month by month and dislikes promises made without figures attached. He remembers visiting Briarcombe as a boy, when Mrs. Ashcombe was affectionate but inclined to treat the conservatory as a world apart from the people who kept it alive. He has inherited her house, not her ease in it. Edward is conscientious, reserved in company, and dryly funny when caught off guard. He makes lists on scraps of paper and later cannot find the one he needs. He notices a loose stair rail at once but may overlook a person’s discomfort while considering how to have it repaired. At meals he puts down his fork to think, then is surprised to find everyone else has finished. He can admit ignorance readily about plants; admitting that his own judgment has caused harm takes longer. His chief flaw is the belief that a problem managed quietly is a problem managed kindly. He included the conservatory cabinet in the sale without examining it because he needed a credible offer quickly. When Clara appears, he tries to protect her claim while preserving the agreement and sparing his aunt worry. Those aims cannot all be reconciled, but he is slow to say so. His apology matters only once he corrects the inventory and accepts the financial consequence. Edward is tall, a little stooped from reading ledgers at poor desks, with a face that appears severe until he forgets to arrange it. His clothes are well made but worn at the cuffs. He is careful on a ladder and hopeless on a sloping roof: he wants three points of contact even when there are only two. He turns toward whoever is speaking, a courtesy Clara appreciates before she is certain she likes him. He wants Briarcombe solvent and its staff paid. He is loyal to Lady Beatrice, whose judgment he has relied on, but increasingly questions what the family has considered its own. Mrs. Ashcombe’s death has left him both affectionate memories and an inventory he mistrusts more with each day. He is attracted to Clara’s precision and her refusal to be soothed by a pleasant intention. Loving her will require him to be answerable, not merely helpful. > “I ought to have looked inside the cabinet. There is no more respectable way to say it.” > > *She spoke of the house as though it were difficult to enter. He had spent three weeks discovering how difficult it was to leave anything out.* # Ruth Vale Ruth died the winter before the story begins, aged in her fifties. The story will know her through Clara’s memories, the garden she shaped, and marks left on paper, rather than through a portrait that settles what sort of woman she was. She came to Briarcombe as a skilled gardener, not a scholar with a formal title, and knew more about some specimens than the people invited to discuss them over dinner. She was capable, playful when work went well, and guarded about disappointment. She gave stubborn plants unflattering private names. Her labels were beautifully legible; her own sketches could be awkward, especially early ones, and she saw no reason to conceal that. She taught Clara to look again before rubbing out a line. She also revised Clara’s drawings without always asking and accepted delayed payment from Mrs. Ashcombe rather than risk losing access to the conservatory. Clara resents that choice even as she begins to understand it. Ruth was broad-handed, strong through the shoulders, and often smelled faintly of damp soil and the soap she used trying to remove it. She moved carefully among seedlings but could close a greenhouse door with a bang. When she was intent on a plant, she would speak to someone without looking up, then remember her manners several minutes later. Her first allegiance was to Clara’s security. She valued Mrs. Ashcombe’s friendship and patronage but understood its limits more clearly than she let Clara see. Her notes for the book show an artist and gardener concerned with getting the plants right, not someone composing evidence for a future dispute. > “Draw the leaf you have, not the leaf the book expects.” > > *If we wait for everything to be settled fairly, Clara, the flowers will be dead before we begin.* # Lady Beatrice Ashcombe Lady Beatrice is Edward’s aunt and the late Mrs. Ashcombe’s sister-in-law. She lives elsewhere but has helped the family through lean years and considers Briarcombe’s debts a shared concern. She is neither secretly cruel nor secretly delighted by Clara’s talent. She wants a sale completed because bills and wages cannot be paid in admiration for a conservatory. Beatrice is brisk, socially astute, and impatient with language meant to make a decision sound easier than it is. She can remember a housemaid’s ailing son while failing to ask whether that same housemaid has been consulted about a change. She sends useful things rather than affectionate letters. When she worries, she becomes more precise about appointments and quantities, which makes others think she is unmoved. She is upright, neatly dressed, and economical in gesture. She removes her gloves finger by finger before difficult conversations and looks directly at Edward when she suspects he has omitted a figure. With Clara she is courteous, though at first her courtesy has the chill of someone addressing an unexpected complication. Beatrice loves Edward and believes she is teaching him to survive as the owner of an indebted estate. She loved Mrs. Ashcombe too, but was frequently exasperated by her spending and vague promises. She feels responsible for the staff whose wages are at risk. She has no wish to steal Clara’s drawings; she resists changing the sale because she knows what losing money will mean and doubts Clara has reckoned with it. Her respect for Clara can grow without turning her into an approving matchmaker. > “I do not dispute whose hand held the pencil. I am asking which bill you propose we leave unpaid.” > > “Your aunt called many things *nearly arranged*, Edward. It was among her costlier habits.” # Mrs. Finch Mrs. Finch is Briarcombe’s senior housemaid, in her late forties, and has worked there since before Clara was born. She knew which windows Ruth and Clara used, which floors complained underfoot, and when Mrs. Ashcombe chose not to notice a breach of household form. She has no taste for being treated as an all-knowing keeper of secrets. Much of what she knows comes from being present while other people assumed she was not listening. She is practical, affectionate in carefully limited doses, and protective of her time. She keeps a needle in the hem of her apron for repairs and dislikes discovering that someone else has used the good scissors on string. She has been known to place a dry cloth within reach of a dripping visitor without interrupting her account. Clara’s return pleases her, but it also brings muddy marks to floors she has just cleaned. Mrs. Finch is compact, brisk, and rarely still when there is work to do. Her expression gives away little until she permits it to. She addresses Edward correctly even while correcting him, and speaks to Clara with the familiarity of someone who once made her wash before tea. Her loyalty is to the household as a place where people earn their living, not simply to the Ashcombe name. She wants Edward to keep the staff paid and Clara to receive what is hers. She liked Ruth, though they sometimes disagreed, and remembers that Ruth was capable of making compromises herself. Mrs. Finch will point Clara toward the former workroom because it is useful; she will not rearrange the entire mystery for the younger people. > “I saw you at the window, Miss Vale. So did the person polishing the window. It was me.” > > “You may spread those papers on the table, sir. You may not spread them on the clean floor.”

# Chapter One: A Familiar Route One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows. Clara Vale had learned it at twelve, when Mrs. Ashcombe required a flowering specimen in her upstairs workroom and Clara’s mother had refused to carry a tub of wet earth across the drawing-room carpet. The conservatory roof joined the house just below the workroom windows. There had been a drainpipe, a broad stone ledge, and a little iron catch Clara could lift with her thumb. At twelve, she had considered this an excellent arrangement. At twenty-six, with a drawing case banging against her hip and rain collecting in the seams of the glass, she was less certain. She had first tried the front door. A young footman admitted her into the hall, where she stood beneath a portrait of a spaniel while he went to inquire. He returned with Mrs. Finch, who had taught Clara to wipe her shoes before entering that same hall. “I am sorry, Miss Vale,” Mrs. Finch said. “Mr. Ashcombe has had the upstairs rooms closed for the inventory.” “I need only my mother’s portfolio.” “I told him so.” Clara adjusted the strap of her case. “And?” “He will be home after three. You may come back then.” It was nearly noon. The post would leave the village at four with Clara’s reply to a publisher who wanted to see six finished plates within a fortnight. She had brought three. The other studies were somewhere in Briarcombe Hall. “Did he say the portfolio was still here?” Mrs. Finch glanced toward the footman. “He did not know what I meant by it.” That was worse than a refusal. Clara thanked her and went out with such good manners that she hoped Mrs. Finch recognized them as a warning. Round the side of the house, the kitchen gardens were smaller than Clara remembered. Half the frames stood empty. Her mother’s espaliered pear still gripped the wall, though nobody had cut back the new growth. Clara stopped beneath it. Ruth would have disliked the untidy branches; she would also have found a reason to wait until tomorrow before touching them. The conservatory door was locked. Above it, the panes rose in a slant to the stonework of the house. Clara had come prepared to ask, not to climb. She had worn a plain walking dress, sensible boots, and the good coat on which she had recently spent more money than wisdom permitted. She took off the coat and folded it beneath a bench. The narrow service path behind the conservatory led to the low wall. There was no ladder. She used a stack of empty plant pots to gain the first foothold, put a boot onto the iron framework, and pulled herself up. At twelve, someone else had carried the heavy things. Ruth, usually. Halfway across, Clara found that the old drainpipe had been replaced. The new one stood several inches farther from the wall. She could still reach the ledge if she stepped onto a rib of iron between two panes. She tested it. It held. The sky darkened, and her dry papers seemed suddenly very far away, on the ground in their case. She moved quickly. The stone ledge took her weight, but a piece broke from its outer edge and dropped through a pane below. Glass rang out in the empty conservatory. Clara flattened herself against the wall. No one called out. Rain ticked against the roof. She found the catch with cold fingers and lifted it. The window did not move. Mrs. Ashcombe had complained for years that it stuck. Apparently someone had listened at last. The frame was new, painted cream. Clara tried the next window along; its lower sash rose an inch, then two. She got her fingers beneath it and pushed. A warm, dusty room opened beyond. It was not the workroom. She could see a writing desk, several covered chairs, and a pair of men’s boots beside the hearth. Clara looked down at the broken pane. She could not cross the roof again without someone seeing her. She swung her case through first and followed, catching her skirt under one knee. “May I ask,” a man said, “whether you generally arrive like this?” Clara remained kneeling on the window seat. He stood just inside the door, hat in hand, looking more astonished than angry. He was tall, with rain on the shoulders of a dark coat and an expression that suggested he had been interrupted in the middle of a calculation. “No,” she said. “Generally the window opens on the workroom.” His gaze moved to her muddy boot. “That explains very little.” “I am Clara Vale. Mrs. Finch told me you would not be home until three.” “She expected me after three. I had not expected to find anyone in my bedroom before then.” Clara looked at the boots by the hearth. There was little to say to that. She pulled her skirt free and climbed down, keeping hold of the drawing case. “You must be Mr. Ashcombe.” “I am. You have broken a conservatory pane.” “Yes.” “And entered my house without permission.” “Yes. I came for my mother’s portfolio. I asked at the door.” He set his hat on the desk. “Mrs. Finch sent word that you wished to collect some drawings. The rooms are being inventoried. Had you waited, I could have looked into it.” Clara had heard many versions of *looked into it* since Ruth’s death. Some people meant to help; others had already forgotten what they were to look for. “The publisher cannot wait as easily as I can,” she said. “And I was told the conservatory is to be sold.” His expression sharpened. “Who told you that?” “I asked in the village.” “The building is not for sale. Some of its contents are.” “Then I had better find out whether my mother’s work is among them.” “You cannot simply take what you find.” “I know what her portfolio looks like.” “That may not settle what belongs to you.” Clara opened her mouth, then closed it. He was right, and he had the advantage of saying so in a room she had entered through his window. Edward Ashcombe looked at the case against her side. “What is in there?” “My drawings. Copies of three studies we made here. The originals are in the portfolio—blue cloth, with a broken leather fastening. My mother kept the watercolour sheets between blotters because the roof leaked above her table.” She heard her voice catching on the last sentence and steadied it. “I need to compare them before I send the plates.” Edward went to the desk. Beneath a folded list lay a sheet of pale paper. He held it by its edges, turning it toward her. A branch of quince crossed the page. Ruth’s tidy letters named the specimen at the bottom; beside them, in Clara’s smaller hand, was the date. “I found this among my aunt’s papers,” he said. “Is it one of them?” Clara came closer but did not touch it. She remembered drawing the thorns. Ruth had made her do them again. “Yes,” she said. “There should be a sheet of early blossom with it. And one showing the fruit cut open.” Edward looked down at the list. Rain came harder against the window Clara had left raised. She went to lower it, but the new sash caught above her head. “Leave it,” he said. “I shall see to it.” He came over, reached past her, and worked the sash down with both hands. Clara stepped aside, annoyed to be grateful. “The drawings have been listed with a cabinet,” he said. “I had thought it contained my aunt’s papers.” “Where is the cabinet?” “In the conservatory.” They both looked toward the rain-streaked glass. Somewhere below, through the broken pane, water was falling onto the tiled floor. Edward picked up his hat again. “We will go down and look. By the stairs, Miss Vale.”

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished opening chapter that demonstrates genuine craft across nearly every dimension. Let me work through the piece carefully. The prose style is controlled and precise without being cold. The writer has found a voice that suits the period and the character simultaneously—dry, observational, with a light ironic touch that never tips into parody. "She had worn a plain walking dress, sensible boots, and the good coat on which she had recently spent more money than wisdom permitted" is exactly the kind of sentence that does multiple things at once: it establishes Clara's financial situation, her vanity, her practicality, and her self-awareness, all without a word of explanation. This is the opposite of tell-don't-show. The chapter follows its plan faithfully. Clara arrives, is refused entry, climbs the conservatory roof (with the old foothold crumbling, as planned), enters the wrong room, and Edward finds her. The portfolio is named, and Edward recognizes it from the inventory. Every beat from the plan is executed, and executed with specificity rather than summary. Character work is strong. Clara is established through action and detail rather than description: she folds her coat under a bench before climbing, she steadies her voice when it catches on a sentence about her mother, she opens her mouth to argue and then closes it when she recognizes Edward is right. These are the marks of a character with genuine interiority. Edward is introduced economically—"an expression that suggested he had been interrupted in the middle of a calculation"—and his line "She expected me after three. I had not expected to find anyone in my bedroom before then" is both funny and character-revealing. The dialogue is particularly strong. It's terse, purposeful, and carries subtext. "I know what her portfolio looks like." / "That may not settle what belongs to you." This exchange does real work: it establishes the central conflict, shows Edward's legal-mindedness, and shows Clara's instinct to assert ownership through knowledge rather than documentation. The final exchange—"We will go down and look. By the stairs, Miss Vale"—is a small, perfect comic beat that also establishes the power dynamic without belaboring it. The period detail is handled exactly as the plan promised: through objects and actions. Drawing paper, a broken pane, a new cream-painted window frame, a quince branch on pale paper, blotters protecting watercolor sheets. None of this is explained; it's simply present. The emotional register is well-calibrated. The moment where Clara's voice catches on "because the roof leaked above her table" is the chapter's most affecting beat, and it's earned because the writer has been so restrained up to that point. The grief for Ruth is present without being announced. If there are weaknesses, they are minor. "Rain ticked against the roof" is a slightly familiar image. The observation that "the kitchen gardens were smaller than Clara remembered" is a well-worn device for establishing time's passage, though it's used briefly and not overworked. The chapter is perhaps slightly front-loaded with setup before the climb, though this is necessary and handled efficiently. The metaphorical language is sparse and almost always earns its place. There's no purple prose, no forced poetry. The writer resists the temptation to make the windows into heavy symbols—they're just windows, used practically, which is exactly what the plan called for. Mrs. Finch's brief appearance is perfectly calibrated: she's present, she's knowing, she's loyal to both parties, and she doesn't overstay her welcome. The chapter ends at exactly the right moment, with the two characters about to descend together, the broken pane letting in rain, and the conflict properly established. It's a clean, confident close. # Chapter Two: What Is in the Inventory Clara followed Edward down a staircase wide enough to have accommodated the cabinet entire. At its foot, Mrs. Finch was standing beside the front door with Clara’s good coat over one arm. “I found this outside,” she said. Clara took it. The hem was dry, which meant Mrs. Finch had brought it in before the rain began in earnest. “There is glass in the conservatory,” Edward said. “I broke a pane.” Mrs. Finch looked from him to Clara’s muddy boots and back. “Shall I have someone clear it, sir?” “Please. I want to examine the cabinet this afternoon.” “It is covered, sir, but I should keep off that stretch of floor.” She went to find a broom without asking why they meant to examine it together. Edward waited until she was out of hearing. “You need not have let me claim the pane.” “I did break it.” “I shall pay to mend it. It is my pane.” “That is a convenient principle.” He opened the door to the conservatory. “I thought so.” Rain blurred the glass overhead, but little reached the plants. A sheet of canvas lay over part of the tiled floor, wet beneath the broken pane. Clara smelled damp earth and the sharp, familiar scent of crushed geranium leaves. The warmth was gone. Several tubs had been moved away from the walls, and a bare space showed where Ruth had kept her propagation bench. Edward led her to a tall cabinet against the inner wall. A card tied to its handle bore a number. The same number appeared in the inventory book he carried. “‘One glazed specimen cabinet,’” he read, “‘with contents comprising botanical papers and materials.’” “Botanical papers,” Clara repeated. “That is one way of putting it.” “The buyer asked for the conservatory fittings. I included the cabinet after my aunt’s secretary put it on the list. I did not inspect what was inside.” Edward unlocked it. On its upper shelves stood jars of seeds, two small presses, and an assortment of packets tied with string. Below were stacks of paper folded in wrappers. Clara found a study of a white clematis on top of one pile. The colour had browned around the edges, but Ruth’s notes were unmistakable. “There must have been a hundred sheets,” she said. “This is only a dozen.” Edward opened another wrapper. Inside were instructions for mixing washes, written in Mrs. Ashcombe’s hand, and a bill for new glass dating from fifteen years ago. “The papers may have been moved,” he said. “Or thrown out.” “I have asked for nothing to be discarded until the inventory is finished.” “Someone may have asked before you.” She heard how sharply she had said it. Edward replaced the papers in their wrapper, taking care to align the corners. He had done nothing more than inherit a room left in disorder. “Who was Mrs. Ashcombe’s secretary?” Clara asked. “Mr. Pike. He left last month for a position in Bath. My aunt dictated to him when her hands troubled her.” “Did he know my mother?” “He knew her name. I cannot say how well.” Clara lifted a packet of dried specimens. Beneath it was a row of wooden labels, each with a plant’s name, a date, and a short description of where it had been grown. Ruth wrote the letters with small straight strokes. Clara could see her bent over the kitchen table on a winter evening, turning a label to catch the light while she sharpened the pencil with a knife. “This one was under the north glass,” she said, holding up a label. “It never thrived here. She kept moving it because Mrs. Ashcombe wanted a drawing before it flowered.” Edward looked along the shelves. “My aunt told me she grew most of these plants.” “She chose what she wished to grow.” Clara set the label down. “Mother found a place for it, and kept it alive when the place was wrong.” He looked at her, then returned his attention to the cabinet. “I did not know there was such a distinction.” “You have not been here long.” “No.” He offered no defense of his aunt, and Clara found it difficult to stay angry with him while he held a heavy wrapper open so she could read what was inside. At the far end of the conservatory she spotted the pear’s reflection, its unruly branches dark against the glass. Ruth had complained about that tree every spring. It was easier to think of her with a knife in her hand than to read the careful labels and remember she would never make another. “Does the buyer know about the papers?” she asked. “He has my description in the agreement.” “When is he coming?” “On Thursday.” It was Monday. Clara laid down the packet. Edward closed the inventory book. “I can write today and tell him there may be drawings to remove. We should find the portfolio first.” “There *are* drawings to remove.” “We have found drawings. We have not established that everything in the cabinet belongs to you.” She stared at him. “I made the quince sheet.” “I believe you made it.” He glanced at the open shelves. “I also know my aunt kept her correspondence here, and that your mother worked on the book. I need to see what was agreed.” The distinction would take time Clara did not have. She could copy from the quince sheet today, if he would let her take it, but the clematis was too damaged and the others were missing. “I must answer the publisher by four,” she said. “Can you tell him you are retrieving the studies?” “I can tell him anything. I would rather know whether it is true.” Mrs. Finch returned with a housemaid and a broom. She stopped at the edge of the canvas. “There are more papers upstairs,” she said. “Mrs. Ashcombe used the little workroom in the east wing once the roof over this one began to drip.” Clara turned. “The room above the pear wall?” “That’s the one. We took a press up there last winter.” Mrs. Finch handed the broom to the younger woman. “I cannot tell you what was in it.” “May we look?” Clara asked Edward. He checked his watch, then the open cabinet. “After we put these back. Mrs. Finch, would you mind fetching the key?” “I know where it is, sir.” When she had gone, Clara began tying the wrappers. Edward took up the next pile without being asked. Across the glass roof, the rain eased, and the cabinet’s empty lower shelf came slowly into view.

The transition from Clara's grief to the practical question about the buyer is slightly abrupt, though one could argue this is true to Clara's character. The chapter is perhaps slightly low on tension for a middle chapter—the conflict is present but the stakes feel muted compared to what the plan promises. The prose is clean and controlled throughout. # Chapter Three: The People Who Remember The key to the east-wing workroom was not where Mrs. Finch expected it to be. “I put it on the hook myself,” she said, regarding the empty hook beside the linen cupboard. “Mr. Pike took keys when he made his list. He returned all the others.” Edward tried the key to the adjoining room. It turned halfway and stuck. “Please don’t force it,” Clara said. “The lock always did that when Mother was cross with it.” “What did she do?” “She sent for Mrs. Finch.” Mrs. Finch gave Clara a look, then reached past Edward and lifted the door by its handle as she turned the key. The lock gave. Inside, the air smelled of paste and cold ashes. A worktable stood beneath the window, its top scored by knife cuts. There were shelves of boxes, a washstand, and a chair with one leg propped on a folded card. Clara remembered sitting in that chair, though it had been even less steady then. Mrs. Ashcombe had kept a cushion on it for visitors; Ruth had never bothered with the cushion. Mrs. Finch crossed to the window. “Your mother took her press away from the damp, Miss Vale. I saw her carry it up.” “When?” “The winter before she left. Mrs. Ashcombe had a cough, and your mother came to set out some of the drawings while she was confined upstairs.” Ruth had said little about that winter except that the cold had spoiled the conservatory’s early bulbs. Clara went to the table. Its shallow drawers held pencils, jars of dried paint, and a block of paper with three sheets remaining. In the deepest she found a folder of loose studies. The first showed the quince Edward had brought downstairs. Clara laid it aside. Under it was a page of seedpods drawn in Ruth’s hand, followed by an iris Clara had made at nineteen. She remembered the iris. The petals had pleased her; the bent stalk had not. On the sheet, the stalk had been corrected, not erased but drawn over with a clean, confident line. Ruth’s line. “She changed it.” Edward came to stand on the other side of the table. “Is it damaged?” “No. Better.” Clara held up the page. “I’d asked her not to touch this one.” Mrs. Finch, examining a stack of boxes, said, “She was pleased with it. She showed me when the paint was dry.” “She might have told me she had improved it.” “I daresay she meant to.” Clara set the iris down. Ruth had been able to argue for twenty minutes over the proper shape of a leaf; she could also avoid a conversation for a year if it was likely to wound. Clara had inherited at least one of those habits. Edward opened a folded sheet he had found beneath the folder. It was a list headed *Plates for the Briarcombe Volume*. Mrs. Ashcombe had written names of plants in one column. In the next, she had put *Mrs. Vale* against several studies and *Clara* against others. For the iris she had written *both*. “There,” Edward said. Clara came round to look. “There should be more than these.” “There’s no portfolio here.” It was encouraging to see her name on the list. It was less encouraging that Mrs. Ashcombe had not written what would happen to the drawings when they were finished. Clara looked at the blank space beneath the last entry. “Did your aunt ever begin the book?” she asked. “Mr. Pike said she discussed it with a publisher some years ago. I found no contract.” Mrs. Finch shut a box. “She discussed it whenever the plants were blooming. In winter she said she would settle it in spring.” “She was ill at the end,” Edward said. “Yes, sir. Before that, she was busy.” Mrs. Finch’s tone was respectful. Clara did not think Edward had missed the difference. He took the list to the window for better light. “The publisher you wrote to—is he the same one?” “No. Mrs. Ashcombe’s man lost interest long ago. I found another through a bookseller in town.” “Will he want work you made with your mother?” “He asked for my plates. I told him I could supply them.” Edward looked up. “I can,” Clara said. “If I can find the originals and make the finished drawings in time. I did not tell him they were in a house I could not get into.” Mrs. Finch drew the chair away from the table. “You might use that for copying, Miss Vale. It still needs the card under the leg.” Clara gave her a grateful glance and opened her drawing case. She had brought tracing paper, pencils, and clean sheets. The publisher wanted to judge her hand; she could at least send copies of work that was hers. Edward spread the loose pages across the table. “Which do you need?” Clara chose the iris and two studies of quince fruit. Mrs. Finch brought a board from the cupboard so Clara could work without marking the table. Edward tried to make room for her elbows and knocked a jar of chalk against his cuff. For half an hour they were quiet. Clara had nearly finished the iris when she noticed he was still sorting drawings, putting those marked in Ruth’s hand beside those marked in hers. “You can tell them apart?” she asked. “Your mother wrote the plant names before drawing them. You left space for the names afterward.” Clara looked at the sheet beneath her hand. It was true. Ruth liked to know precisely what she meant to draw. Clara liked to see what the plant offered first. Mrs. Finch came in to announce that the post boy would call shortly. Clara blotted the last line and packed the copies. “I can take these,” she said to Edward. “The copies, I mean.” “Yes. You made them here, in front of us.” He lifted the iris original with care. “I should like to keep these safe until we find the others.” Clara nodded. She wished she could take it, altered stalk and all, but the paper was dry here and she knew where it lay. At the door, Edward said, “I will speak to the buyer once we know what has happened to the portfolio. It may be simplest not to mention the matter elsewhere until then.” “Mrs. Finch already knows.” “She is hardly likely to start a rumour.” “I wasn’t thinking of rumours.” Clara tucked her case under her arm. “I will tell the publisher which drawings I have and which I’m looking for. He ought to know what I can deliver.” Edward stood aside to let her pass. Mrs. Finch was waiting at the stairs with Clara’s coat. Down in the hall, the young footman opened the front door for her without being asked.

The pacing is even throughout, which is a strength for coherence but means there are no peaks of intensity. # Chapter Four: The Portfolio The publisher’s reply arrived on Wednesday morning. He liked the three studies Clara had sent. Could she bring him the original sheets next week, together with four more suitable for reproduction? He had underlined *next week*. Clara read the letter twice at her lodgings, then walked to Briarcombe before she could draft an answer she would regret. Mrs. Finch admitted her by the front door. “Mr. Ashcombe is upstairs,” she said. “I’ve found the east-room key, though it took the cook to tell me where Mr. Pike had put it.” “Where?” “In the drawer marked *keys*. We had stopped looking there after the first day.” Edward met them on the landing. He had a ledger under one arm and ink on the side of his hand. “I found the account for the roof repairs,” he told Clara. “There is a charge for moving your mother’s press and a large wooden case. The workmen put them in the dry room above the conservatory.” “The workroom we searched?” “No. The room on the other side of the passage. It was locked when my aunt became ill.” Mrs. Finch held up the key. “I shall fetch the dust sheets. It has not been opened for months.” The dry room contained little beyond a broken screen, two rolled carpets, and a press under a cloth. They moved the screen and found a lighter rectangle on the floor where the wooden case had once stood. “Someone took it away,” Edward said. “Or moved it again.” Clara knelt to examine two parallel scuffs. They ran toward the wall beneath the window. There, a recess had been boarded over with shelves. “That window used to open onto the roof,” she said. “Mother brought the press in that way when the stairs were full of builders. There was space behind the shelves then.” Edward pulled at the lowest shelf. It lifted free. So did the one above it. Behind them stood a narrow wooden case, wedged between the wall and a length of old pipe. Clara reached in. The case would not budge. “We may have to take the rest down,” Edward said. “The pipe catches at the back. If I can get round to the window, I can push it clear.” He looked at the window, then at the roof outside it. “This one is painted shut.” Clara set her bag down and took a thin knife from her pencil case. She ran its blade along the seam. “You carry that for drawing?” “For sharpening pencils. And opening windows, when people paint over the catches.” “I see you have learned from experience.” The sash rose a few inches and stuck. Edward joined her, pulling carefully while Clara pressed at the swollen frame. With a groan, it opened far enough for her to climb through. “Mrs. Finch will object to the mud,” Edward said. “Then don’t fall on her carpets.” Clara stepped onto the narrow strip of roof. There was no rain today, only a wind that caught at her skirt. She moved to the outer side of the recess and found a gap where the old window frame met the wall. The wooden case had been pushed in at an angle; its corner pressed against the pipe. “Can you see it?” Edward called. “I can reach it. Push from your side when I say.” He braced himself behind the shelves. Clara wedged her fingers against the case, lifted, and felt it shift. Edward pushed. The wood scraped across the floor inside. “Stop. You’ll catch the portfolio under it.” She could see a strip of blue cloth beneath the case. Edward eased it back while she pulled the cloth free, inch by inch. The broken leather fastening came after it. For a moment she could only hold the portfolio against the wall. The cloth was dusty and faded where the light had reached it. Ruth had sewn the small tear at one corner with brown thread. “Have you got it?” Edward asked. “Yes.” Clara climbed back in. Edward cleared a space on the floor and fetched two boards to lay across the trestles left by the builders. He did not ask to open the portfolio. Clara undid the fastening herself. Inside were studies of quince, iris, hellebore, and dozens more, separated by blotting paper. She turned them slowly, checking for damp. Ruth’s annotations crowded some margins. Clara’s drawings were there too, including seven sheets she could take to the publisher with little more work. “She kept them flat,” Clara said. “She took more trouble with them than with the roof.” That surprised a laugh out of her. Edward smiled, then began lifting the old case away from the trestles. At the back of the portfolio lay a packet tied with blue ribbon. Its wrapper read *For the Briarcombe Volume*, in Mrs. Ashcombe’s hand. Clara opened it. There were proposed page layouts, lists of plants, and passages of text describing how each specimen had been grown. Edward leaned over a page. “I remember her writing at that desk.” Clara read the opening paragraph. Mrs. Ashcombe called the garden her own experiment. Farther on she thanked “my excellent Mrs. Vale” for her care of the plants. Clara searched the remaining pages for Ruth’s observations and found them copied into the text, often word for word. There was no note saying so. “She meant to give her thanks,” Edward said quietly. “She did give them.” Clara touched a line Ruth used to say aloud while she worked. “Mother told her this. I remember.” He read it again. “It ought to have her name beside it.” They turned another page. A proposed list of plates credited Mrs. Ashcombe as editor. The space beside *illustrations* was blank. “Perhaps she had not decided,” Edward said. “Perhaps not.” Clara slipped the page back beneath its wrapper. “May I take the drawings I need on Monday?” “We will make a list before you go. I’ll have the buyer’s agreement brought here so we know exactly what must be changed.” “Thank you.” She meant it. She also wished the answer had been simpler. Mrs. Finch appeared in the doorway carrying dust sheets. She looked at the open window, Clara’s dusty skirt, and the portfolio on the boards. “You found it,” she said. “We did.” “Good. I’ve brought cloths for your hands. Tea is ready when you’ve finished deciding what to do with it.” Clara took a cloth. There was dust in the stitching of the portfolio, and a brown thread had come loose at one end. She tucked it back with her fingernail before closing the cover.
