# Chapter 1 — The Back Room The bell over the door rang so violently that Carys looked up expecting broken glass. A man in a dark coat came in sideways, glanced at the front window, and said, “Have you got a back door?” “Yes.” “Could I use it?” “No.” “Excellent. A woman of principle.” He took a breath. “Is there somewhere I could stand for thirty seconds where I can’t be seen from the street?” Two men with cameras hurried past the window. The man flattened himself against a display of cookbooks, upsetting a paperback about soup. Carys set down their pencil. “Do you want to buy anything?” He snatched the first book off the table. “Desperately.” “You’re holding it upside down.” He turned it. “Now I want it even more.” “Through there.” Carys pointed to the curtain behind the counter. “Don’t touch the boxes. They’re stacked badly.” He slipped through it. His coat caught on the curtain rail; Carys heard him swear, then catch the falling rail before it struck the floor. The two photographers came back. One tried the door while the other peered through the glass. Carys went to the front before either could enter. “Looking for someone?” they asked. “A bloke in a black coat,” said the first man. “Came down here.” “Several have.” “This one you’d remember.” “That isn’t always a recommendation.” The second man, still searching the shelves with his eyes, asked, “Has he gone through?” Carys considered the storeroom, which had no exit. “Nobody’s gone through the shop.” After another look down the street, the men moved on. Carys waited until their footsteps had faded. “You can come out.” Rhys Vale emerged holding the curtain rail. “Where does this go?” “Above the curtain.” “I’d gathered that much.” Carys took it from him and laid it on the counter. Up close, he looked less like his posters: rain in his hair, a red mark on his cheek where the coat collar had pressed it. Carys had seen three of his films and an interview last night, after a customer mentioned he was coming to town. None of that was information he needed. “You owe me for the book,” they said. “And a curtain rail, apparently. I’m Rhys.” “Yes.” His smile widened. “You can say it. Most people do.” “Rhys.” For a moment he seemed pleased. Then he caught their expression. “What did I pick?” He turned the book over. *Small Hours: Poems from the Welsh Coast*. “How fortunate. I’m a man of enormous literary seriousness.” “It was beside a cookbook about soup.” “I was torn between them.” “Eight pounds.” He took out his wallet. “Eight pounds for saving my life?” “The hiding was free.” “And the rail?” “Depends whether I can put it back.” He paid with a twenty. Carys opened the till and discovered they had pulled out the five-pound notes. They put them back, found a ten, then managed to drop two pound coins under the counter. Rhys politely looked elsewhere while they retrieved them. It made things worse. “Do they come in often?” Carys asked, handing him his change. “The photographers? It’s our first date. I’m hoping there won’t be a second.” “They might still be outside.” “Then perhaps I should browse.” “You’ve bought something.” “I could be a slow browser.” Carys indicated the aisles. “Try not to break any more fittings.” He moved toward the shelves, but stopped beside the table. “You knew who I was when I came in.” “Yes.” “And you hid me anyway.” “I’d have hidden anyone with those two after them.” “That’s generous.” “I was going to say it was bad for business having photographers in the doorway.” “Ah.” He held a hand against his chest. “You know, most people let me keep the nicer explanation.” Carys looked down at the rail. One end was bent; Mair had put it up years ago, insisting she could manage without a drill. “Would you prefer I lied?” Rhys’s answer came too quickly. “I’m used to it.” He seemed to hear himself. “Sorry. That sounded mysterious. Very annoying of me.” “It did a bit.” “I’ve had a long morning.” Carys fetched the step stool. Rhys caught it by one leg when it snagged on a rug. “May I?” he asked. “You’ve already demonstrated your way with the rail.” “I also caught it.” “Hold the stool, then.” Carys climbed up and pushed the rail into its brackets. It settled, crooked but secure. Rhys stood beneath with both hands on the stool and his face tipped toward them. “Is it straight?” Carys asked. “Almost.” “Honest answer?” “Left side’s low.” They adjusted it. “Now?” “Better.” Carys climbed down. The shop felt strangely close, though Rhys had stepped away. He examined a shelf of local history. “I used to come in here when it belonged to your aunt.” Carys turned. “You knew Mair?” “She told me I couldn’t read the comics on the floor because people would trip over me. I was about twelve.” “That sounds like her.” “She let me sit behind the counter when it rained.” “She’d deny it.” “She did. Every time.” He smiled, but this one arrived slowly. “I was in the pub over the road this morning. Three people asked if I was glad to be home.” “It’s an ordinary question.” “I know. I told all three yes.” He ran his thumb along the book’s spine. “One of them knew me when I lived here. I couldn’t remember his name.” Carys thought of the men with cameras, and of the film-star smile Rhys had worn even while crouching behind the cookbooks. “You could ask him next time,” they said. Rhys laughed once. “That’s what my mother said.” “She sounds sensible.” “She’ll be delighted you think so.” Outside, a van stopped to unload crates at the café. Rhys moved to the window, then checked himself and stood back. “They’ve gone,” Carys said. “I’d have told you.” “I know.” He looked at the book in his hand. “Do you recommend it?” Carys opened their mouth to recommend *Small Hours*, then saw its cover and felt heat rise in their face. “You’ve got it already.” “So I have.” “The third poem’s good,” they said. “The first one tries too hard.” He glanced at the first page. “I’ll trust you.” “You haven’t read it.” “No. I meant your opinion.” At the door, he paused. “Thank you, Carys.” They had not told him their name. Following their glance, he pointed to the small handwritten sign behind the till: **ASK CARYS FOR RECOMMENDATIONS**. “Good advertising,” he said, and went out into the rain.

[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of creative writing that demonstrates genuine craft across nearly every dimension. Let me examine it carefully. **Dialogue and Voice** The dialogue is the chapter's greatest strength. Rhys and Carys have genuinely distinct voices that never blur into each other. Rhys's lines carry the practiced ease of someone who has learned to charm: "Eight pounds for saving my life?" and "I was torn between them" are exactly the kind of light, deflecting wit the profile demands. Carys's responses are economical and dry without being cold: "The hiding was free" and "Depends whether I can put it back" are perfectly calibrated. The exchange about the curtain rail is particularly good — it establishes their dynamic through action and banter simultaneously. The dialogue does real work. It reveals character, advances the scene, and contains genuine wit that lands rather than straining. The line "I'm used to it" followed by Rhys catching himself — "Sorry. That sounded mysterious. Very annoying of me" — is a small masterpiece of characterization: the ego, the self-awareness, the performance of self-awareness. **Character Consistency** Both characters are rendered faithfully to their profiles. Rhys's fragile ego appears in "Most people let me keep the nicer explanation" and his checking whether the photographers are gone before catching himself. His charm is present but not cartoonish. Carys's interior fluster is shown through the dropped coins, the misrecommended book, the heat rising in their face — all small, specific, earned moments. The detail about Carys having watched an interview "last night, after a customer mentioned he was coming to town" is a perfect quiet revelation of their interest. **Following the Plan** The chapter follows its plan closely: Rhys ducks in, Carys hides him with a technically truthful answer, the compliments meet brisk replies, Carys privately flusters (the coins, the book recommendation), Rhys notices they haven't mentioned a film, and he admits tiredness about being asked if he's glad to be home. He leaves before Carys can answer. The accidental purchase is taken. All boxes checked, but never mechanically. **Prose Quality** The prose is spare and controlled. There is no purple prose, no forced metaphor. The few descriptive touches are precise and functional: "rain in his hair, a red mark on his cheek where the coat collar had pressed it." The observation that he looked "less like his posters" is economical characterization. The line "The shop felt strangely close, though Rhys had stepped away" is the chapter's most poetic moment — and it earns its place because it's grounded in physical reality and emotional truth simultaneously. **Minor Criticisms** The chapter is nearly flawless, which makes small issues stand out. The Mair backstory is introduced smoothly but the transition from banter to genuine conversation (the "glad to be home" admission) happens slightly quickly — though this may be intentional given the chapter's length constraints. The ending with the name sign is clever but perhaps slightly too neat, a touch of writerly tidiness that resolves the small mystery a little too comfortably. These are minor quibbles. **Creativity** The scenario is familiar (famous person hides in small shop) but the execution is fresh. The curtain rail as a running physical gag that also creates proximity is inventive. The technically truthful misleading answer to the photographers is handled with admirable restraint — shown in two lines rather than belabored. The book recommendation mistake is a perfect small comedy of embarrassment. **Overall** This is professional-quality literary fiction. It executes its plan faithfully, renders its characters with nuance and consistency, writes dialogue that crackles with distinct voice, and maintains tonal control throughout. The lightness is genuinely earned. It is not a masterpiece — the scenario remains somewhat conventional and the emotional stakes are necessarily limited in a first chapter — but it is excellent work. Rhys Vale held yesterday’s purchase against his chest. His hair was damp, though he had apparently remembered to fasten his coat. “You were right,” he said. “About the third poem?” “About the first. Can I exchange the book?” “You’ve read it.” “Some of it.” “There’s a crease in the spine.” “It came like that.” Carys looked at him. “I put the crease in the spine,” he said. “I’d still like another book.” “That’s a different request.” The rose gardener approached the till with two volumes, one notably more expensive than the other. “This says it’ll tell me what’s eating the leaves.” “Does it have pictures?” Carys asked. “Appalling ones.” “Then I’d start there.” Carys rang up the sale. Rhys stood to one side, turning *Small Hours* in his hands without opening it. Once the customer left, he put the book on the counter. “I don’t need my money back.” “That’s a relief. I’ve spent it.” “I thought I might try the one you’d have given me if I’d come in on purpose.” “You’d have to tell me what you like.” “That seems fair.” Carys considered his face. He looked expectant, and they felt the familiar, foolish urge to make him laugh. “You could tell me what you didn’t like about this one.” “The first poem knew how I was supposed to feel before I’d started it.” He tapped the cover. “The one about the ferry was good.” “It’s about a bus.” “The ferry one, then, is better than I realised.” Carys laughed before they could stop themselves. Rhys looked so gratified that they turned toward the shelves. The bell rang again. “Rhys?” said the man coming in. He wore a green wool hat and carried a parcel under one arm. “Well, look at you. Mrs Bowen said you were back.” Rhys turned. His smile appeared at once, broad and easy. “Hello.” “Gareth Pritchard. You used to help us stack chairs after the summer concert. Or you were meant to.” “Gareth! Of course.” “You hid under the stage with a packet of crisps.” “That sounds much more likely.” Gareth laughed and turned to Carys. “I’ve got those maps your assistant asked about. I’ll leave them here?” “Thanks. Elin will be in Saturday.” He set the parcel down but did not go. “My wife’s seen all your films,” he told Rhys. “She says you’re far too thin in person.” “I’ll take that up with the camera.” “You remember the concert hall? They’ve done up the roof at last.” “I heard.” Rhys nodded. “It was about time.” “Course, you were there when it leaked onto the piano.” Rhys hesitated. Only Carys, watching him, seemed to notice. “Every summer, wasn’t it?” he said. “Just the one. You and Sian carried the piano bench out while old Mr Davies held an umbrella over the keys.” “Yes,” Rhys said. “Sian. I’d forgotten the umbrella.” Gareth smiled, satisfied. “Tell your mother I asked after her. And don’t be a stranger at the concert on Friday.” “I won’t.” After he left, Rhys kept looking at the door. Then he picked up the book and examined its price sticker. “You didn’t remember him,” Carys said. “I know him now.” “You’re very convincing.” Rhys set the book down. “Would you rather I’d said I didn’t know who he was?” “No. I meant you handled it kindly.” “That isn’t how you said it.” Carys crossed their arms. “I spoke before I’d thought.” “It must be lovely, being certain what everyone else ought to do.” They stared at him. Rhys’s jaw tightened. “That wasn’t fair.” “No,” Carys said. “It wasn’t.” He looked toward the door again, but a delivery van pulled up outside. Carys recognised the driver and swore under their breath. “What?” “Stock. He’s early.” “Do you want a hand?” “I can manage.” The driver came in carrying a cardboard box nearly as wide as the doorway. “Where do you want the rest?” “How much rest?” Carys asked. “Four more like this.” Carys had cleared space for them at the back, but had not moved the returns piled in front of it. Rhys saw the boxes, then looked away while Carys considered the distance. “One box,” they told him. “Understood.” “You’ll have to take your coat off.” He did, hanging it on a peg already occupied by Carys’s scarf. They shifted books for ten minutes. Rhys carried two boxes despite the agreement, but left the third when Carys pointed at it. The driver brought in the rest. “These have been labelled children’s,” Rhys said, opening the top of a box. Inside were three dense volumes on maritime law. “Demanding children.” “Don’t open any more. I need to check the invoice first.” He folded the flap down. “I was trying to be useful.” “You were. Thank you.” His hands stayed on the box a moment longer. “You could have said so while I was being useful.” Carys glanced at him. “Would you have carried them faster?” “Probably.” “That explains why you needed telling.” He gave them a reluctant smile. It was easier to see the tiredness around his eyes without the coat and the hurried smile he had given Gareth. “I was sharp with you,” Carys said. “Before.” “So was I.” Rhys straightened. “Gareth’s a nice man. I remembered the concert as soon as he mentioned the piano. Not him.” “You don’t have to explain it to me.” “I know.” He rubbed dust from his palms. “That makes it slightly easier to do.” Carys went to the fiction shelves and pulled out a slim, battered novel. “This one,” they said. “No one in it knows what they’re doing, and the writer doesn’t pretend otherwise.” Rhys took it. “A pointed recommendation?” “You asked what I liked.” He read the back cover. “Can I buy it without returning the other?” “Yes. And there’s no charge for the box.” “That’s generous.” “It’s also still in the doorway. Could you move it before you go?”

Carys's observation of this, their initial misreading of it as performance, and their correction ("I meant you handled it kindly") followed by Rhys's sharp retort and near-immediate recognition that it was unfair — all of this tracks precisely with the profiles. Rhys's ego wound when Carys's tone seems contemptuous, his cutting remark, and his awkward acknowledgment of it ("That wasn't fair" / "No. It wasn't.") is handled with admirable restraint. The Welsh setting is present through Gareth and the concert hall reference without being touristically described. OVERALL: This is confident, disciplined literary fiction with genuine romantic tension. The characters feel real, the dialogue crackles, and the chapter advances both plot and relationship with economy and intelligence. # Chapter 3 — Other People’s Business By six o’clock on Thursday, Carys had counted seven chairs, eight cups and nine books on the table. Mrs Pritchard always brought her own copy, but there was still a book too many. “Elin put it there,” said Mrs Pritchard, following their gaze. “She said your actor might come.” “He’s not my actor.” “I didn’t say he was.” “You said it in a very particular way.” Mrs Pritchard settled into the armchair by the window. “I’ve never said anything in a general way.” Rhys arrived as Carys was filling the kettle. He stood just inside the door with his coat dripping onto the mat and the little novel Carys had sold him tucked under his arm. “Is this an invitation-only gathering?” he asked. “No,” said Carys. “Though we usually take our coats off before sitting down.” “I could stand.” “You’ll drip standing, too.” He took off the coat. Mrs Pritchard watched him find the peg, then returned pointedly to her book. Carys handed him a cup. “Tea?” “Yes, please.” “Milk?” “Yes.” “Sugar?” “None.” “I’ve asked you enough questions to start charging admission.” “I nearly asked where the toilets were.” “Back room. Don’t pull down the curtain.” It was the first time he had heard them mention it since Tuesday. He smiled into his cup. The others came in out of the rain: Iwan from the pharmacy, two sisters who argued over every novel, and Megan, who taught music at the primary school. Carys introduced Rhys by his name and did not say what he did for a living. Nobody asked. Mrs Pritchard waited until they had all found seats before saying, “Gareth says you helped carry stock yesterday.” “I did a box,” Rhys said. “Two,” said Carys. “He’s been telling everyone I’m a model of industry.” “He said you looked cold.” Rhys glanced at the radiator. “Both can be true.” They were reading *Small Hours*. Carys had chosen it the month before Rhys had come into the shop, a coincidence Mrs Pritchard had already noticed aloud. When they reached the poem about a bus turning inland from the coast, Rhys raised his hand. “You don’t have to do that,” Carys said. “I thought I might, after what happened last time I talked about it.” “You thought it was a ferry.” “I maintain there’s a boat somewhere in those last four lines.” “There isn’t,” said Megan. “He knows,” Carys told her. “Go on, Rhys.” “I think he’s pleased the bus doesn’t go home. That’s the part I like.” Mrs Pritchard set down her cup. “Pleased? He spends the whole poem looking out the back window.” “Yes, but that’s where you can see something getting smaller.” “Or where you watch it go because you wish you’d stayed.” “He could’ve got off.” “Not after that stop, he couldn’t. Read it again.” Rhys opened his book and read the final verse. He did it beautifully, which irritated Carys until he reached the last line and stumbled over an ordinary word. “Sorry,” he said. “I rushed that.” “You did,” said Mrs Pritchard. He read it again, more slowly. Afterward he sat listening while the two sisters disagreed about the bus driver. He started to speak once, then let one of them finish. Carys was more aware of that small pause than they had been of his first reading. By the time the others left, Mrs Pritchard had made Rhys promise to tell his mother Gareth had sent the maps round. She gave Carys a different look on the way out, which Carys chose not to understand. “You survived,” they said, collecting cups. “I’ve had worse reviews.” “Mrs Pritchard doesn’t review people.” “She asked me to read it twice.” “Because she thought you’d missed it.” “That was worse.” Rhys took two chairs and folded them. “I had.” Carys brought the cups to the sink in the back room. Rhys followed as far as the curtain, then stopped. “May I put these in here?” “Against the wall.” He carried them through, careful of the rail. A stack of invoices lay on the desk beneath it. Carys moved them to make room, but Rhys had already seen the figures pencilled in the margin. “I hadn’t realised you did all this alone,” he said. “Elin’s here on Saturdays.” “That’s not what I meant.” “Mair and I used to split it.” “You could close an extra day.” “I might.” Carys folded another chair. “I’m trying shorter hours first.” Rhys’s mouth opened, then shut. Carys appreciated the restraint, even if they could guess the sort of offer it had prevented. Outside, the rain had stopped. Rhys held up his coat. “Are you going toward the harbour?” “My flat’s that way.” “I’m at the hotel.” “That isn’t.” “I know. I’ve lived here.” “You’ve mentioned.” “Frequently, by the sound of it.” They set out. The pavements were slick, and the sea was visible only in gaps between buildings. For a while they talked about Megan’s interpretation of the poem. Then Rhys said, “Gareth and I spent a summer making a raft below the harbour steps. I went down there today. The steps have been replaced.” “They were rotten.” “They probably were when we used them.” Carys watched him tuck the novel more securely under his arm. “Does it look wrong?” “It looks perfectly good. That’s the trouble. I couldn’t find the bit I remembered.” They reached the turning for the hotel. Carys pointed up the hill. “That’s your quickest route.” “Thank you.” Neither moved. “Did you finish the novel?” Carys asked. “Nearly. I’ve got a question about the last chapter, but I’d spoil it for myself.” “Then don’t ask me.” “I wasn’t going to.” He fell into step beside them again, going the long way round.

The poetry discussion is the chapter's centrepiece and works well — Rhys's reading of the poem, stumbling on an ordinary word, then being asked to read it again by Mrs Pritchard, is a quietly devastating small moment. The argument about the bus poem feels genuinely literary without being pretentious, and both positions are defensible, which is a mark of real craft. **Character Consistency** Rhys is rendered faithfully to his profile: he performs, then falters, then recovers imperfectly. The stumble in the reading is exactly right — his beauty of delivery followed by a mundane error humanises him without melodrama. His restraint when he sees the financial figures ("Rhys's mouth opened, then shut. Carys appreciated the restraint, even if they could guess the sort of offer it had prevented.") is perfectly calibrated to his character — the impulse to rescue, checked. Carys's interiority is handled with appropriate economy: "Carys was more aware of that small pause than they had been of his first reading" is a lovely, understated revelation of attraction. **Following the Chapter Plan** The plan called for: Rhys appearing at the reading group, not being its star, disagreeing with a regular, listening when pushed back, helping stack chairs, Carys learning he no longer knows which memories are his, Rhys learning about the shorter hours, and the near-plain-speaking walk toward the harbour. All of these are delivered. The ending — Rhys taking the longer route — is exactly as planned and lands with quiet satisfaction. **Emotional Engagement** The chapter earns its emotional beats. The harbour steps memory ("I couldn't find the bit I remembered") is genuinely moving and connects to the chapter's thematic concern with memory, performance, and authenticity. The final exchange — "Neither moved" followed by Rhys falling into step beside them — is well-earned and avoids sentimentality. **Mrs Pritchard** The introduction of Mrs Pritchard as a minor character is handled well. She is distinct, has her own voice, and her interaction with Rhys (making him read the poem twice, the look she gives Carys on the way out) adds texture without overwhelming the central dynamic. **Weaknesses** The chapter is almost too controlled. There are moments where the restraint tips into a slight flatness — the walk to the harbour, while thematically resonant, moves through its beats a little quickly. The line "Carys chose not to understand" regarding Mrs Pritchard's look is slightly telling rather than showing, though it's brief. The chapter's emotional register is consistently low-key, which is appropriate but occasionally risks monotony. The "sea was visible only in gaps between buildings" is a nice image but the chapter doesn't lean heavily on setting, which is both a strength (avoiding purple prose) and occasionally a missed opportunity for grounding. The plan mentioned Carys learning "he once knew the town well but no longer knows which memories belong to him and which have become anecdotes other people tell" — this is delivered through the harbour steps moment, but it's somewhat compressed. The plan also mentioned "they almost speak plainly about why he keeps returning" — this is present but very oblique, perhaps appropriately so. **Overall** This is accomplished, disciplined literary fiction with genuine wit and emotional intelligence. It avoids the common pitfalls of romance writing (sentimentality, over-explanation, purple prose) while delivering real feeling through restraint. The dialogue is among the best elements — natural, characterful, and doing real narrative work. # Chapter 4 — An Errand, Not a Date On Saturday morning, Carys was arguing with a length of parcel tape when Rhys came in. “If you’ve come for the end of the novel,” they said, “she doesn’t go back to him.” “I’d worked that out.” He looked at the parcel. “Who’s winning?” “The tape. What do you want?” “To ask if you still need to collect those books from Penllech.” Carys found the loose end and pulled. Half the tape came away in a long twist. “I didn’t tell you where they were.” “Elin did. I came in for coffee yesterday and she was here.” “Elin tells people far too much.” “She also said the bus doesn’t run back until four.” “I know.” “I have a car.” “I had gathered you weren’t offering to carry a box twenty miles.” Rhys took the parcel tape from Carys’s hand and folded the end over so they could find it again. “I’m offering a lift.” Carys considered him. The books belonged to a retired teacher who was moving into a smaller house; she wanted them collected before her nephew arrived on Sunday. Carys had planned to borrow Elin’s father’s van, but he had not called back. “I’ll pay for petrol,” they said. “You don’t have to.” “Then you don’t have to take me.” “Petrol it is.” “And it isn’t a date.” “I hadn’t said it was.” “You were about to.” “I was about to ask what time to meet you.” “Noon.” Rhys’s car was parked two streets away, where the road widened. It was small, expensive, and filled with parking receipts. He swept them off the passenger seat. “I’ll have you know it was immaculate before I drove it here.” “Were these issued on the way?” He glanced at the receipts in his hand. “I bought coffee.” “Every day since Christmas?” “Are you always like this with people doing you favours?” “Only the ones who ask Elin about my travel arrangements.” Rhys started the engine. “That’s fair.” The road to Penllech ran above the sea, though mist hid it for much of the journey. Rhys kept both hands on the wheel and did not ask Carys to fill the silence. At a roundabout, he missed their turning. “You needed the second exit,” Carys said. “I know.” “You took the third.” “I thought I recognised a shorter way.” “This is the road to the quarry.” “I remember it being useful.” “When?” Rhys made the turn into a lay-by. “Possibly when I was seventeen and wanted to avoid my mother.” “That would account for it.” They found the teacher’s house half an hour late. Mrs Evans had packed the books into five crates and made tea despite Carys’s assurances that they could not stay. She recognised Rhys after ten minutes and asked if he was in a television programme she liked. He said he was not, but that the actor in it had excellent hair. She agreed and offered them both another biscuit. Back in the car, Carys held a list against one of the crates on their lap. “Shouldn’t you check them before we go?” Rhys asked. “Mrs Evans has put them in order. If there’s a mistake, I’ll ring her.” “You trust her?” “Yes.” “She thought I was someone else.” “She was right about the books.” Rhys laughed. “You missed a chance to tell her.” “She was happy to see you. Or him. I didn’t want to interfere.” “She’d have been equally happy if you had.” “Would you?” He glanced across at them, then back at the road. “I said I hadn’t done the programme.” “True.” “I liked that she didn’t mind.” Carys folded the list. “You liked her thinking she knew you.” “I do sometimes.” Rhys slowed for a cyclist. “I know what I said about Gareth. Both things can be true. I like being recognised until somebody wants me to remember them back.” “That sounds difficult.” “It’s also a very good living.” He gave a brief smile. “I make it sound awful when I want you to be nice to me.” “I’ve been nice to you.” “You have. You’re just careful I don’t notice.” Carys watched a field slide past the window. “I watched *The Magpie Affair* on Wednesday.” Rhys took his eyes off the road long enough to check their expression. “Ah.” “You’re good in it.” “‘Good’?” “Would you prefer ‘enormous literary seriousness’?” “I would not.” His fingers shifted on the wheel. “What did you think?” “It’s very silly. I liked the scene in the kitchen.” “I spent the entire shoot convinced that scene was terrible.” “It isn’t.” “Thank you.” He said it without any of the flourish Carys had expected. When they returned to Aberglas, Rhys helped unload the crates. Elin was behind the till, finishing a handwritten recommendation for a customer. She raised her eyebrows at Carys, who ignored her. Once the last crate was inside, Rhys picked up his coat from the passenger seat. “Have dinner with me.” “Elin’s right there.” “She’s pretending to arrange bookmarks.” “I’m doing it very well,” Elin called. Rhys kept his attention on Carys. “Tomorrow? Somewhere you like.” “Yes,” Carys said. He blinked. “Right.” “You don’t have to look so surprised.” “I was prepared to argue.” “I know. That’s why I didn’t let you.” Elin dropped a bookmark. Rhys and Carys both turned, and she bent to retrieve it with unnecessary concentration. Outside, the pavement was narrow. Rhys stood close enough that Carys could see a faint dent in his cheek where Mrs Evans’s reading glasses had caught it when she hugged him goodbye. Carys reached up to show him, then stopped with their hand between them. “What?” he asked. “Your face.” “I’ve heard that before.” “Mrs Evans’s glasses.” “Where?” They touched the mark. Rhys went still. Carys’s hand stayed there; his own rose, not quite reaching theirs. A flash lit the shop window. Rhys turned toward it and smiled before he looked back. Carys lowered their hand. Across the street, a photographer checked his camera. “Elin needs help with the crates,” Carys said, and went inside.

# Chapter 5 — A Busy Day By nine on Monday morning, Carys had sold two copies of *Small Hours* to people who had not looked inside it. The photograph had appeared on a celebrity account the night before. Rhys stood in the shop doorway with Carys’s hand against his cheek, both of them caught just before the flash. The caption read: **RHYS VALE FINDS ROMANCE BACK HOME?** Carys had looked at it long enough to notice the reflection of Elin behind them, carrying a crate. Then they had put their phone away. At ten, a woman asked whether Rhys came in often. At eleven, a man photographed the shop window until Carys went outside and asked him to stop. He bought a postcard and left without apologising. Elin tore a fresh strip of paper for the card machine. “We’ve taken more this morning than we did last Monday.” “We’ve also sold out of stamps.” “Two women bought them because they thought he might send you a letter.” “They asked you that?” “They asked me whether he knew your address. I said you’re in the phone book.” “Elin.” “You aren’t in the phone book.” “That isn’t the point.” “I know.” Elin fitted the roll into the machine. “I wanted them to hear how stupid the question was.” Carys could not fault the impulse. They had briefly enjoyed telling the woman who bought *Small Hours* that Rhys had disliked its first poem. The woman had laughed and bought it anyway. Now Carys wished they had kept that much to themselves. Mrs Pritchard came in just after noon. She took one look at the people gathered near the poetry table and remained on the mat. “I can come back,” she said. “They’re leaving soon,” Carys said. The visitors did not appear to be leaving. One was asking Elin which book Rhys had bought on Thursday. “Have you got the maps Gareth brought?” Mrs Pritchard asked. “In the back. I’ll get them.” “No hurry. I’ve got the butcher to visit.” She looked past Carys at the crowded aisle. “Tell Elin I’ll see her Saturday.” Carys watched her go. By the time they reached the maps, they had forgotten whether Gareth’s parcel was under the counter or beside the desk. Rhys came in at half past one. The bell rang, and three people turned toward him at once. “Hello,” he said to Carys. Someone asked for a photograph. He gave it to them, standing so they would not block the till. Carys served another customer while the phone rang unanswered. When Rhys was free, he came behind the poetry table. “I saw the picture,” he said. “I’m sorry.” “So did I.” “I tried ringing.” “I was working.” “I could see that.” He glanced at the queue of two, at the gap where the copies of *Small Hours* had stood. “Has it been like this all morning?” “Yes.” “I can ask people not to take photographs in here.” “I’ve already asked them.” “I’ll say it too.” “Elin’s taking card payments. Could you let that customer through?” He stepped aside at once. The customer slipped past with an armful of books and gave Carys an apologetic look. Rhys lowered his voice. “Have they been buying anything?” “Some of them.” “Well, at least there’s that.” Carys put down the book they were holding. “Is there?” “I didn’t mean it makes the rest all right.” “Mrs Pritchard wouldn’t come in.” “I can speak to her.” “What would you say?” “That I’m sorry she felt—” He stopped. “I don’t know. I was trying to help.” “You keep saying that.” “I said it once.” “You offered to ask people not to take photographs. I told you I had. Now you want to explain Mrs Pritchard to herself.” “I didn’t say that.” Elin looked up from the till. Carys wished she had not heard, then wished more strongly that they had chosen somewhere else to have this conversation. Rhys glanced at the customers. “Could we talk in the back?” “I can’t leave Elin alone with this.” “She seems perfectly capable.” “She is. She shouldn’t have to.” “I didn’t ask any of them to come.” Carys stared at him. “I know you didn’t take the photograph.” “Then I don’t know what you want me to say.” “Nothing about the till, for a start.” Rhys looked toward it, then back at Carys. “I was glad to see the day hadn’t been entirely awful.” “It’s my shop. I get to decide what sort of day it’s been.” “I’m not taking that away from you.” His voice had grown as quiet as theirs. “I came because I was worried. You’ve hardly looked at me since I walked in.” “You smiled for the camera.” “I know. I saw it coming and did what I always do.” “That’s what worries me.” He stepped back. For a moment Carys could see the rest of the sentence forming; he pressed his lips together instead. Elin came over with a receipt that needed a signature, and Carys signed it without reading it. When she returned to the till, Rhys said, “Are you embarrassed to be seen with me?” “No.” “I saw you go inside.” “Because I didn’t want him taking another picture.” “You could have told me that.” “The photographer was still there.” “So you left me to guess.” Carys thought of Mrs Pritchard on the mat and the messages waiting on their phone. Rhys had been caught outside too; Carys knew that. They could not find a way to say it that would not begin another argument. “I need to work,” they said. Rhys looked at the people browsing near them. “I’m not keeping you.” “You are. Please go.” He took a breath. “All right.” At the door, he nearly turned toward the window with that ready smile. Carys saw him catch himself. He pulled his coat collar up and went out without looking for a camera. Elin finished with a customer and came to Carys’s side. “Mrs Pritchard’s maps are under the desk,” she said. “I know.” “I thought you were looking for them.” “I was.” Elin returned to the till. Carys brought out the parcel and set it behind the counter, where Mrs Pritchard would find it when she came back.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] Chapter 5 is a tightly controlled piece of conflict writing that largely succeeds on its own terms. The chapter follows its plan closely: the photograph circulates, visitors flood the shop, a regular (Mrs Pritchard) is driven away, Rhys arrives hoping to help, misreads the situation, and they argue before Carys asks him to leave. The plan's key beats—Carys being unsettled yet embarrassed to feel pleased by sales, Rhys saying the attention "might at least be useful," Carys hearing dismissal, and Rhys leaving angry enough to want photographers to see him go—are all present, though the last beat is softened: Rhys catches himself before performing for the camera, which is actually a more interesting choice than the plan's angrier version. The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. Both voices are distinct and consistent with their profiles. Rhys's line "Well, at least there's that" is exactly the kind of thing his character would say—well-intentioned, tone-deaf, and immediately regretted. Carys's responses are economical and cutting without being theatrical. The exchange about Mrs Pritchard ("What would you say?" / "That I'm sorry she felt—" / He stopped.) is particularly good: it shows Rhys's impulse to fix things through charm colliding with the reality that charm has no purchase here. The line "It's my shop. I get to decide what sort of day it's been" is one of the chapter's best—it captures Carys's core character in a single sentence. The chapter also handles interiority with restraint. We get Carys's perspective through small actions: putting down the book, forgetting where the maps are, signing a receipt without reading it. These are well-chosen details that show distraction and distress without announcing them. The Elin subplot is handled deftly—she functions as a witness and a practical anchor without becoming a device. Where the chapter is slightly less successful: the argument's emotional logic is occasionally compressed to the point of opacity. The line "You smiled for the camera" / "That's what worries me" is the chapter's emotional crux, but it arrives and passes quickly. The reader understands intellectually what Carys means—that Rhys's automatic performance reflex is the problem—but the moment doesn't quite land with the weight it deserves given how much the chapter has been building toward it. A beat more of interiority here would have earned the darkness. The ending is quietly effective. Rhys catching himself before turning to the window is a small but significant moment of genuine self-awareness, and Carys noting it without comment is the right choice. The final image of Mrs Pritchard's maps being set out for her return is a good closing gesture—it grounds the chapter in the shop's ordinary life and suggests Carys's loyalty to their regulars without sentimentality. There is no purple prose, no forced metaphor, and no amateurish reaching for effect. The prose is spare throughout, occasionally to the point of being slightly flat, but this is a deliberate stylistic choice that suits the material. The chapter is not particularly surprising in its structure—argument, failed reconciliation, departure—but it executes that structure with enough specificity and character consistency to avoid feeling formulaic. One minor weakness: the chapter's opening section (the morning rush, Elin's lines about the phone book) is slightly more charming than the rest of the chapter's register, and the tonal shift into the argument feels slightly abrupt. The Elin-phone-book exchange is the chapter's only moment of genuine lightness, and it's well-earned, but the transition from that to the argument could be smoother. Overall, this is confident, controlled writing that serves its characters and its plan well. It is not a masterpiece, but it is a very competent chapter that avoids most of the pitfalls of the genre. # Chapter 6 — The Wrong Kind of Help Rhys woke to three messages from Nia and one from his mother. His mother’s said, *Gareth says you were in the bookshop again. Ring me before somebody else tells me why.* He called Nia first. “You’re up,” she said. “That saves me coming to find you.” “Can you get the photograph taken down?” “The original? I’ve asked. Reposts, no.” “Can you ask harder?” “I can ask more people.” “Please.” Nia was quiet for a moment. “Rhys, did you tell Carys I could put out a statement?” “No.” “Good. Don’t.” “I know that much.” “I’m checking. Yesterday you wanted me to say the shop was grateful for the attention.” “I said I thought it might be.” “And then?” “And then Carys told me I was wrong.” “Were you?” “I haven’t seen the accounts.” “You know what I’m asking.” He pulled the curtains back an inch. A woman across the street was walking a dog; neither looked up at his window. “The shop’s been busy,” he said. “Some of them bought books. I noticed because I wanted it to be one less thing I’d done to Carys.” “Did you tell them that?” “No. I said at least people were buying something.” Nia made a sound he had heard often during press tours. “Don’t go round there today.” “I need to apologise.” “You can apologise without making them stop work to listen.” After they hung up, Rhys called his mother. She was halfway through asking about the photograph when the kettle boiled on her end, and she set the phone down. He listened to a cupboard opening and spoons rattling. “Is Carys all right?” she asked when she returned. “I don’t think so. I said something stupid.” “How unusual.” “I’m asking for sympathy.” “I’ve got some. Tell me what you said.” He told her. She let him finish, including the part where Carys had gone inside after the flash. “I thought they were ashamed,” he said. “Of you?” “Yes.” “And now?” “I think they saw the camera and wanted to get away from it.” “That sounds likely.” “I was standing right there.” His mother stirred her tea. “You were both standing there.” At the shop, Carys discovered a damp patch spreading across the back-room ceiling. It lay just to the left of the bucket they had placed under the old leak. They moved the bucket, called the roofer, and carried two crates out of reach. By lunchtime the rain had stopped, the roofer had promised Thursday, and a customer had returned a novel because it contained pencil marks. “They were there when I bought it,” he said. “I’m sorry. I should have checked.” “I don’t want another copy. I’m moving tomorrow.” Carys gave him his money back. Elin would have said that people put pencil marks in books because they cared about them, but Elin was at college on Tuesdays. Carys rubbed out three lines before deciding the marks were easier to live with than the damaged paper. Their phone buzzed. There was a message from Rhys, written the previous night. *Are you all right? I’m sorry about what I said. I can ring when you close.* Carys had not answered it. They set the phone beneath a stack of invoices and went to unlock the door after lunch. Rhys had written five versions of a new message by then. One offered to pay for the bracket he had broken. Another offered to pay for the roof after he remembered the invoices on Carys’s desk. He deleted both. An apology on his phone was becoming a place to put every offer Carys had already refused. He walked to the shop near closing time. There was no one outside with a camera. Inside, Carys stood on a stool reaching over the travel shelf, a pencil tucked behind one ear. He waited until they had climbed down before he opened the door. “You’re closed,” Carys said. “The door wasn’t locked.” “I was about to do it.” “I can go.” Carys looked at him, then at the wet pavement behind him. “What did you come to say?” Rhys kept one hand on the door. “I saw the photograph coming. I smiled. I wish I hadn’t.” “Did Nia ask for it to be taken down?” “Yes. She says it’ll keep turning up.” Carys nodded. “I thought so.” “I didn’t ask her to say anything about you.” “Thank you.” He glanced at the bucket visible behind the curtain. “Has it been another bad day?” “The roof’s leaking. That part isn’t your fault.” “I know.” “Then why are you looking at it like that?” “Because I’m here, and I’d rather carry a bucket than have this conversation.” Carys’s mouth moved, nearly a smile. “The bucket’s fine.” “I was hurt when you went inside,” he said. “Yesterday I wanted you to know that, so I made it the most important thing in the shop. It wasn’t.” Carys took the pencil from behind their ear. “I should have told you why I’d gone.” “Perhaps. You don’t owe an explanation to someone with a camera pointed at you.” “It was pointed at both of us.” “Yes.” He looked down at his hand on the door, then let it fall. “I’m sorry I said the sales might make up for it.” “They did help with the roofer.” “I noticed the roof.” “I know. That’s why I’m telling you before you offer.” Rhys gave a short, embarrassed laugh. “I nearly did.” For a moment they stood without speaking. Someone passed outside carrying a folded umbrella. “I meant it about dinner,” Rhys said. “Before all this.” “I know.” “I’m not asking you tonight.” “Good. I’m not ready.” He nodded and moved back onto the pavement. “I’ll let you lock up.” Carys turned the key after he left. Through the glass, they watched him walk to the corner without looking back. Then they went to move the bucket another inch.

The chapter follows its plan closely: Rhys consults Nia, calls his mother, considers and rejects the wrong kinds of help (the money offer, the statement), and eventually arrives at the shop for an awkward but genuine apology that Carys accepts without fully reopening the door. The dinner is deferred. The chapter ends on a small, telling action—Carys moving the bucket another inch—that earns its symbolic weight without overreaching. The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. Each character speaks in a distinct register. Nia's clipped professionalism ("I'm checking. The mother's dry warmth ("How unusual") is perfectly calibrated. The central exchange between Rhys and Carys at the shop door is particularly well-handled: short sentences, careful admissions, neither character performing. "I'd rather carry a bucket than have this conversation" is a good line—it's funny, self-aware, and character-consistent. "They did help with the roofer" / "I noticed the roof" / "I know. Rhys's impulse to offer money, his recognition that it would land badly, his embarrassment at having nearly done it anyway—all consistent with a man whose ego-management instincts sometimes override his better judgment. Carys's precision ("That part isn't your fault") and their tendency to deflect with practicality are well-maintained. The detail of Carys rubbing out pencil marks in a returned book, then deciding the marks are easier to live with than the damaged paper, is a small, excellent piece of characterization that doesn't announce itself. The chapter's weaknesses are minor but worth noting. The pacing is very even—almost too controlled. There's little variation in emotional temperature; the chapter moves from one quiet moment to another without much friction. The plan called for Rhys's apology to be "awkward and does not ask for reassurance," which is achieved, but the scene could have pushed further into discomfort before the partial resolution. The moment where Rhys "gave a short, embarrassed laugh" is the closest thing to a tell-don't-show lapse, though it's mild. The woman walking a dog outside his window is a slightly generic establishing detail. The chapter avoids purple prose entirely. There are no forced metaphors or strained poetic leaps. The prose is spare and functional, occasionally rising to something more resonant (the final image of Carys moving the bucket) without overreaching. The lightness—the near-smile, the embarrassed laugh, the amiable exchange about the roof—is genuinely earned by the preceding tension. One small concern: the chapter is perhaps too tidy in its emotional resolution. Both characters behave with considerable maturity and self-awareness for people who were in genuine conflict the previous day. The plan notes that "neither will deliver a perfect diagnosis of the other," but in this chapter they come quite close. At five, Mrs Pritchard collected her maps. At twenty past five, Carys sent Rhys a message. *If you’re free, come by after closing. I’ve got the first volume back in stock.* He replied: *I’ll come by.* Carys considered adding that he was not obliged to buy anything. Instead, they put the phone away and helped a customer choose a book for her brother. Rhys arrived as Carys was turning the sign. He had brought an umbrella and had used it; for once his hair was dry. “Which first volume?” he asked. “There isn’t one.” “Oh.” He folded the umbrella. “I spent the walk trying to remember what I’d ordered.” “You haven’t ordered anything.” “I was beginning to suspect that.” Carys set the umbrella in the stand. “I wanted to talk without making you stand in the doorway.” “That’s fair.” They sat at the reading-group table. Carys had cleared away the cups but missed a biscuit crumb; Rhys brushed it onto a saucer and waited. “I didn’t answer your message on Monday,” Carys said. “I read it. I was cross, and I didn’t want to tell you I was all right.” “I’d guessed you were cross.” “I know. I’m telling you what I did with it.” He nodded. “The shop was busy again today,” Carys said. “Not like Monday. Two people asked about you. One bought the book.” “Which book?” “The one you bought when you first came in. I told her where it was. That’s all.” “Did you want to tell her more?” “I wanted to tell her to buy the bus poem for herself and leave us out of it. I didn’t.” Rhys looked down at the saucer. “I can ask Nia to make sure I’m not photographed here again.” “Can she?” “She can tell the ones she deals with to leave the shop alone. She can’t keep everyone away.” “Then tell her that. I’d appreciate it.” “I will.” Carys had expected to feel relieved. Instead they noticed how readily he had agreed, and wondered if he was waiting for them to say they were pleased. “There’s something else,” they said. “I went inside because of the photographer. I also knew that if you came in after me, everyone would see you following.” “I thought you wanted me to come in.” “I hadn’t decided. I didn’t give you much chance to ask.” “I could have asked afterward,” Rhys said. “I could have followed you in for that, instead of smiling at him.” “Would you have?” “I don’t know. I’d already seen the camera. I’m quicker at giving them a picture than I am at thinking.” Carys found that easier to believe than a promise about what he would do next time. Rhys picked up the crumb he had missed and placed it on the saucer. “On Monday, when you didn’t look at me, I kept thinking you’d changed your mind about dinner.” “I had.” “Yes.” He looked up. “You were entitled to. I still wanted you to tell me it wasn’t because you were embarrassed.” “I was embarrassed.” He sat back. “Not by you,” Carys said. “By how much I’d wanted to kiss you with Elin watching from the till.” Rhys’s smile appeared, then disappeared as he tried not to look too pleased. “She was watching?” “She dropped a bookmark to make us turn away.” “That was considerate of her.” “She’ll be unbearable if she knows it worked.” He laughed. Carys liked the sound, though they had meant to keep talking. “I liked it when you came back with that terrible excuse about the book,” they said. “It was a good excuse.” “You’d read half of it.” “I’d read all of it by then.” “You told me you’d read some.” “I was trying to sound as though I could still leave.” Carys rested their hands on the table. “You don’t have to stay here because I’ve asked you to come.” “I know.” Rhys watched their fingers. “I want to.” Outside, someone tried the shop door. Both turned. A woman looked through the glass, saw the CLOSED sign, and mouthed an apology before walking on. Carys waited until she had passed the window. “I need to be able to ask you to go,” they said. “Even if I wanted you here yesterday.” “You can.” “You weren’t pleased on Monday.” “No.” He let the answer stand. “I went.” Carys remembered him leaving, and how much they had wanted him to turn around once the door was shut. “You did.” “I’d like to take you to dinner,” he said. “If you still want to go. You can pick somewhere quiet, or somewhere everyone knows me. I can manage either.” “I know a place.” “When?” “Tomorrow. If the roof holds.” “That’s a condition I can’t influence.” “Exactly.” Rhys reached across the table, palm up. Carys put their hand in his. He had a tiny cut beside his thumbnail, almost healed. “You’re staring,” he said. “At your hand.” “That’s new.” “You’ve got dust in the cut.” “I carried two boxes here. Against medical advice.” Carys shook their head. When he leaned closer, they both stopped. Rhys glanced at the window; Carys pulled down the blind. “Subtle,” he said. “The woman’s gone. I wanted the room to myself.” He stood. Carys was close enough to see his smile return, uncertain this time. They kissed him before he could find something clever to say. His hand settled against their back; somewhere behind them, the old curtain rail gave a small metallic rattle. Neither moved to check it.

Rhys lowered the bookmark. “I am.” “Would you mind a picture? My daughter won’t believe I saw you in here.” He looked toward Carys. The woman looked too. Carys felt the familiar jolt: the room waiting for them to say something about Rhys. “Ask him,” Carys said. “He’s the one in the picture.” “I don’t mind,” Rhys said, “if we take it by the door. On her way out, she paused beside Rhys. “Your mother says you’re going to the concert tomorrow.” “I am.” “Don’t hide under the stage.” “I’ll try not to.” When the door shut, Elin fetched three mugs. “Mrs Vale can have hers at home. You can have a photograph taken.” “I could say no when I’m in here.” “Some days I’d be grateful. Today I’m only telling you how it felt.” “All right.” Elin came back with the tea. “What’s all right?” “The postcards,” Carys said. “You can finish them after your break.” Elin surveyed them both, then took her mug to the back room without further questions. Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Task: write a short story over several chapters. Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The first chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. The remainder of the story is open to your choices & direction.

# Brainstorming **Possible centres of the story** - **A land-rights dispute:** Arthur Neegan’s modest homestead sits above an immense Azra vein. His claim may give him the right to refuse extraction—but only if a century-old first-settler charter still applies. The plot could turn on whether law has any force when fleets need fuel. - **A scientific mystery:** Azra accelerates radioactive decay, yet the rate varies from sample to sample. Arthur’s mining records might reveal what laboratories have missed: the vein’s surrounding rock governs how violently it acts. - **A labour struggle:** Corporations lease indentured miners as readily as drilling machines. Arthur could use his leverage to demand the cancellation of those leases, while discovering that a sudden halt to mining would also strand workers in company habitats. - **An interplanetary bluff:** Antares could want the vein as much for its effect on rivals’ calculations as for its metal. Arthur might try to make every claimant believe a different story about what lies beneath his land. **People who might pull Arthur in different directions** - An Antares envoy who speaks with immaculate courtesy while an armed diplomatic retinue waits outside the door. - A Mars lease-company director who argues that the colony cannot survive without its mines and supply contracts. - An indentured surveyor or technician who knows the workings beneath Arthur’s property better than he does, and challenges his habit of saying *my land* when others will bear the cost of mining it. - An independent physicist who can test Arthur’s discovery but cannot keep it secret. - A local magistrate with a narrow legal power that becomes important if Arthur can make the rival interests acknowledge it. **Possible turns and images** - Chapter One could alternate polite negotiation aboard an off-world-bound transfer vessel with Arthur’s memory of the armed arrival at his home. Through the port: the ochre curve of Mars, its mines visible as tiny artificial lights. - A tabletop atomic clock runs unexpectedly fast beside an unshielded Azra sample—an intimate demonstration of a force coveted for engines and weapons. - Old paper claim maps survive because they cannot be altered remotely; calculating machines, punch cards and planetary videophones give the setting a retrofuturistic texture. - The apparent “immense vein” may be a branching formation. Extracting it carelessly could accelerate decay in buried radioactive tailings beneath nearby worker settlements. - Antares’s offer could be reasonable in its stated terms: protection, wealth and a research station. Its troubling clause would give Antares sole authority to decide what counts as a security threat. - Arthur’s eventual gambit might be neither selling nor hiding Azra, but forcing its hazards and the labour contracts into one public negotiation, where no power can take the prize without accepting obligations. **Possible eight-chapter rhythm** The story could move from invitation and offer, through investigation and competing bids, to a discovery that changes the value of the vein. The last chapters would test whether Arthur can turn that knowledge into a durable agreement rather than a momentary victory. A quieter ending—workers reading new contract terms while the great powers continue to watch Mars—would suit the tension between individual lives and interstellar politics. # Reflection The strongest direction combines **the land-rights dispute, the scientific mystery and the leased workers**. Any one of them alone risks making Arthur’s choice too simple. If he merely owns the vein, he can auction it; if he merely knows a dangerous fact, he can reveal it. Together, they give him leverage while making every possible use of that leverage costly. Arthur should remain a mining engineer, not become a physicist or a master strategist overnight. His advantage can come from patient observations: bore depths, waste-rock composition, instrument readings and an old map others considered obsolete. He can make a consequential inference, then depend on other people to verify and act on it. That also gives the indentured technician a necessary role rather than making the workers only the beneficiaries of Arthur’s decision. The Antares envoy will work best if the offer is genuinely tempting and partly defensible. A purely sinister diplomat would flatten the political contest. Antares may understand the danger of an arms race, while still intending to place the metal—and the authority to define “security”—under its own control. The corporate director likewise has a real argument about keeping Mars supplied, even as the lease system makes that argument self-serving. The opening needs particular care. The armed descent on Arthur’s home is the inciting event, but **Chapter One begins aboard the transfer vessel**, with Arthur wondering what he has entered into. A brief recollection can show the retinue’s arrival without displacing that starting point. Most of the chapter can then be a dialogue-heavy meeting with the unknown Antares party, broken by the vessel’s cabin, its instruments, the view of Mars and small details of diplomatic coercion. That setting lets the story show a man’s kitchen table and an interstellar arms race in the same conversation. For roughly 1,000 words per chapter, the plot should have one principal turn in each chapter. The scientific rule should be clear and limited: **Azra accelerates radioactive decay; surrounding material affects how strongly it does so**. The story need not solve all of Azra’s secrets. Its climax should instead hinge on a testable danger and a political choice. A public agreement can end this particular contest without pretending to end corporate power or the arms race.
